Review article

Stroke syndromes: localizing the lesion from the cortex to the spinal cord

Stroke symptoms follow the anatomy of the lesion rather than its cause. Cerebral syndromes reflect the ACA, MCA, PCA, and watershed territories, brainstem syndromes produce crossed signs, and spinal cord lesions separate motor, pain, and proprioceptive pathways. Hemorrhagic strokes add features of raised ICP and meningeal irritation. Here, we review these syndromes and their complications, and consider how to distinguish those that resemble each other.

Key points

  • Brainstem strokes are crossed: cranial nerve signs are ipsilateral, and limb signs are contralateral.
  • ACA favors the leg, whereas MCA favors the face and arm.
  • Dominant MCA lesions cause aphasia; non-dominant lesions cause neglect.
  • Thunderclap headache with meningeal signs suggests SAH.

Cerebral ischemic syndromes

ACA syndrome causes contralateral leg weakness, greater than arm, contralateral leg sensory loss, urinary incontinence, abulia, and a grasp reflex. MCA syndrome causes contralateral face and arm weakness, greater than leg, gaze toward the lesion, contralateral face and arm sensory loss, and contralateral homonymous hemianopia; dominant lesions add aphasia and Gerstmann syndrome, and non-dominant lesions add extinction, hemispatial neglect, and anosognosia. PCA syndrome usually causes no weakness, with contralateral sensory loss if the thalamus is involved, contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, alexia without agraphia (dominant), and prosopagnosia (non-dominant). MCA/ACA watershed syndrome, from low perfusion or ICA stenosis, causes proximal arm and shoulder weakness sparing the hand and face ("man in a barrel" if bilateral), mild proximal arm sensory loss, and transcortical motor aphasia (dominant). MCA/PCA watershed syndrome usually causes no weakness and mild sensory change, with visual field loss, transcortical sensory aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant), and Balint syndrome if bilateral.

Dominant-hemisphere lesions cause characteristic aphasias. Broca aphasia, from the inferior frontal gyrus, is nonfluent with intact comprehension and impaired repetition. Wernicke aphasia, from the posterior superior temporal gyrus, is fluent but paraphasic, with impaired comprehension and repetition. Conduction aphasia, from the arcuate fasciculus, is fluent with relatively intact comprehension but impaired repetition, and global aphasia affects all three. Transcortical motor and sensory aphasias resemble Broca and Wernicke aphasia but preserve repetition.

Lacunar infarcts follow lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of small penetrating arteries, mainly with hypertension and diabetes, and lack cortical signs. Pure motor stroke, the most common at 45%, involves the posterior limb of the internal capsule, corona radiata, or ventral pons; pure sensory stroke involves the thalamus; sensorimotor stroke involves the thalamus and internal capsule; ataxic hemiparesis involves the internal capsule, pons, or corona radiata; and dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome involves the pons or internal capsule. Amaurosis fugax, a painless, curtain-like loss of vision in one eye that resolves, usually follows emboli from the carotid bifurcation and warns of stroke.

Brainstem strokes

In the midbrain, supplied by P1 paramedian branches and the top of the basilar, Weber syndrome (ventromedial) causes ipsilateral CN III palsy with a dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis. Benedikt syndrome (paramedian) causes ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral tremor and ataxia, with or without contralateral hemiparesis, and contralateral vibration and proprioception loss, combining Weber and Claude features. Claude syndrome causes ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral ataxia, with no weakness. In the pons, ventromedial pontine syndrome, from basilar paramedian branches, causes contralateral hemiparesis, dysarthria, and ataxic hemiparesis, and its caudal form (Raymond syndrome) adds ipsilateral CN VI palsy. Ventral pontine (Millard-Gubler) syndrome causes contralateral hemiplegia, ipsilateral CN VI and CN VII palsy (forehead included), and horizontal diplopia. Inferior medial pontine (Foville) syndrome causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and CN VII palsy (forehead included), contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral vibration and proprioception loss, and eyes that deviate toward the weak side; both are supplied by basilar paramedian and short circumferential branches. Lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome causes ipsilateral CN VII palsy (forehead included) and ataxia with preserved strength, crossed pain and temperature loss (ipsilateral face and contralateral body), and ipsilateral hearing loss, vertigo, and Horner syndrome. Marie-Foix syndrome, a lateral pontine syndrome from basilar perforators and the AICA, adds contralateral hemiparesis and contralateral vibration and proprioception loss to ipsilateral limb ataxia, CN VII palsy, hearing loss, vertigo, and nystagmus. Locked-in syndrome, from bilateral ventral pons injury via the basilar artery, causes quadriplegia and anarthria, usually with preserved sensation, consciousness, vertical eye movements, and blinking. In the medulla, lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, from the vertebral artery or PICA, causes ipsilateral palate, pharynx, and vocal cord weakness and ataxia with preserved strength, crossed pain and temperature loss, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome, vertigo, dysphagia, and hiccups. Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome, from the anterior spinal artery, causes contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face, ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation toward the lesion, and contralateral vibration and proprioception loss.

Spinal cord lesions

Central cord syndrome, from hyperextension injury and syringomyelia, causes arm weakness greater than leg, with the hands worst, cape-like pain and temperature loss, and sacral sparing. Anterior cord syndrome, from the anterior spinal artery, causes bilateral weakness and pain and temperature loss below the lesion, preserved vibration and proprioception, and bladder and bowel dysfunction. Posterior cord syndrome, from the posterior spinal artery, tabes dorsalis, and B12 deficiency, causes sensory ataxia with preserved strength, bilateral vibration and proprioception loss, and a positive Romberg sign. Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection), from penetrating trauma and compression, causes ipsilateral weakness and vibration and proprioception loss below the lesion, contralateral pain and temperature loss, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome if at or above T1.

Hemorrhagic strokes

Intracerebral hemorrhage causes headache and cortical focal neurologic deficits. Subarachnoid hemorrhage causes thunderclap headache and meningeal signs: photophobia, neck stiffness, and positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Both cause raised ICP, with nausea and vomiting, posturing, and Cushing triad, along with loss of consciousness in intracerebral hemorrhage and CN deficits in subarachnoid hemorrhage. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is complicated by rebleeding, highest early before the aneurysm is secured; vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia on days 3–14; hydrocephalus; hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; and seizures.

Complications

Stroke complications are cerebral edema (malignant MCA infarct, with herniation in the first several days), hemorrhagic transformation, aspiration pneumonia from dysphagia, seizures, DVT and PE from immobility, spasticity and contractures, post-stroke depression, and central post-stroke pain, often from a thalamic infarct but possible after any sensory pathway lesion.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both can cause focal deficits, and non-contrast CT head separates them.

Lateral pontine vs lateral medullary. Both cause crossed pain and temperature loss, ataxia, vertigo, and Horner syndrome with preserved strength. CN VII palsy and hearing loss favor the pons; dysphagia, hiccups, and palate weakness favor the medulla.

Midbrain syndromes. All three share CN III palsy. Contralateral hemiparesis means Weber, contralateral ataxia means Claude, and tremor with sensory loss means Benedikt.

Medial medullary vs ventral pontine. Both cause contralateral hemiparesis. Ipsilateral tongue weakness points to the medulla, and CN VI and CN VII palsy to the pons.

Anterior vs posterior cord. Anterior cord lesions lose strength and pain and temperature but preserve vibration and proprioception, whereas posterior cord lesions lose vibration and proprioception but preserve strength.

Acute Ischemic Stroke

Pathophysiology

Blocked or inadequate arterial blood flow leads to cerebral ischemia, causing an infarct core surrounded by a salvageable penumbra.

  1. Blocked or inadequate flowEmbolus, thrombus, low flow, or vessel wall disease
  2. Cerebral ischemiaDecreased oxygen delivery
  3. Core and penumbraThe core dies, and the penumbra can recover

What ischemia does

  • AArterial occlusionAn embolus or thrombus stops flow downstream
  • BInfarct coreFlow is too low for cells to survive → irreversible injury
  • CPenumbraFlow stops function but not survival → deficits that reperfusion can reverse
  • DCerebral edemaFailing ion pumps swell cells → malignant MCA infarct, with herniation in the first several days
  • EHemorrhagic transformationReperfusion of injured vessels → blood within the infarct

Etiology

  • Embolus Most common
  • 1Cardiac embolus ImportantLeft atrial thrombus: A-fib or flutter, mechanical valve, or RHD
    Left ventricular thrombus: LV aneurysm from MI, anterior or lateral MI, or HFrEF
  • 2Infective endocarditisCardiac embolus; a contraindication to thrombolysis
  • 3Paradoxical embolusASD, patent foramen ovale, or atrial septal aneurysm; a right-to-left shunt lets a venous thrombus reach arterial circulation
  • Thrombus
  • 4Large vessel thrombusAtherosclerotic thrombus in the ICA, MCA, or vertebrobasilar arteries
  • 5Small vessel thrombusLacunar infarct from lenticulostriate arteries or small pontine branches, occluded by lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, mainly from hypertension and diabetes
  • Low flow
  • 6Global hypoperfusionCardiac arrest, acute respiratory failure, or ICA stenosis with low BP; decreased cerebral oxygen delivery causes watershed infarcts
  • Vessel wall
  • 7VasculitisAutoimmune, infections, or primary CNS vasculitis; arterial wall inflammation
  • 8DissectionTrauma, iatrogenic, or connective tissue diseases; intimal tear with thrombus and embolus

Diagnosis

  1. Glucose and non-contrast CT headRule out hypoglycemia and hemorrhage
  2. CT angiogram of the head and neckLook for large vessel occlusion
  3. CT perfusion or MRIIf 4.5–24 hours or onset unknown; look for penumbra

Find the cause

  • 1Cardiac embolusECG, telemetry, and echocardiogram: A-fib, thrombus
  • 2Infective endocarditisBlood cultures and echocardiogram
  • 3Paradoxical embolusBubble echocardiogram: PFO
  • 4Large vessel thrombusCT angiogram or carotid duplex: ICA stenosis
  • 5Small vessel thrombusMRI: lacunar infarct
  • 7VasculitisESR, CRP, autoimmune serology, and CSF
  • 8DissectionCT or MR angiogram of the neck
  • +Vascular risk factorsLipids and HbA1c

Stroke mimics

ForFavored byObtain
HypoglycemiaLow glucose; deficits resolve with glucoseGlucose
Seizure with Todd paralysisWitnessed seizure, tongue biting, and a post-ictal stateEEG
Migraine with auraSpreading symptoms over minutes, positive symptoms, and past similar attacksMRI if unclear
Functional neurologic disorderInconsistent signs, positive Hoover sign, and normal imagingMRI
Brain tumor or abscessGradual onset; fever with an abscessCT or MRI with contrast
Bell palsyIsolated facial weakness that includes the foreheadClinical examination
Peripheral vertigoIsolated vertigo with a reassuring HINTS examinationHINTS examination; MRI if unclear

Note: NIHSS grades stroke severity.

Treatment

Acute treatment

  • IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset
  • Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion, up to 24 hours with penumbra
  • Aspirin within 24–48 hours; wait 24 hours after thrombolysis
Onset4.5 hours24 hours48 hours
Supportive care
  • Swallow screen before oral intake
  • Treat fever and glucose
  • DVT prophylaxis

Blood pressure: below 185/110 for thrombolysis; otherwise allow up to 220/120.

Thrombolysis contraindications

  • Hemorrhage on CT
  • Head trauma within 3 months
  • Intracranial or spinal surgery within 3 months
  • Active bleeding
  • Platelets under 100000/µL
  • INR over 1.7
  • Infective endocarditis
  • aPTT over 40 seconds
  • Therapeutic LMWH within 24 hours
  • Recent DOAC use with possible ongoing effect
  • Suspected aortic dissection
  • Intracranial neoplasm with high bleeding risk

Prior ischemic stroke is weighed case by case rather than excluding thrombolysis.

Dual antiplatelets

  • Minor stroke (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIAAspirin plus clopidogrel within 24 hours for 21 days, then one antiplatelet
  • Who qualifiesNot treated with thrombolysis, and not cardioembolic

Prevent recurrence

  • 1Cardiac embolusAnticoagulation: DOAC; warfarin for mechanical valve
  • 2Infective endocarditisABX
  • 3Paradoxical embolusAntiplatelet; PFO closure if under 60 with no other cause
  • 4Large vessel thrombusAntiplatelet and high-intensity statin; carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic ICA stenosis of 70–99%
  • 5Small vessel thrombusAntiplatelet, statin, and BP control
  • 6Global hypoperfusionTreat the cause of low perfusion
  • 7VasculitisImmunosuppression; treat any infection
  • 8DissectionAntiplatelet or anticoagulation

Review article

Acute ischemic stroke: embolic, thrombotic, and low-flow injury and the race to reperfuse

Blocked or inadequate arterial blood flow leads to cerebral ischemia, causing an infarct core surrounded by a salvageable penumbra. Embolus is the most common mechanism; the others are thrombus, global hypoperfusion, vasculitis, and dissection. Management is a race to reperfuse within fixed time windows, followed by prevention tailored to the cause. Here, we review its causes, imaging, acute treatment, and recurrence prevention, and consider how it relates to hemorrhagic stroke.

Key points

  • Glucose and non-contrast CT head come first, to rule out hypoglycemia and hemorrhage.
  • IV alteplase or tenecteplase is given within 4.5 hours of onset.
  • Thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion extends up to 24 hours with penumbra.
  • Prevention of recurrence is chosen by cause.

Pathophysiology

Blocked or inadequate flow causes cerebral ischemia with decreased oxygen delivery. An embolus or thrombus stops flow downstream. In the infarct core, flow is too low for cells to survive, so injury is irreversible, whereas in the penumbra, flow stops function but not survival, so reperfusion can reverse deficits. Failing ion pumps swell cells, causing cerebral edema, with malignant MCA infarct and herniation in the first several days, and reperfusion of injured vessels can cause hemorrhagic transformation, with blood within the infarct.

Etiology and mechanisms

Cardiac embolus, an important cause, arises from a left atrial thrombus in A-fib or flutter, mechanical valve, or RHD, or from a left ventricular thrombus in LV aneurysm from MI, anterior or lateral MI, or HFrEF. Infective endocarditis is a separate source of cardiac embolus and a contraindication to thrombolysis. Paradoxical embolus occurs with ASD, patent foramen ovale, and atrial septal aneurysm, where a right-to-left shunt lets a venous thrombus reach arterial circulation. Global hypoperfusion from cardiac arrest, acute respiratory failure, or ICA stenosis with low BP decreases cerebral oxygen delivery, causing watershed infarcts. Large vessel thrombus is atherosclerotic thrombus in the ICA, MCA, and vertebrobasilar arteries. Small vessel thrombus causes lacunar infarcts from the lenticulostriate arteries or small pontine branches, occluded by lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, mainly from hypertension and diabetes. Vasculitis from autoimmune disease, infections, or primary CNS vasculitis causes arterial wall inflammation and can affect any artery. Dissection from trauma, iatrogenic injury, or connective tissue diseases causes an intimal tear with thrombus and embolus.

Diagnosis

Glucose and non-contrast CT head rule out hypoglycemia and hemorrhage. If there is no hemorrhage, CT angiogram of the head and neck looks for large vessel occlusion, and CT perfusion or MRI looks for penumbra if onset is 4.5–24 hours ago or unknown. Cardiac embolus is sought with ECG, telemetry, and echocardiogram, looking for A-fib and thrombus. Paradoxical embolus is sought with bubble echocardiogram, looking for PFO. Large vessel thrombus is assessed by CT angiogram or carotid duplex for ICA stenosis, small vessel thrombus by MRI for lacunar infarct, vasculitis by ESR, CRP, autoimmune serology, and CSF, dissection by CT or MR angiogram of the neck, and infective endocarditis by blood cultures and echocardiogram. Vascular risk factors are assessed with lipids and HbA1c. NIHSS grades stroke severity.

Stroke mimics

Stroke mimics must be recognized without delaying reperfusion. Hypoglycemia causes deficits that resolve with glucose. A seizure with Todd paralysis is favored by a witnessed seizure, tongue biting, and a post-ictal state. Migraine with aura spreads over minutes, with positive symptoms and past similar attacks. Functional neurologic disorder shows inconsistent signs, a positive Hoover sign, and normal imaging. Brain tumor or abscess has a gradual onset, with fever in an abscess, and is seen on CT or MRI with contrast. Bell palsy causes isolated facial weakness that includes the forehead, peripheral vertigo causes isolated vertigo with a reassuring HINTS examination, and systemic illness such as sepsis, hyponatremia, or drugs can unmask an old deficit.

Management

Reperfusion uses IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset, and mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours with penumbra. Aspirin is given within 24–48 hours, waiting 24 hours after thrombolysis. Supportive care comprises a swallow screen before oral intake, treating fever and glucose, and DVT prophylaxis. BP is kept below 185/110 for thrombolysis, and otherwise allowed up to 220/120. Thrombolysis contraindications are hemorrhage on CT, head trauma within 3 months, intracranial or spinal surgery within 3 months, active bleeding, platelets under 100000/µL, INR over 1.7, infective endocarditis, aPTT over 40 seconds, therapeutic LMWH within 24 hours, recent DOAC use with possible ongoing effect, suspected aortic dissection, and an intracranial neoplasm with high bleeding risk. Prior ischemic stroke is weighed case by case rather than excluding thrombolysis. After a minor non-cardioembolic stroke (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIA not treated with thrombolysis, aspirin plus clopidogrel is started within 24 hours and continued for 21 days before changing to one antiplatelet.

Prevention of recurrence

Cardiac embolus is treated with anticoagulation: DOAC, or warfarin for a mechanical valve. Infective endocarditis is treated with ABX. Paradoxical embolus is treated with antiplatelet therapy, with PFO closure if under 60 with no other cause. Large vessel thrombus is treated with antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statin, with carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic ICA stenosis of 70–99%. Small vessel thrombus is treated with antiplatelet therapy, statin, and BP control. Global hypoperfusion is treated by treating the cause of low perfusion. Vasculitis is treated with immunosuppression and treating any infection. Dissection is treated with antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation.

In A-fib, the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score estimates stroke risk to guide anticoagulation, with 1 point each for congestive heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease, age 65–74, and female sex, and 2 points each for age 75 or older and prior stroke or TIA; a score of 2 or more marks high risk.

Relationships to other conditions

. Non-contrast CT separates them, and BP goals are opposite: ischemic stroke tolerates up to 220/120, whereas hemorrhage is actively lowered. Hemorrhagic transformation links the two.

. Thunderclap headache with meningeal signs favors SAH, and hemorrhage on CT contraindicates thrombolysis.

. Deficits localize the vessel, and watershed syndromes follow low perfusion or ICA stenosis.

Infective endocarditis. It causes ischemic stroke by embolism and contraindicates thrombolysis, and it causes hemorrhage through mycotic aneurysms.

Embolic disease elsewhere. A-fib also embolizes to the SMA, causing acute mesenteric ischemia.

Intracerebral Hemorrhage

Pathophysiology

Vessel rupture bleeds into the brain parenchyma, forming a hematoma that compresses tissue and raises ICP.

  1. Weakened vesselHypertension, amyloid, and other causes
  2. Vessel ruptureInto the brain parenchyma
  3. HematomaCompresses tissue and raises ICP

What the hematoma does

  • ATissue compressionThe hematoma presses on brain tissue → cortical focal neurologic deficits
  • BHematoma growthBleeding can continue → worsening deficits, so BP control and reversal limit it
  • CSurrounding edemaInjured tissue swells around the hematoma, adding to its mass
  • DRaised ICPAdded mass → headache, nausea and vomiting, loss of consciousness, posturing, and Cushing triad
  • EHydrocephalusBlood or mass effect blocks CSF flow, so an EVD may be needed

Etiology

  • Deep
  • 1Hypertension Most common causeBasal ganglia Important, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum; cortex is less common
  • Cortex
  • 2Cerebral amyloid angiopathy Lobar bleeds in older adultsCortical bleeds; may present with dementia
  • 3Cerebral venous sinus thrombosisFactor V Leiden, decreased AT-III, decreased protein C or S, APS, OCP, and pregnancy; obstructed venous drainage → venous infarction or hemorrhage near the cortex
  • Any site
  • 4CoagulopathyWarfarin, heparin, DOACs, tPA, aspirin, clopidogrel, and liver disease
  • 5Hemorrhagic transformationIschemic stroke conversion from tPA or reperfusion injury
  • 6MalignancyMelanoma, RCC, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid carcinoma are highly angiogenic and bleed
  • 7Arteriovenous malformationVascular abnormality in young patients
  • 8Mycotic aneurysmInfective endocarditis vegetation deposits

Primary or secondary

  • Primary85% of cases; hypertension or amyloid angiopathy, a diagnosis of exclusion
  • SecondaryAn identifiable cause, such as a vascular malformation, tumor, or bleeding diathesis
  • Hypertensive damageLipohyalinosis and Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms in penetrating arterioles

Diagnosis

  1. Non-contrast CT headHyperdense blood in the parenchyma
  2. BloodsFBC, PT/INR, aPTT, and LFTs
  3. CT angiogramIf young, lobar, or no hypertension

Find the cause

  • 1HypertensionNon-contrast CT head: deep location
  • 2Cerebral amyloid angiopathyMRI with SWI: lobar microbleeds
  • 3Cerebral venous sinus thrombosisCT or MR venography: empty delta sign
  • 4CoagulopathyFBC, PT/INR, aPTT, and LFTs
  • 5Hemorrhagic transformationCT head after stroke or thrombolysis: blood within the infarct
  • 6MalignancyMRI with contrast: enhancing mass
  • 7Arteriovenous malformationCT angiogram; catheter angiography to confirm
  • 8Mycotic aneurysmBlood cultures, echocardiogram, and CT angiogram

Prognosis

  • MortalityUp to 50% at 30 days; most deaths occur in the first 24 hours
  • PredictorsHematoma size and location, GCS on admission, and intraventricular extension or hydrocephalus

Note: The ICH score estimates 30-day mortality.

ICH score

  • GCS 3–42 points
  • GCS 5–121 point
  • Age 80 or older1 point
  • Infratentorial origin1 point
  • Volume 30 mL or more1 point
  • IVH1 point
  • UseA higher score predicts higher 30-day mortality; volume is estimated as A × B × C / 2 on CT

Treatment

Acute treatment

Limit hematoma growth
  • IV nicardipine, clevidipine, or labetalol
  • Reverse any coagulopathy
Lower ICP
  • Head of bed at 30°
  • Hypertonic saline or mannitol
  • EVD for hydrocephalus
Decompression
  • Surgical evacuation for a cerebellar bleed over 3 cm with brainstem compression, decreased consciousness, or hydrocephalus
Supportive care
  • ICU admission
  • Treat fever and hyperglycemia
  • Antiseizure medication only for seizures
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression

Blood pressure: if systolic is 150–220, lower it to a target of 140.

Reverse coagulopathy

  • Warfarin4-factor PCC and IV vitamin K, to an INR below 1.4; PCC acts faster than FFP
  • HeparinProtamine
  • DabigatranIdarucizumab
  • Apixaban or rivaroxabanAndexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC
  • tPACryoprecipitate
  • Aspirin or clopidogrelStop the offending drug
  • Liver diseaseVitamin K and FFP

Treat the cause

  • 1HypertensionLong-term control below 130/80
  • 2Cerebral amyloid angiopathyAvoid antithrombotics where possible
  • 3Cerebral venous sinus thrombosisAnticoagulation, even with hemorrhage
  • 4CoagulopathyReverse as above
  • 5Hemorrhagic transformationStop antithrombotics
  • 6MalignancySurgery, radiation, or systemic therapy
  • 7Arteriovenous malformationSurgical resection, embolization, or radiosurgery
  • 8Mycotic aneurysmIV ABX for infective endocarditis; endovascular or surgical repair if ruptured

Review article

Intracerebral hemorrhage: causes by location, and limiting hematoma growth

Vessel rupture bleeds into the brain parenchyma, forming a hematoma that compresses tissue and raises ICP. Hypertension is the most common cause, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a common cause of lobar bleeds in older adults, with location helping to separate them. Management aims to limit hematoma growth, reverse coagulopathy, and control ICP. Here, we review its causes, workup, and treatment, and consider how it relates to ischemic stroke and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Key points

  • Hypertension bleeds in deep structures, especially the basal ganglia; amyloid angiopathy bleeds in the cortex.
  • If systolic is 150–220, lower it to a target of 140.
  • Reversal is matched to the drug.
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation, even with hemorrhage.

Pathophysiology

A weakened vessel ruptures into the brain parenchyma, forming a hematoma. The hematoma presses on brain tissue, causing cortical focal neurologic deficits, and bleeding can continue, causing worsening deficits, which is why BP control and reversal limit it. Injured tissue swells around the hematoma, adding to its mass. This added mass raises ICP, causing headache, nausea and vomiting, loss of consciousness, posturing, and Cushing triad, and blood or mass effect can block CSF flow, causing hydrocephalus that may need an EVD.

Etiology and mechanisms

Hypertension, the most common cause, bleeds in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, and less commonly the cortex. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy, a common cause of lobar bleeds in older adults, bleeds in cortical structures and may present with dementia. Coagulopathy follows warfarin, heparin, DOACs, tPA, aspirin, clopidogrel, and liver disease. Hemorrhagic transformation follows ischemic stroke, through conversion from tPA or reperfusion injury. Arteriovenous malformation is a vascular abnormality of young patients. Mycotic aneurysm follows infective endocarditis vegetation deposits. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis follows factor V Leiden, decreased AT-III, decreased protein C or S, APS, OCP, and pregnancy, with obstructed venous drainage causing venous infarction or hemorrhage near the cortex. Malignancy, including melanoma, RCC, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid carcinoma, disrupts the BBB. Causes from coagulopathy onward can bleed at any site. Primary ICH, from hypertension or amyloid angiopathy, accounts for 85% of cases and is a diagnosis of exclusion, whereas secondary ICH has an identifiable cause, such as a vascular malformation, tumor, or bleeding diathesis. Chronic hypertension causes lipohyalinosis and Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms in penetrating arterioles.

Clinical presentation

Patients have headache and cortical focal neurologic deficits, with raised ICP causing nausea and vomiting, loss of consciousness, posturing, and Cushing triad.

Diagnosis

Non-contrast CT head shows hyperdense blood in the parenchyma, bloods comprise FBC, PT/INR, aPTT, and LFTs, and CT angiogram is obtained if the patient is young, the bleed is lobar, or there is no hypertension. Hypertension shows a deep location on CT. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is evaluated by MRI with SWI, showing lobar microbleeds. Coagulopathy is evaluated by those bloods. Hemorrhagic transformation is seen on CT head after stroke or thrombolysis as blood within the infarct. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is evaluated by CT or MR venography, with the empty delta sign. Malignancy is evaluated by MRI with contrast, showing an enhancing mass. Arteriovenous malformation is evaluated by CT angiogram, with catheter angiography to confirm. Mycotic aneurysm is evaluated by blood cultures, echocardiogram, and CT angiogram. The ICH score estimates 30-day mortality. Mortality reaches 50% at 30 days, with most deaths in the first 24 hours, and depends on hematoma size and location, GCS on admission, and intraventricular extension or hydrocephalus.

The ICH score predicts 30-day mortality from five items: GCS 3–4 (2 points) or 5–12 (1 point), age 80 or older, infratentorial origin, volume of 30 mL or more, estimated as A × B × C / 2 on CT, and IVH, each 1 point.

Management

Hematoma growth is limited with IV nicardipine, clevidipine, or labetalol, and reversal of any coagulopathy; if systolic is 150–220, it is lowered to a target of 140. ICP is lowered with head of bed at 30°, hypertonic saline or mannitol, and EVD for hydrocephalus. Surgical evacuation is used for a cerebellar bleed over 3 cm with brainstem compression, decreased consciousness, or hydrocephalus. Supportive care comprises ICU admission, treating fever and hyperglycemia, antiseizure medication only for seizures, and intermittent pneumatic compression. Warfarin is reversed with 4-factor PCC and IV vitamin K to an INR below 1.4, with PCC acting faster than FFP, heparin with protamine, dabigatran with idarucizumab, apixaban or rivaroxaban with andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC, and tPA with cryoprecipitate. For aspirin or clopidogrel, the offending drug is stopped. Liver disease is treated with vitamin K and FFP. By cause, hypertension needs long-term control below 130/80; amyloid angiopathy needs antithrombotics avoided where possible; hemorrhagic transformation needs antithrombotics stopped; venous sinus thrombosis needs anticoagulation, even with hemorrhage; malignancy needs surgery, radiation, or systemic therapy; arteriovenous malformation needs surgical resection, embolization, or radiosurgery; and mycotic aneurysm needs IV ABX for infective endocarditis, with endovascular or surgical repair if ruptured.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause focal deficits and CT separates them. Thrombolysis and antithrombotics that treat ischemia can cause hemorrhage, and BP goals differ.

. Blood lies in the parenchyma here and in the subarachnoid space there. AVM and mycotic aneurysm cause both, and thunderclap headache with meningeal signs favors SAH.

Dementia. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy can present with dementia as well as lobar bleeds.

. Hemorrhagic transformation is both a complication of ischemic stroke and a cause of intracerebral hemorrhage.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

Pathophysiology

Vessel rupture, from trauma or a weakened wall such as an aneurysm, bleeds into the subarachnoid space, causing meningeal irritation and raised ICP.

  1. Trauma or weakened wallSuch as an aneurysm
  2. Vessel ruptureTriggered by exercise, straining, or anger
  3. Blood in the subarachnoid spaceSpreads through the CSF

What the blood does

  • AMeningeal irritationBlood irritates the meninges → thunderclap headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness
  • BRaised ICPAdded blood volume → nausea and vomiting, CN deficits, posturing, and Cushing triad
  • CHydrocephalusBlood blocks CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
  • DVasospasmBlood around arteries narrows them on days 3–14 → delayed cerebral ischemia
  • ERebleedingThe unsecured aneurysm can rupture again; risk is highest early

Etiology

  • Traumatic
  • 1TraumaticBlunt force or penetrating injury
  • Non-traumatic
  • 2AneurysmalSaccular (berry), giant, fusiform, dissection pseudoaneurysm, and mycotic
  • 3Vessel wall injuryHypertension, smoking, and sympathomimetics; alcohol, OCP, and pregnancy are less certain → hemodynamic stress and inflammation at bifurcations → thin or absent tunica media
  • 4AVMArteriovenous malformation
  • 5Inherited conditionsEhlers-Danlos syndrome, PKD, fibromuscular dysplasia, coarctation of the aorta, and Marfan syndrome

Aneurysm location

  • 1ACommAnterior communicating artery; the most common site
  • 2PCommPosterior communicating artery; also common

Triggers

  • Coffee or cola
  • Physical exercise
  • Sneezing
  • Straining
  • Sexual intercourse
  • Anger
  • Being startled

Diagnosis

  1. Non-contrast CT headBlood in the subarachnoid space
  2. Lumbar punctureIf CT is negative and suspicion remains: xanthochromia
  3. CT angiogramFind the source; catheter angiography if negative

Ottawa SAH rule

For alert patients over 15 years with a new severe headache peaking within 1 hour, investigate if any of these is present:

  • Neck pain or stiffness
  • Age 40 or older
  • Witnessed LOC
  • Onset during exertion
  • Thunderclap headache
  • Limited neck flexion

Early CT

  • Within 6 hoursSensitivity near 100%, so a normal scan can rule out SAH without a lumbar puncture
  • After 6 hoursSensitivity falls, so a lumbar puncture follows a normal scan

Hunt and Hess scale

  • Grade 1Asymptomatic, or minimal headache and slight neck stiffness
  • Grade 2Moderate to severe headache and neck stiffness; no deficit except CN palsy
  • Grade 3Drowsiness, confusion, or mild focal deficit
  • Grade 4Stupor, moderate to severe hemiparesis, and possibly early decerebrate rigidity
  • Grade 5Deep coma, decerebrate posturing, and a moribund appearance

Note: A higher Hunt and Hess grade means a worse prognosis.

Treatment

Acute treatment

  • Secure the aneurysmEndovascular coiling or surgical clipping, preferably within 24 hours
  • Control BPIV nicardipine or labetalol until the aneurysm is secured
  • Prevent ischemiaNimodipine
  • Lower ICPHead of bed at 30°, hypertonic saline or mannitol, and EVD for hydrocephalus
  • Supportive careICU admission, pain relief, and reverse any coagulopathy

Blood pressure: keep systolic below 160 until the aneurysm is secured.

Before the aneurysm is secured

  • Rebleeding risk9–17% in the first 72 hours, highest in the first 6 hours
  • If repair is delayedAn antifibrinolytic for no more than 72 hours
  • AntithromboticsStop them, and reverse anticoagulation
  • Pain reliefParacetamol; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs

Treat complications

  • RebleedingSecure the aneurysm
  • VasospasmNimodipine and euvolemia; endovascular therapy if refractory
  • HydrocephalusEVD
  • HyponatremiaTreat the cause; avoid fluid restriction
  • SeizuresAntiseizure medication

Treat the cause

  • 1TraumaticSupportive care; treat associated injuries
  • 3Vessel wall injuryControl hypertension; stop smoking, alcohol, and sympathomimetics
  • 4AVMSurgical resection, embolization, or radiosurgery
  • 5Inherited conditionsScreen for aneurysms

Review article

Subarachnoid hemorrhage: aneurysmal rupture and the threats that follow

Vessel rupture, from trauma or a weakened wall such as an aneurysm, bleeds into the subarachnoid space, causing meningeal irritation and raised ICP. Patients describe a thunderclap headache, and triggers include exercise, straining, and anger. Aneurysms favor the AComm, then the PComm. Severity is graded by Hunt and Hess, and management centers on securing the aneurysm and preventing delayed complications. Here, we review its causes, workup, and treatment, and consider how it relates to other stroke types.

Key points

  • Thunderclap headache with meningeal signs is the classic presentation.
  • If CT is negative and suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looks for xanthochromia.
  • Securing the aneurysm early prevents rebleeding.
  • Nimodipine prevents ischemia, and vasospasm occurs on days 3–14.

Pathophysiology

Trauma or a weakened wall such as an aneurysm leads to vessel rupture, triggered by exercise, straining, or anger, and blood spreads through the CSF of the subarachnoid space. Blood irritates the meninges, causing thunderclap headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness, and added blood volume raises ICP, causing nausea and vomiting, CN deficits, posturing, and Cushing triad. Blood blocks CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations, causing hydrocephalus, and blood around arteries narrows them on days 3–14, causing vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia. The unsecured aneurysm can rupture again, with the highest risk early.

Etiology and mechanisms

Traumatic SAH follows blunt force or penetrating injury. Non-traumatic causes are aneurysms (saccular or berry, giant, fusiform, dissection pseudoaneurysm, and mycotic); hypertension, smoking, and sympathomimetics, with alcohol, OCP, and pregnancy less certain, which cause hemodynamic stress and inflammation at bifurcations and leave a thin or absent tunica media; AVM; and inherited conditions (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, PKD, fibromuscular dysplasia, coarctation of the aorta, and Marfan syndrome). About 85% of aneurysms arise in the anterior circulation, most often at the AComm, with the PComm also common. Triggers are coffee or cola, physical exercise, sneezing, straining, sexual intercourse, anger, and being startled.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients have a thunderclap headache, meningeal signs (photophobia, neck stiffness, and positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs), and raised ICP (nausea and vomiting, CN deficits, posturing, and Cushing triad). Complications are rebleeding, highest early before the aneurysm is secured; vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia on days 3–14; hydrocephalus; hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; and seizures.

Diagnosis

Non-contrast CT head shows blood in the subarachnoid space. If CT is negative and suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looks for xanthochromia. CT angiogram finds the source, with catheter angiography if negative. The Hunt and Hess scale grades severity: grade 1 is asymptomatic, or minimal headache and slight neck stiffness; grade 2 is moderate to severe headache and neck stiffness, with no deficit except CN palsy; grade 3 is drowsiness, confusion, or mild focal deficit; grade 4 is stupor, moderate to severe hemiparesis, and possibly early decerebrate rigidity; and grade 5 is deep coma, decerebrate posturing, and a moribund appearance. A higher grade means a worse prognosis. By the Ottawa SAH rule, alert patients over 15 years with a new severe headache peaking within 1 hour are investigated if they have neck pain or stiffness, are aged 40 or older, had a witnessed LOC, developed the headache during exertion, describe a thunderclap headache, or have limited neck flexion. CT within 6 hours of onset has a sensitivity near 100%, so a normal scan can rule out SAH without a lumbar puncture; after 6 hours, sensitivity falls, and a lumbar puncture follows a normal scan.

Management

The aneurysm is secured early by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping. BP is controlled with IV nicardipine or labetalol until then, keeping systolic below 160. Nimodipine prevents ischemia. ICP is lowered with head of bed at 30°, hypertonic saline or mannitol, and EVD for hydrocephalus. Supportive care comprises ICU admission, pain relief, and reversal of any coagulopathy. Rebleeding is prevented by securing the aneurysm; vasospasm is treated with nimodipine and euvolemia, with endovascular therapy if refractory; hydrocephalus is treated with EVD; hyponatremia is treated by treating the cause and avoiding fluid restriction; and seizures are treated with antiseizure medication. By cause, trauma needs supportive care and treatment of associated injuries; vessel wall injury needs hypertension control and stopping smoking, alcohol, and sympathomimetics; AVM needs surgical resection, embolization, or radiosurgery; and inherited conditions need screening for aneurysms. The aneurysm is secured preferably within 24 hours, because rebleeding occurs in 9–17% of patients in the first 72 hours, with the highest risk in the first 6 hours. If repair is delayed, an antifibrinolytic may be given for no more than 72 hours. Until the aneurysm is secured, antithrombotics are stopped, anticoagulation is reversed, and pain is treated with paracetamol, avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs.

Relationships to other conditions

. AVM and mycotic aneurysm cause both. Blood in the subarachnoid space with meningeal signs favors SAH, and focal deficits with parenchymal blood favor ICH.

. Vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia on days 3–14 link the two, which is why nimodipine is given to prevent ischemia.

. Seizures appear in both complication lists, whereas rebleeding and vasospasm are listed only for SAH.

Polycystic kidney disease. PKD is grouped with the inherited conditions that need screening for aneurysms.

Seizures

Pathophysiology

Excess excitation (glutamate) or lost inhibition (GABA) lowers the seizure threshold, so cortical neurons fire in excessive synchrony, causing a seizure.

  1. Excess excitation or lost inhibitionFrom an etiology, with or without a trigger
  2. Lowered seizure thresholdNeurons fire more easily
  3. Synchronous firingCauses the seizure

How firing builds and spreads

  • AExcitationGlutamate opens Na+ and Ca2+ channels → depolarization
  • BInhibitionGABA opens Cl− channels → hyperpolarization
  • CSynchronyWhen excitation wins, neurons fire together rather than independently
  • DFocal seizureFiring starts in one hemisphere, so symptoms match that region; spread to both makes it focal to bilateral tonic-clonic
  • EGeneralized seizureFiring rapidly engages networks in both hemispheres

Etiology

Etiology: VITAMIN DEFG

  • VVascularAIS, ICH, SAH, PRES from increased BP, and anoxic brain injury from global hypoxia
  • IInfectiousMeningitis, encephalitis, and brain abscess
  • TTraumaticEpidural and subdural hematomas
  • AAutoimmuneSLE and paraneoplastic syndrome → autoimmune encephalitis
  • MMetabolicDecreased vitamin B1, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, hyponatremia or hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, increased urea and metabolic waste, increased ammonia, and increased thyroid hormones
  • IIatrogenic or idiopathicDrugs: opioids, TCAs, isoniazid, salicylate, cocaine, cefepime, amphetamine, metronidazole, penicillin, bupropion, lithium, and benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawalEpilepsy: non-adherence to medications, West syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
  • NNeoplasticGlioblastoma, meningioma, and metastatic cancer
  • DDegenerative or demyelinatingAlzheimer disease and MS
  • EEclampsia
  • FFever
  • GGenetic

Triggers

  • Stress
  • Sleep deprivation
  • Bright lights and sounds

Triggers act on top of an etiology, pushing the brain over the seizure threshold.

Febrile seizures

  • WhoChildren aged 6 months to 5 years with fever of 38 °C or more, without CNS infection

  • ComplexFocal features, 15 minutes or more, or more than one within 24 hours

  1. AuraIn some focal seizures
  2. Ictal eventFocal or generalized
  3. Post-ictal stateAfter some seizure types

Motor seizure types

  • AAtonicSudden loss of muscle tone, in a limb or the whole body
  • BTonicSustained contraction, with stiff posturing of the limbs
  • CClonicRepeated, rhythmic jerking of a body part, from brief contractions alternating with silent periods
  • DMyoclonicSudden, brief, shock-like jerks of a muscle, a group of muscles, or the whole body; irregular, not rhythmic
  • ETonic-clonicA tonic phase of stiffening, often with a cry, then a clonic phase of rhythmic jerking; usually with LOC

Focal seizures

  • 1Motor (frontal)Atonic, tonic, clonic, or myoclonic (A–D), and Jacksonian march
  • 2Sensory (parietal, occipital, and temporal)Pain or paresthesia, and visual, auditory, smell, or taste hallucinations
  • 3Autonomic and psychological (temporal and insular)ANS: increased HR and BP, urinary incontinence, salivation, and sweatingEmotions: fear, dread, anxiety, or pleasureDéjà vu, depersonalization, and derealization

Spread

  • Jacksonian marchTwitching or tingling moves to neighboring body parts in the order of the homunculus, such as from the hand up the arm, as the seizure spreads along the cortex
  • Focal to bilateral tonic-clonicThe seizure spreads to both hemispheres and becomes tonic-clonic (E); the most common seizure type

Reticular formation and thalamus

  • InvolvedLOC, often with automatisms, and a post-ictal state
  • Not involvedNo LOC or post-ictal state

Aura

  • Déjà vu
  • Nausea

Generalized seizures

  • OnsetRapidly involves both hemispheres; a focal seizure that spreads stays focal
  • MotorAny of A–E, with LOC and a post-ictal state
  • AbsenceUsually ages 5–15: brief staring, daydreaming, and automatisms, with no loss of muscle tone and no post-ictal state; EEG shows a 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern
May feature
  • Involuntary cry or scream
  • Upgaze
  • Pooling of oral secretions
  • Tongue biting
  • Urinary or fecal incontinence
  • Increased HR and BP

Post-ictal state

  • FollowsFocal seizures with impairment, generalized motor seizures, and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures

Diagnosis

Find the cause

Treatment

During a seizure

  • Protect the patientRecovery position; nothing in the mouth
  • StabilizeAirway, oxygen, and IV access
  • Check glucoseGive glucose if low, with thiamine if alcohol use is likely

Status epilepticus

  • Definition5 minutes or more of continuous seizure activity, clinical or on EEG, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them
  • ConvulsiveGeneralized tonic-clonic movements with impaired mental status
  • NonconvulsiveImpaired mental status with seizure activity on EEG, but few or no motor signs
  • RefractorySeizures continue despite appropriate antiseizure drugs
  1. 0–5 minutesStabilize and check glucose
  2. 5–20 minutesIV lorazepam or IM midazolam
  3. 20–40 minutesIV levetiracetam, valproate, or fosphenytoin
  4. Over 40 minutesIntubation, ICU, and anesthetic infusion with EEG

Treat the cause

  • VVascularTreat the stroke; lower BP in PRES
  • IInfectiousABX or antivirals; drain a brain abscess
  • TTraumaticNeurosurgical evacuation of hematomas if needed
  • AAutoimmuneCorticosteroids and IVIG; treat any underlying tumor
  • MMetabolicCorrect the abnormality; give thiamine for decreased vitamin B1
  • IIatrogenic or idiopathicStop the drug; benzodiazepines for withdrawal; restart missed medications
  • NNeoplasticSurgery, radiation, or chemotherapy
  • DDegenerative or demyelinatingTreat the underlying disease

  • FFeverTreat the fever and its cause
  • GGeneticAntiseizure medication by seizure type

Long-term antiseizure medication

  • FocalLevetiracetam, lamotrigine, or carbamazepine
  • Generalized motorValproate, levetiracetam, or lamotrigine
  • AbsenceEthosuximide
  • Juvenile myoclonic epilepsyValproate or levetiracetam

How the drugs work

  • Sodium channel blockersCarbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, and lacosamide
  • T-type calcium channel blockersEthosuximide; valproate weakly
  • GABA enhancersBenzodiazepines and phenobarbital at the GABA-A receptor; vigabatrin blocks GABA breakdown
  • SV2A bindingLevetiracetam
  • Multiple mechanismsValproate and topiramate

Avoid valproate in those who could become pregnant where possible, because it is teratogenic.

Adverse effects

  • PhenytoinGingival hyperplasia; nystagmus and ataxia at high levels; SJS; fetal hydantoin syndrome; zero-order kinetics at high doses

Review article

Seizures: lowered thresholds, the patterns they produce, and stepwise control

Excess excitation or lost inhibition lowers the seizure threshold, so cortical neurons fire in excessive synchrony. An etiology raises excitability, and triggers such as stress, sleep deprivation, and bright lights and sounds can then push the brain over the threshold. Seizures are focal or generalized, and their features follow the region involved. Management stabilizes the patient, stops prolonged seizures in timed steps, treats the cause, and selects long-term medication by seizure type. Here, we review these mechanisms, causes, patterns, and treatments, and consider how seizures relate to other neurologic conditions.

Key points

  • Causes follow VITAMIN DEFG, and triggers act on top of an etiology.
  • Focal seizures follow their lobe: motor in the frontal lobe, sensory in the parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, and autonomic and psychological in the temporal lobe and insula.
  • Reticular formation or thalamic involvement brings LOC, often with automatisms, and a post-ictal state.
  • Absence seizures have no post-ictal state, and EEG shows a 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern.
  • A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus and is treated in timed steps.

Pathophysiology

Glutamate opens Na+ and Ca2+ channels, causing depolarization, and GABA opens Cl− channels, causing hyperpolarization. When excitation wins, the seizure threshold falls and neurons fire together rather than independently. In a focal seizure, firing starts in one region, so symptoms match that region; a focal seizure that spreads to both hemispheres is a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. In a generalized seizure, firing rapidly engages networks in both hemispheres.

Etiology

Vascular causes are AIS, ICH, SAH, PRES from increased BP, and anoxic brain injury from global hypoxia. Infectious causes are meningitis, encephalitis, and brain abscess, and traumatic causes are epidural and subdural hematomas. Autoimmune causes are SLE and paraneoplastic syndrome, leading to autoimmune encephalitis. Metabolic causes are decreased vitamin B1, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, hyponatremia or hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, increased urea and metabolic waste, increased ammonia, and increased thyroid hormones. Iatrogenic causes are opioids, TCAs, isoniazid, salicylate, cocaine, cefepime, amphetamine, metronidazole, penicillin, bupropion, lithium, and benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal. Idiopathic causes are epilepsy, with non-adherence to medications, West syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Neoplastic causes are glioblastoma, meningioma, and metastatic cancer, and degenerative or demyelinating causes are Alzheimer disease and MS. Eclampsia, fever, and genetic causes complete the list. Triggers are stress, sleep deprivation, and bright lights and sounds.

Febrile seizures occur in children aged 6 months to 5 years with fever of 38 °C or more and no CNS infection. Most are simple, a single generalized seizure of 15 minutes or less; complex febrile seizures have focal features, last 15 minutes or more, or recur within 24 hours. Most resolve without complications, although a subset carries a higher risk of epilepsy.

Clinical presentation

A seizure can pass through an aura, an ictal event, and a post-ictal state. Motor seizures take five forms: atonic seizures are a sudden loss of muscle tone, in a limb or the whole body; tonic seizures are sustained contraction with stiff posturing; clonic seizures are repeated, rhythmic jerking of a body part, from brief contractions alternating with silent periods; myoclonic seizures are sudden, brief, shock-like, irregular jerks; and tonic-clonic seizures are a tonic phase of stiffening, often with a cry, then a clonic phase of rhythmic jerking. Focal motor seizures arise in the frontal lobe and are atonic, tonic, clonic, or myoclonic. In a Jacksonian march, twitching or tingling moves to neighboring body parts in the order of the homunculus, such as from the hand up the arm, as the seizure spreads along the cortex. Focal sensory seizures arise in the parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes and cause pain or paresthesia, and visual, auditory, smell, or taste hallucinations. Focal autonomic and psychological seizures arise in the temporal lobe and insula and cause increased HR and BP, urinary incontinence, salivation, and sweating; fear, dread, anxiety, or pleasure; and déjà vu, depersonalization, and derealization. If the reticular formation or thalamus is involved, there is LOC, often with automatisms such as rapid blinking, chewing, and lip smacking, and a post-ictal state, and if not, there is neither. Auras include déjà vu and nausea.

Generalized seizures and the post-ictal state

A focal seizure that spreads to both hemispheres stays focal, as a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, the most common seizure type. Motor seizures are atonic, tonic, clonic, myoclonic, or tonic-clonic, with LOC and a post-ictal state, and may feature an involuntary cry or scream, upgaze, pooling of oral secretions, tongue biting, urinary or fecal incontinence, and increased HR and BP. Absence seizures, usually at ages 5–15, are non-motor, with staring, daydreaming, automatisms, and no loss of muscle tone. A post-ictal state follows focal seizures with impairment, generalized motor seizures, and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, and features confusion, lethargy, and amnesia. Todd paralysis is temporary weakness of a limb or one side, usually the side involved in the seizure, lasting minutes to 1–2 days and resolving without lasting damage; it follows focal or generalized tonic-clonic seizures and can look like a stroke, and mistaking it for one can lead to unneeded thrombolysis.

Diagnosis

Glucose and vital signs come first, so that hypoglycemia is treated. Bloods comprise FBC, electrolytes, urea, LFTs, and drug levels. Non-contrast CT head is the first imaging after a new seizure, EEG classifies the seizure, and MRI finds structural causes. A normal EEG between seizures does not exclude epilepsy. By cause, vascular disease is assessed with CT head, CT angiogram, and MRI for PRES; infection with lumbar puncture, CSF analysis, and blood cultures; trauma with non-contrast CT head; autoimmune disease with ANA and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in blood and CSF; metabolic disease with glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, urea, ammonia, and TFTs; drugs and epilepsy with a toxicology screen, antiseizure medication levels, and EEG; tumors with MRI with contrast; degenerative or demyelinating disease with MRI and cognitive assessment; eclampsia with a pregnancy test, BP, and urine protein; fever with temperature and a search for infection; and genetic causes with family history and genetic testing.

Prolactin rises 10–20 minutes after a generalized convulsive seizure but not after PNES; it also rises after convulsive syncope, and a normal level does not confirm PNES.

Seizure mimics

Syncope is favored by a trigger, a prodrome of lightheadedness, brief jerks, and rapid recovery, and is assessed with ECG and orthostatic BP. Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures show closed eyes, side-to-side head movement, asynchronous limb movement, and no post-ictal state, and are confirmed by video EEG. Cardiac arrhythmia is suggested by palpitations, exertional collapse, or a family history of sudden death. TIA causes negative symptoms such as weakness or numbness, without a march, whereas migraine with aura spreads over minutes and is followed by headache. Sleep disorders occur only during sleep, and panic attacks and movement disorders preserve awareness.

Management

During a seizure, the patient is placed in the recovery position with nothing in the mouth, the airway, oxygen, and IV access are secured, and glucose is given if low, with thiamine if alcohol use is likely. Status epilepticus is 5 minutes or more of continuous seizure activity, clinical or on EEG, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them; convulsive status epilepticus has generalized tonic-clonic movements with impaired mental status, nonconvulsive status epilepticus has impaired mental status with seizure activity on EEG but few or no motor signs, and refractory status epilepticus continues despite appropriate antiseizure drugs. At 0–5 minutes, the patient is stabilized and glucose is checked; at 5–20 minutes, IV lorazepam or IM midazolam is given; at 20–40 minutes, IV levetiracetam, valproate, or fosphenytoin is given; and after 40 minutes, the patient needs intubation, ICU care, and an anesthetic infusion with EEG. The cause is treated: the stroke, with BP lowered in PRES; ABX or antivirals, draining any brain abscess; neurosurgical evacuation of hematomas if needed; corticosteroids and IVIG, treating any underlying tumor; correction of metabolic abnormalities, with thiamine for decreased vitamin B1; stopping a drug, benzodiazepines for withdrawal, and restarting missed medications; surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy; treatment of degenerative or demyelinating disease; magnesium sulfate and delivery in eclampsia; and treatment of fever and its cause. Long-term medication follows seizure type: levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or carbamazepine for focal seizures; valproate, levetiracetam, or lamotrigine for generalized motor seizures; ethosuximide for absence; valproate or levetiracetam for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; ACTH or vigabatrin for West syndrome; and valproate, lamotrigine, or rufinamide for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Refractory epilepsy may need surgery, vagus nerve stimulation, or a ketogenic diet. By mechanism, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, and lacosamide block sodium channels; ethosuximide, and weakly valproate, block T-type calcium channels; benzodiazepines and phenobarbital act at the GABA-A receptor, and vigabatrin blocks GABA breakdown; levetiracetam binds SV2A; and valproate and topiramate have multiple mechanisms. All patients avoid triggers and take medications as prescribed, and valproate is avoided where possible in those who could become pregnant, because it is teratogenic.

Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, nystagmus and ataxia at high levels, SJS, and fetal hydantoin syndrome, and follows zero-order kinetics at high doses. Carbamazepine causes agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, hyponatremia, and SJS, so patients of Han Chinese ancestry are tested for HLA-B*1502. Valproate raises the risk of neural tube defects about 10-fold and causes hepatotoxicity, especially under age 2.

Relationships to other conditions

. AIS, ICH, and SAH are vascular causes of seizures, and seizures are listed among stroke complications, so both belong in the first assessment. Non-contrast CT head helps with both, and Todd paralysis after a seizure is the feature most likely to be confused with a stroke deficit.

Focal seizures with impairment vs absence seizures. Both can cause staring and automatisms. An aura and a post-ictal state favor a focal seizure, whereas no post-ictal state and a 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern on EEG favor absence.

Focal motor vs generalized motor seizures. Both can be atonic, tonic, clonic, or myoclonic. A Jacksonian march favors a focal seizure, whereas LOC with an involuntary cry, upgaze, or tongue biting favors a generalized one, and a focal seizure can spread as a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

Epilepsy vs provoked seizures. Metabolic, toxic, and withdrawal causes are corrected directly, whereas epilepsy needs long-term antiseizure medication, and non-adherence is itself a cause.

and . Both are degenerative or demyelinating causes of seizures, so treatment targets the underlying disease as well.

Eclampsia. A seizure in pregnancy with increased BP and urine protein favors eclampsia, which is treated with magnesium sulfate and delivery rather than standard antiseizure medication.

Multiple Sclerosis

Pathophysiology

Autoreactive T cells release cytokines that bring macrophages across the BBB, where they destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes are injured, forming myelin plaques that slow nerve conduction.

  1. Autoreactive T cellsIn a genetically susceptible person
  2. IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-αOpen the BBB and recruit cells
  3. Macrophage phagocytosisOf myelin, with oligodendrocyte injury
  4. Myelin plaquesSlow nerve conduction

What the immune attack does

  • ACytokine releaseT cells release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α
  • BAdhesion moleculesIncreased adhesion molecules → immune cells stick to the vessel wall
  • CVasodilation and permeabilityVasodilation and increased vascular permeability → immune cells cross the BBB
  • DChemotaxisCytokines draw macrophages to the site
  • EPhagocytosisMacrophages destroy myelin, and oligodendrocytes are injured → myelin plaque formation
  • FSlowed conductionDemyelinated axons conduct poorly → symptoms that depend on the plaque's site

Etiology

  • Environmental
  • 1EBV
  • 2HHV-6
  • 3Decreased vitamin D
  • 4Smoking
  • 5Obesity
  • 6Higher latitude
  • Genetic and demographic
  • 7HLA-DR2
  • 8Female, 20–40 years old

Where lesions cause symptoms

  • 1Optic neuritisDecreased visual acuity, reduced color vision, and RAPD
  • 2MLF damageBilateral INO
  • 3Pseudobulbar palsyDecreased chewing, increased jaw jerk, absent facial expressions, dysphagia, dysphonia, increased gag reflex, dysarthria, and spastic tongue
  • 4Cerebellar signsAtaxia and intention tremor
  • 5Lhermitte signElectric shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion
  • 6Uhthoff phenomenonSymptoms worsen with heat
  • 7Upper motor neuron signsMuscle weakness, increased tone, hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign
  • 8Dorsal column lossLoss of fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception
  • 9Spinothalamic lossLoss of pain and temperature
  • 10Bladder dysfunctionIncontinence (SNS damage) or retention (PNS damage)

Charcot triad

  • NystagmusFrom brainstem or cerebellar involvement
  • Intention tremorGrows as the hand nears a target; in 58–77% of patients
  • Scanning speechDysarthria from cerebellar involvement

Disease courses

Each course is also described as active or not active, by relapses or new MRI lesions, and progressive courses as progressing or not. CIS is a first episode that does not yet meet dissemination in time.

Note: Uhthoff phenomenon has no single site, so it is not on the diagram.

Diagnosis

  1. MRI brain and spineWith gadolinium
  2. SpacePlaques in at least 2 of 5 sites
  3. TimePlaques of different ages, or a substitute
  4. Exclude mimicsBloods, evoked potentials, and OCT

MRI

  • PlaquesT2 plaques in periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, and optic nerve sites; active plaques enhance with gadolinium

McDonald criteria (2024)

MS is diagnosed when MRI shows plaques spread in space, across different sites, and in time, of different ages, once other causes are excluded.

  • SpacePlaques in at least 2 of the 5 sites
  • TimeA new plaque on a later MRI, or enhancing and non-enhancing plaques together
  • Instead of timeCSF oligoclonal bands or kappa free light chains, 4 or more sites, or 6 plaques with a central vein sign
  • Only 1 siteTime or positive CSF, plus a central vein sign or a paramagnetic rim plaque
  • Incidental MRI findings2 or more sites, plus time, positive CSF, or a central vein sign
  • 2017 criteria4 sites, without the optic nerve; time or oligoclonal bands always needed

Lumbar puncture

  • CSFOligoclonal bands or kappa free light chains, if MRI does not meet the criteria

Extra tests

  • Visual evoked potentialsSlowed conduction in the optic nerve
  • OCTInter-eye difference in retinal thickness shows optic nerve involvement
  • Bloods to exclude mimicsFBC, B12, TFTs, ESR, ANA, syphilis serology, HIV, and AQP4 and MOG antibodies

MS mimics

ForFavored byObtain
NMOSDSevere optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesionsAQP4 antibodies
MOGADBilateral optic neuritis, often with disc swellingMOG antibodies
ADEMOne episode after an infection, with encephalopathy, usually in childrenMRI
B12 deficiencyDorsal column and corticospinal signs, with anemiaB12
SLERash, joint pain, and kidney diseaseANA
NeurosarcoidosisLung disease and CN palsiesCXR and serum ACE
InfectionsNeurosyphilis, HIV, and Lyme diseaseSerology
Small vessel diseaseOlder age and vascular risk factors; no oligoclonal bandsMRI and CSF

Note: The criteria need other causes to be excluded first.

Treatment

Acute relapse

  • First lineIV methylprednisolone for 3–7 days
  • If refractoryPlasma exchange

Chronic disease-modifying therapy

  • InjectableInterferon beta and glatiramer acetate
  • OralDimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, and fingolimod
  • High-efficacyNatalizumab, ocrelizumab, and alemtuzumab
S1P receptor modulators Fingolimod
  • AS1P and lymph nodesS1PR1 signaling lets lymphocytes leave lymph nodes for the blood
  • BFingolimodBinds S1PR1, which is degraded, so lymphocytes stay in lymph nodes and fewer reach the CNS
  • CS1P and capillariesS1PR1 on endothelial cells tightens junctions and lowers permeability; prolonged fingolimod can increase permeability
  • HeartS1P receptors on the SA and AV nodes slow the heart, so fingolimod causes bradycardia
  • More selective drugsSiponimod, ozanimod, and ponesimod

Treatment strategies

  • Escalation (ascending)Start with moderate-efficacy drugs, and move up if the disease stays active
  • High-efficacy (sustained)Natalizumab, S1P receptor modulators, or anti-CD20 drugs from the start
  • Induction (descending)Short-term mitoxantrone, alemtuzumab, cladribine, or stem cell transplant, then maintenance
  • Early high-efficacy suitsYoung people with active disease, many T2 lesions, and no irreversible disability

Chronic symptom control

  • SpasticityBaclofen
  • Bladder dysfunctionOxybutynin for incontinence; catheterization for retention
  • Neuropathic painGabapentin
  • Uhthoff phenomenonAvoid heat

Natalizumab can cause PML, so JC virus status is checked first.
