Review article

Multiple sclerosis: immune demyelination and lesions scattered in space and time

Autoreactive T cells release cytokines that bring macrophages across the BBB, where they destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes are injured, forming myelin plaques that slow nerve conduction. Environmental and genetic factors contribute, and the typical patient is a woman aged 20–40 years. Symptoms depend on the site of each plaque, and diagnosis rests on showing dissemination in space, usually with dissemination in time. Management treats acute relapses, modifies the disease, and controls symptoms. Here, we review these mechanisms, the symptoms they produce, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how multiple sclerosis relates to other neurologic conditions.

Key points

  • IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α increase adhesion molecules, vasodilation, vascular permeability, and chemotaxis.
  • Macrophages destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes are injured, forming myelin plaques.
  • MRI comes first, and the 2024 McDonald criteria need dissemination in space, plus dissemination in time or a substitute.
  • CSF oligoclonal bands support the diagnosis if MRI is not diagnostic.
  • Acute relapses are treated with IV methylprednisolone, and disease-modifying therapy is long term.

Pathophysiology

In a genetically susceptible person, autoreactive T cells release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α. These cytokines increase adhesion molecules, so immune cells stick to the vessel wall, and cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, so immune cells cross the BBB. Chemotaxis draws macrophages to the site, where they destroy myelin and oligodendrocytes are injured, causing myelin plaque formation. Demyelinated axons conduct poorly, so symptoms depend on the site of the plaque.

Etiology

Environmental factors are EBV, HHV-6, decreased vitamin D, smoking, obesity, and higher latitude. Genetic and demographic factors are HLA-DR2 and being female and aged 20–40 years.

Clinical presentation

Optic neuritis causes decreased visual acuity, reduced color vision, and RAPD, and MLF damage causes bilateral INO. Pseudobulbar palsy causes decreased chewing, increased jaw jerk, absent facial expressions, dysphagia, dysphonia, increased gag reflex, dysarthria, and spastic tongue. Cerebellar involvement causes ataxia and intention tremor. Lhermitte sign is an electric shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion, and in Uhthoff phenomenon, symptoms worsen with heat. Upper motor neuron signs are muscle weakness, increased tone, hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign. Dorsal column damage causes loss of fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception, and spinothalamic damage causes loss of pain and temperature. Bladder dysfunction causes incontinence with SNS damage and retention with PNS damage. Most people have a relapsing-remitting course, with relapses over days to weeks and stability between them. Gradual worsening after 10–15 years, with or without relapses, marks the secondary progressive course, and a small subset has a primary progressive course, with worsening from onset. Each course is also described as active or not active, by relapses or new MRI lesions, and progressive courses as progressing or not, and CIS is a first episode that does not yet meet dissemination in time.

The Charcot triad of intention tremor, dysarthria with scanning speech, and nystagmus reflects cerebellar and brainstem involvement, and tremor affects 58–77% of patients.

Diagnosis

MRI brain and spine with gadolinium shows T2 plaques in periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, and optic nerve sites, with active plaques enhancing. The McDonald criteria diagnose MS when plaques are spread in space, across different sites, and in time, of different ages, once other causes are excluded. The 2024 McDonald criteria need dissemination in space, with plaques in at least 2 of the 5 sites, and dissemination in time, with new plaques over time or enhancing and non-enhancing plaques together. CSF oligoclonal bands, kappa free light chains, 4 or more sites, or 6 plaques with a central vein sign can substitute for time. With only 1 site, the diagnosis needs dissemination in time or positive CSF, plus a central vein sign or a paramagnetic rim plaque. Incidental MRI findings qualify with 2 or more sites, plus dissemination in time, positive CSF, or a central vein sign. The 2017 criteria used 4 sites, without the optic nerve, and always needed dissemination in time or oligoclonal bands. Other causes must be excluded first. Lumbar puncture tests CSF for oligoclonal bands or kappa free light chains if MRI does not meet the criteria. Extra tests are visual evoked potentials, which show slowed conduction in the optic nerve, OCT, which shows an inter-eye difference in retinal thickness, and bloods to exclude mimics: FBC, B12, TFTs, ESR, ANA, syphilis serology, HIV, and AQP4 and MOG antibodies.

MS mimics

NMOSD causes severe optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesions, with AQP4 antibodies, and MOGAD causes bilateral optic neuritis, often with disc swelling, with MOG antibodies. ADEM is one episode after an infection, with encephalopathy, usually in children. B12 deficiency causes dorsal column and corticospinal signs with anemia. SLE is suggested by rash, joint pain, and kidney disease, with ANA, and neurosarcoidosis by lung disease and CN palsies, with CXR and serum ACE. Neurosyphilis, HIV, and Lyme disease are found by serology. Small vessel disease occurs with older age and vascular risk factors, with no oligoclonal bands.

Management

An acute relapse is treated with IV methylprednisolone for 3–7 days, with plasma exchange if refractory. Chronic disease-modifying therapy includes the injectable drugs interferon beta and glatiramer acetate, the oral drugs dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, and fingolimod, and the high-efficacy drugs natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and alemtuzumab. Natalizumab can cause PML, so JC virus status is checked first. S1PR1 signaling lets lymphocytes leave lymph nodes for the blood. Fingolimod binds S1PR1, which is then degraded, so lymphocytes stay in lymph nodes and fewer reach the CNS. On endothelial cells, S1PR1 tightens junctions and lowers capillary permeability, although prolonged fingolimod can increase permeability, and S1P receptors on the SA and AV nodes explain fingolimod-induced bradycardia. Siponimod, ozanimod, and ponesimod are more selective. Two strategies guide treatment: escalation, or ascending therapy, starts with moderate-efficacy drugs and moves up if the disease stays active, whereas early high-efficacy treatment uses natalizumab, S1P receptor modulators, or anti-CD20 drugs from the start, and induction, or descending therapy, uses short-term mitoxantrone, alemtuzumab, cladribine, or stem cell transplant before maintenance. Early high-efficacy treatment suits young people with active disease, many T2 lesions, and no irreversible disability. Symptoms are controlled with baclofen for spasticity, oxybutynin for incontinence, catheterization for retention, gabapentin for neuropathic pain, and avoiding heat in Uhthoff phenomenon.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause focal deficits, including upper motor neuron signs and brainstem signs. Deficits that follow one arterial territory and appear suddenly favor stroke, whereas plaques separated in space and time favor multiple sclerosis.

. Both cause loss of vibration and proprioception, and B12 deficiency is a cause of posterior cord syndrome, which is why B12 is checked. Low B12 favors deficiency, whereas MRI plaques and CSF oligoclonal bands favor multiple sclerosis.

AQP4 antibody disease and . These are mimics that also cause demyelination, so positive antibodies point away from multiple sclerosis.

. Multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating cause of seizures, so treatment targets the underlying disease as well.

Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)

Pathophysiology

Antibodies against AQP4, the water channel on astrocyte end-feet, activate complement and destroy astrocytes, and the inflammation that follows damages oligodendrocytes and axons in the optic nerves, spinal cord, and area postrema.

  1. AQP4-IgGMade by plasmablasts, which IL-6 sustains
  2. Entry to the CNSThrough a BBB opened by inflammation
  3. Binding to AQP4On astrocyte end-feet around vessels
  4. ComplementClassical pathway; neutrophils and eosinophils
  5. Astrocyte lossThen oligodendrocyte and axon damage

What AQP4 is

  • AAQP4A water channel whose tetramers cluster into orthogonal arrays of particles, packed on the astrocyte end-feet that surround vessels; dense in the optic nerve, spinal cord, and area postrema
  • BAQP4-IgGMade by plasmablasts, which IL-6 keeps alive; reaches AQP4 where the BBB is open, binds its extracellular loops, and favors clustered AQP4
  • CComplementThe classical pathway and its membrane attack complex kill astrocytes, so lesions lose AQP4 and GFAP
  • DNeutrophils and eosinophilsInfiltrate with macrophages and can cause necrosis
  • EGlutamateBinding pulls AQP4 into the cell along with EAAT2, the glutamate transporter, so glutamate builds up
  • FOligodendrocytes and axonsDamaged as bystanders, so demyelination is secondary; axon damage often comes first

Why the damage stays in the CNS

  • Where AQP4 is denseOptic nerve, spinal cord, and the area postrema and other regions around the ventricles
  • Area postremaA route for antibodies into the CNS in animal models
  • Outside the CNSAQP4 is also in the kidney, stomach, and skeletal muscle, which are mostly spared, perhaps because CD59 limits complement

NMOSD is an astrocytopathy: demyelination follows astrocyte loss rather than starting it.

Etiology

  • Predisposition
  • 1Other autoimmune diseaseSLE, Sjögren syndrome, myasthenia gravis, autoimmune thyroid disease, and antiphospholipid syndrome; also celiac disease and sarcoidosis
  • 2HLA genesHLA-DRB1*03:01 and complement C4 copy number, a pattern closer to SLE than to MS
  • Triggers
  • 3Infection or vaccinationPrecedes 20–30% of attacks
  • 4Gut bacteriaPart of AQP4 resembles a protein of Clostridium perfringens, which is overabundant in the gut of some patients; a proposed molecular mimicry
  • Sex
  • 5WomenUp to 9:1 in adults and about 3:1 in children

Who gets it

  • AgeOnset usually at 30–40; under 5% are children
  • AncestryMore common with Asian or African ancestry: 1–2% of demyelinating disease in the United States and Italy, but 13.7% in India and over 30% in Thailand
  • PrevalenceAbout 0.7–10 per 100000
  • Possible risksSmoking, low vitamin D, low physical activity, and a diet low in fruit and vegetables

Symptoms and complications

Core clinical characteristics

  • Optic neuritisSevere, often bilateral or reaching the chiasm; altitudinal field defects; acuity can stay at 20/200 or worse
  • Acute myelitisA complete cord syndrome, with paraplegia and paroxysmal tonic spasms
  • Area postrema syndromeIntractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting; 16–43% of patients
  • Acute brainstem syndromeFrom lesions around the fourth ventricle
  • Diencephalic syndromeSymptomatic narcolepsy, with thalamic or hypothalamic lesions
  • Cerebral syndromeWith NMOSD-typical brain lesions

Course

  • Relapsing80–90%; about 60% relapse within a year of a first LETM, though relapses can be over a decade apart
  • Monophasic5–10%; more often without AQP4-IgG
  • TimingOptic neuritis and myelitis can occur together or weeks apart
  • DisabilityBuilds with each attack; a progressive course is very rare
  • PregnancyRelapses increase during pregnancy and after delivery, unlike MS
  • RecoveryWorse with older onset: about 85% at age 20 and 60% at age 60

Complications

  • BlindnessIn one or both eyes in about 60% of relapsing disease
  • ParalysisParaplegia or monoplegia in about half of relapsing disease
  • Respiratory failureIn severe attacks; raises mortality
  • Chronic painIn 80–100%: neuropathic pain, painful attacks, and headache
  • OtherDysautonomia, often worse than in MS; bladder and bowel dysfunction; depression and anxiety

Note: Area postrema syndrome is often seen first by gastroenterologists and misdiagnosed as gastroparesis or reflux.

Diagnosis

  1. Core clinical characteristicMost often optic neuritis, myelitis, or area postrema syndrome
  2. Serum AQP4-IgGCell-based assay
  3. MRIBrain, orbits, and spinal cord
  4. Exclude alternativesRed flags prompt a wider search

2015 criteria

  • With AQP4-IgGAt least 1 core clinical characteristic, with alternatives excluded
  • Without AQP4-IgG, or untestedAt least 2 core characteristics in different regions, from one or more attacks; one must be optic neuritis, myelitis with LETM, or area postrema syndrome with a dorsal medulla lesion; supporting MRI findings required
  • Antibody or lesions aloneAQP4-IgG without an attack, or typical lesions without symptoms, is not NMOSD
  • RetestingSeronegative patients are retested after a relapse and before B-cell or antibody-targeted treatment

Area postrema syndrome

  • SymptomsAcute or subacute intractable nausea, vomiting, or hiccups, alone or together
  • DurationAt least 48 hours, or sooner with a new area postrema lesion on MRI
  • ClueLittle response to antiemetics
  • RequiresAQP4-IgG and exclusion of other causes

AQP4-IgG testing

  • Cell-based assayPreferred; sensitivity about 77%, with 0.1% false positives
  • ELISA or immunofluorescenceSensitivity 63–64%; more false positives, often at low titer
  • TiterDoes not predict severity

MRI

  • Spinal cordLETM over 3 or more vertebral segments, centered on the gray matter, with swelling, T1 hypointensity, and enhancement; can extend into the brainstem; bright spotty lesions
  • Short cord lesions7–14% of first myelitis attacks, especially early or in remission
  • Optic nerveBilateral, posterior, reaching the chiasm, or over half the nerve's length
  • BrainWhere AQP4 is dense, around the third and fourth ventricles: dorsal medulla, thalamus, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, and corpus callosum
  • Lesions like MSNonspecific white matter lesions in up to half, and over 30% meet McDonald criteria, so they do not exclude NMOSD

CSF and other tests

  • OCBUsually absent; their presence is a red flag
  • CellsOver 50 white cells/µL in about 35%, or neutrophils or eosinophils, which favor NMOSD over MS
  • GFAPRaised in CSF for days to weeks after an attack
  • OCTMore RNFL thinning than in MS
  • Visual fieldsCentral or centrocecal scotoma, with reduced color vision

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Multiple sclerosisShort, peripheral cord lesions, Dawson fingers, OCB, and a progressive courseMRI and CSF
MOGADDisc edema, anterior optic nerve lesions, conus lesions, ADEM, and men or childrenMOG-IgG
Gastroparesis, reflux, or food poisoningResponse to antiemeticsBrain MRI for an area postrema lesion

Note: LETM also follows infection, granulomatous disease, tumors, paraneoplastic syndromes, ADEM, spinal cord infarction, and dural arteriovenous fistulas.

Treatment

Acute attack

  • First lineIV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 2–7 days
  • PLEXOften needed, because steroids alone rarely restore baseline; from the start or if steroids fail
  • TimingTreatment within 14 days of onset more often returns patients to baseline
  • Area postrema syndromeAntiemetics rarely help, but IV methylprednisolone or PLEX stops most attacks within 2 days

Relapse prevention

  • WhenLong-term immunosuppression starts after the first attack, because each relapse adds disability
  • Deplete B cellsRTX (anti-CD20), first line, every 6 months; inebilizumab (anti-CD19)
  • Block the IL-6 receptorSatralizumab or tocilizumab
  • Block complement C5Eculizumab, after meningococcal vaccination
  • Broad immunosuppressionAZA with prednisone, first line; MMF, methotrexate, or tacrolimus

Avoid

  • Interferon beta
  • Natalizumab
  • Other MS disease-modifying drugs

Monitoring

  • RTXImmunoglobulin levels before treatment and yearly, since low levels raise infection risk
  • PregnancyHigher relapse risk; RTX has been continued safely in case reports

Note: Satralizumab, tocilizumab, eculizumab, and inebilizumab have proven benefit mainly in AQP4-IgG-positive disease.

Review article

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder: an antibody-mediated astrocytopathy of the optic nerves, spinal cord, and area postrema

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an autoimmune disease of the CNS in which AQP4-IgG binds AQP4, the water channel of astrocyte end-feet, activates complement, and destroys astrocytes, with secondary damage to oligodendrocytes and axons. It causes severe optic neuritis, LETM, area postrema syndrome, and brainstem, diencephalic, and cerebral syndromes, and follows a relapsing course in which disability builds with each attack. Diagnosis rests on the 2015 international consensus criteria, which require one core clinical characteristic with AQP4-IgG, or two with supporting MRI findings without it. Attacks are treated with IV methylprednisolone and PLEX, and relapses are prevented with long-term immunosuppression, including B-cell depletion, IL-6 receptor blockade, and complement inhibition. Here, we review its pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • AQP4-IgG binds AQP4 on astrocyte end-feet and kills astrocytes through complement, so demyelination is secondary.
  • Lesions favor regions dense in AQP4: the optic nerves, spinal cord, area postrema, and tissue around the third and fourth ventricles.
  • The 2015 criteria require one core clinical characteristic with AQP4-IgG, or two without it, including optic neuritis, myelitis with LETM, or area postrema syndrome.
  • Disability builds with each relapse, and a progressive course is very rare.
  • Attacks are treated with IV methylprednisolone and often PLEX, long-term immunosuppression follows the first attack, and interferon beta and natalizumab can worsen the disease.

Pathophysiology

Antibodies against AQP4, the water channel on astrocyte end-feet, activate complement and destroy astrocytes, and the inflammation that follows damages oligodendrocytes and axons in the optic nerves, spinal cord, and area postrema.

AQP4 is a water channel whose tetramers cluster into orthogonal arrays of particles on the astrocyte end-feet that surround vessels, and it is dense in the optic nerve, spinal cord, and area postrema and other regions around the ventricles. AQP4-IgG is made by plasmablasts, which IL-6 keeps alive, and reaches AQP4 where inflammation opens the BBB; in animal models, the area postrema is one route of entry. The antibody binds the extracellular loops of AQP4, favoring clustered AQP4, and activates the classical complement pathway, whose membrane attack complex kills astrocytes, so lesions lose AQP4 and GFAP. Neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages then infiltrate and can cause necrosis.

Binding also pulls AQP4 into the cell together with EAAT2, the glutamate transporter, so glutamate builds up. Oligodendrocytes and axons are damaged as bystanders, so demyelination is secondary and follows astrocyte loss rather than starting it, and axon damage often comes first. AQP4 is also found in the kidney, stomach, and skeletal muscle, but these are mostly spared, perhaps because CD59 limits complement outside the CNS.

Etiology

NMOSD is associated with other autoimmune diseases, including SLE, Sjögren syndrome, myasthenia gravis, autoimmune thyroid disease, and antiphospholipid syndrome, as well as celiac disease and sarcoidosis. HLA-DRB1*03:01 and complement C4 copy number confer risk, in a pattern closer to SLE than to MS. Infection or vaccination precedes 20–30% of attacks, and part of AQP4 resembles a protein of Clostridium perfringens, which is overabundant in the gut of some patients, suggesting molecular mimicry.

Women are affected up to 9 times as often as men in adults, and about 3 times as often in children. Onset is usually at 30–40 years, and fewer than 5% of patients are children. NMOSD is more common with Asian or African ancestry, accounting for 1–2% of demyelinating disease in the United States and Italy but 13.7% in India and over 30% in Thailand, and its prevalence is about 0.7–10 per 100000. Smoking, low vitamin D, low physical activity, and a diet low in fruit and vegetables may add risk.

Clinical presentation

Six core clinical characteristics each implicate one region. Optic neuritis is severe, often bilateral or reaching the chiasm, can cause altitudinal field defects, and can leave acuity at 20/200 or worse. Acute myelitis causes a complete cord syndrome, with paraplegia and paroxysmal tonic spasms. Area postrema syndrome, in 16–43% of patients, causes intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting and is often seen first by gastroenterologists and misdiagnosed as gastroparesis or reflux. Acute brainstem syndrome arises from lesions around the fourth ventricle, diencephalic syndrome causes symptomatic narcolepsy with thalamic or hypothalamic lesions, and cerebral syndrome occurs with NMOSD-typical brain lesions. Optic neuritis and myelitis can occur together or weeks apart.

Most patients, 80–90%, relapse, about 60% within a year of a first LETM, although relapses can be over a decade apart, and the 5–10% with a single attack are more often without AQP4-IgG. Disability builds with each attack, and a progressive course is very rare. Unlike in MS, relapses increase during pregnancy and after delivery, and recovery is worse with older onset, about 85% at age 20 and 60% at age 60. In relapsing disease, about 60% become blind in one or both eyes and about half develop paraplegia or monoplegia, and respiratory failure in severe attacks raises mortality. Chronic pain, including neuropathic pain, painful attacks, and headache, affects 80–100% of patients, and dysautonomia, often worse than in MS, bladder and bowel dysfunction, depression, and anxiety are common.

Diagnosis

Evaluation starts with a core clinical characteristic, then serum AQP4-IgG on a cell-based assay, MRI of the brain, orbits, and spinal cord, and exclusion of alternatives, with red flags prompting a wider search. Under the 2015 international consensus criteria, one core clinical characteristic suffices with AQP4-IgG once alternatives are excluded. Without AQP4-IgG, or when it is untested, at least 2 core characteristics in different regions are needed, from one or more attacks; one must be optic neuritis, myelitis with LETM, or area postrema syndrome with a dorsal medulla lesion, and supporting MRI findings are required. AQP4-IgG without an attack, or typical lesions without symptoms, is not NMOSD, and seronegative patients are retested after a relapse and before B-cell or antibody-targeted treatment. Area postrema syndrome requires AQP4-IgG and acute or subacute intractable nausea, vomiting, or hiccups, alone or together, for at least 48 hours, or sooner with a new area postrema lesion on MRI, with other causes excluded, and little response to antiemetics is a clue.

Cell-based assays are preferred, with a sensitivity of about 77% and 0.1% false positives, whereas ELISA and immunofluorescence have a sensitivity of 63–64% and more false positives, often at low titer, and titer does not predict severity. MRI typically shows LETM over 3 or more vertebral segments, centered on the gray matter, with swelling, T1 hypointensity, and enhancement, sometimes extending into the brainstem, and bright spotty lesions, although 7–14% of first myelitis attacks are shorter, especially early or in remission. Optic nerve lesions are bilateral, posterior, reach the chiasm, or span over half the nerve's length, and brain lesions sit where AQP4 is dense, around the third and fourth ventricles, in the dorsal medulla, thalamus, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, and corpus callosum. Nonspecific white matter lesions occur in up to half, and over 30% meet McDonald criteria, so they do not exclude NMOSD.

CSF OCB are usually absent, and their presence is a red flag, whereas over 50 white cells/µL, in about 35%, or neutrophils or eosinophils favor NMOSD over MS. CSF GFAP is raised for days to weeks after an attack. OCT shows more RNFL thinning than in MS, and visual fields show a central or centrocecal scotoma, with reduced color vision. Short, peripheral cord lesions, Dawson fingers, OCB, and a progressive course favor MS, confirmed with MRI and CSF; disc edema, anterior optic nerve lesions, conus lesions, ADEM, and men or children favor MOGAD, confirmed with MOG-IgG; and response to antiemetics favors gastroparesis, reflux, or food poisoning over area postrema syndrome, which brain MRI can show. LETM also follows infection, granulomatous disease, tumors, paraneoplastic syndromes, ADEM, spinal cord infarction, and dural arteriovenous fistulas.

Management

Attacks are treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 2–7 days. Steroids alone rarely restore baseline, so PLEX is often needed, from the start or if steroids fail, and treatment within 14 days of onset more often returns patients to baseline. Antiemetics rarely help area postrema syndrome, but IV methylprednisolone or PLEX stops most attacks within 2 days.

Because each relapse adds disability, long-term immunosuppression starts after the first attack. B cells are depleted with RTX, an anti-CD20 antibody given every 6 months and a first-line drug, or inebilizumab, an anti-CD19 antibody. Satralizumab and tocilizumab block the IL-6 receptor, and eculizumab blocks complement C5 and is given after meningococcal vaccination. AZA with prednisone is also first line, and MMF, methotrexate, and tacrolimus are alternatives. Satralizumab, tocilizumab, eculizumab, and inebilizumab have proven benefit mainly in AQP4-IgG-positive disease. Interferon beta, natalizumab, and other MS disease-modifying drugs are avoided. With RTX, immunoglobulin levels are checked before treatment and yearly, because low levels raise infection risk. Relapse risk rises in pregnancy, and RTX has been continued safely in case reports.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are relapsing CNS diseases that affect more women and cause optic neuritis and myelitis, and NMOSD was long considered a variant of multiple sclerosis. AQP4-IgG, LETM over 3 or more segments, bilateral or chiasmal optic neuritis, area postrema syndrome, CSF pleocytosis with neutrophils or eosinophils, and severe attacks with poor recovery favor NMOSD, whereas short, peripheral cord lesions, Dawson fingers, OCB, and a progressive course favor multiple sclerosis, whose interferon beta and natalizumab can worsen NMOSD.

. Both are antibody-mediated diseases that cause optic neuritis and LETM, and MOG-IgG was first thought to mark AQP4-negative NMO. AQP4-IgG, area postrema syndrome, posterior and chiasmal optic nerve lesions, other autoimmune disease, and more women favor NMOSD, whereas disc edema, anterior optic nerve lesions, conus lesions, ADEM, children and men, and a monophasic course favor MOGAD, which is a demyelinating disease rather than an astrocytopathy.

. Optic neuritis causes painful vision loss in multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, and MOGAD. Severe, bilateral, or chiasmal optic neuritis with poor recovery favors NMOSD, whereas unilateral optic neuritis with good recovery favors multiple sclerosis.

Review article

MOG antibody-associated disease: an antibody-mediated demyelinating disease distinct from MS and NMOSD

MOG antibody-associated disease is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS in which antibodies target MOG, a glycoprotein on the outermost layer of myelin and on oligodendrocytes. It most often causes optic neuritis, myelitis, or ADEM, alone or in combination, and follows a monophasic or relapsing course without a progressive phase. Diagnosis requires a demyelinating attack, serum MOG-IgG on a live cell-based assay, and exclusion of better diagnoses, including MS. Attacks are treated with corticosteroids, and relapsing disease with immunosuppression. Here, we review its pathophysiology, triggers, clinical syndromes, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • MOG is a transmembrane glycoprotein on the outermost myelin lamellae, with an extracellular, N-terminal, immunoglobulin-like domain.
  • MOGAD is distinct from MS and from AQP4-positive NMOSD, an astrocytopathy.
  • Optic neuritis, myelitis, and ADEM are the most common syndromes.
  • A clear positive titer of 1:100 or more needs no supporting features.
  • MS drugs appear ineffective; relapses are prevented with AZA, MMF, IVIG, or corticosteroids.

Pathophysiology

Antibodies against MOG on the outer surface of myelin recruit complement and immune cells, causing perivenous and confluent demyelination of the optic nerves, spinal cord, and brain.

MOG is a transmembrane glycoprotein of the outermost myelin lamellae and oligodendrocyte surface, with an extracellular, N-terminal, immunoglobulin-like domain. It is a small part of myelin, but because it faces outward, antibodies reach it easily. IgG1 MOG antibodies activate complement and cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and active lesions contain perivascular lymphocytes and myelin-laden macrophages, with perivenous and confluent white matter and cortical demyelination.

MOG-IgG was first thought to mark AQP4-negative NMO, but MOGAD is now a separate disease. AQP4-positive NMOSD targets AQP4 on astrocytes, an astrocytopathy in which axon damage precedes demyelination, whereas MOGAD targets myelin and oligodendrocytes. MOGAD is monophasic or relapsing, without a progressive phase, and affects both sexes equally, whereas NMOSD and MS affect more women, and MS can be progressive.

Etiology

MOGAD can follow infection, mainly viral, including influenza, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, and SARS-CoV-2, and also Mycoplasma, and, extremely rarely, vaccination. Onset has two peaks: children, who make up about a third of cases, and young to middle-aged adults. Men and women are affected equally, MOGAD is not linked to other autoimmune diseases, unlike AQP4 disease, and pregnancy may protect against relapse.

Clinical presentation

Optic neuritis is the most common syndrome and is often bilateral, with disc edema and a long optic nerve lesion. Myelitis causes weakness, a sensory level, and bladder and bowel dysfunction, with LETM or a conus lesion. ADEM, mainly in children, causes encephalopathy with multifocal deficits. Cortical encephalitis often causes seizures, and brainstem or cerebellar deficits can involve the pons and MCP. These syndromes can occur alone, in sequence, or together.

About half of patients have a single attack. Relapse is more likely in adults and with persistent MOG-IgG, and disability comes from attacks, without a progressive phase.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis requires a demyelinating attack, serum MOG-IgG on a live cell-based assay, and exclusion of better diagnoses, including MS. By the 2023 criteria, a clear positive titer of 1:100 or more needs no supporting features. A low positive titer of 1:10 to below 1:100, a positive result without a titer, or antibodies in CSF only requires negative AQP4-IgG and at least one supporting feature.

Supporting features are bilateral optic neuritis, an optic nerve lesion over half its length, disc edema, perineural optic sheath enhancement, LETM, a conus lesion, an H-sign or central cord lesion, ill-defined, fluffy brain lesions, deep gray matter lesions, and a cortical lesion with meningeal enhancement. Well-circumscribed lesions and CSF OCB favor MS, and area postrema syndrome with AQP4-IgG favors NMOSD. Because MOG-IgG is found in only 0.4% of MS, testing everyone with possible MS yields false positives.

Management

Acute attacks are treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, or oral prednisone 1250 mg, and PLEX or immunoadsorption follows if steroids fail. Relapse prevention usually starts after a second attack, with AZA or MMF bridged by prednisolone for the first months, IVIG at 1–2 g/kg every 4 weeks, or oral corticosteroids, whose long-term risks must be weighed. RTX is less effective than in NMOSD, and MS drugs such as interferons, glatiramer acetate, and fingolimod appear ineffective.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are demyelinating diseases that cause optic neuritis and myelitis. Bilateral optic neuritis with disc edema, LETM, a conus lesion, fluffy lesions, and MOG-IgG favor MOGAD, whereas well-circumscribed lesions, CSF OCB, and a progressive course favor multiple sclerosis, whose drugs appear ineffective in MOGAD.

. Both are antibody-mediated diseases that cause optic neuritis and LETM, and MOG-IgG was first thought to mark AQP4-negative NMO. Disc edema, a conus lesion, ADEM, equal numbers of men and women, and a monophasic course favor MOGAD, whereas AQP4-IgG and area postrema syndrome favor NMOSD, an astrocytopathy in which axon damage precedes demyelination.

Glaucoma

Pathophysiology

Aqueous humor drains too slowly, through a resistant trabecular meshwork in open-angle glaucoma or past an iris that blocks the angle in angle closure, so IOP rises and damages the optic nerve, causing peripheral, then central, vision loss.

  1. Outflow obstructionTrabecular meshwork or a closed angle
  2. Increased IOPAbove 21 mmHg
  3. Optic nerve damageGanglion cell axons are lost; the cup enlarges
  4. Visual field lossPeripheral first; irreversible

How aqueous humor flows

  • AProductionThe ciliary body secretes aqueous humor behind the iris; β2 receptors increase secretion, α2 receptors decrease it
  • BThrough the pupilInto the anterior chamber
  • CTrabecular outflowMost drainage, through the meshwork into Schlemm canal; resistance here causes open-angle glaucoma
  • DUveoscleral outflowA minority, through the ciliary muscle; prostaglandin analogs increase it

Open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma

ForOpen angleAngle closure
AngleOpen on gonioscopyIris against the trabecular meshwork
MechanismSlow exit of aqueous humor through the trabecular meshworkIris pushed forward onto the cornea by pupillary block, or a thickened iris base
CourseChronic and painlessAcute emergency, or chronic
ShareMost glaucomaAbout a third, but more often blinding

Note: Glaucoma can occur at normal pressure, and pressure above 21 mmHg does not always cause it.

Etiology

  • Open angle
  • 1Trabecular resistanceAqueous humor exits slowly although the angle is open
  • Angle closure
  • 2Pupillary blockThe iris presses on the lens, aqueous humor builds behind it, and the iris bows forward onto the cornea; the most common cause
  • 3Thickened iris baseMydriatics contract the radial dilator muscle, and the bunched iris base narrows the angle
  • 4Thick lensThe lens thickens with age, or swells with cataract, and pushes the iris forward

Risk factors

  • Open angleOlder age, African ancestry (4-fold), family history, myopia, thin cornea, and type 2 diabetes
  • Angle closureAge 55–65, women (2–4 times), East Asian and Inuit ancestry, hyperopia, and a shallow anterior chamber
  • Triggers of closureDilating drops, such as atropine and cyclopentolate; topiramate and sulfonamides; darkness
  • Secondary glaucomaSteroids, pseudoexfoliation, neovascularization, trauma, and cataract

Symptoms and complications

Open-angle glaucoma

  • EarlyNo symptoms; over half of cases are undetected
  • Visual fieldsGradual peripheral and arcuate loss, with central vision kept until late
  • Optic discCup-to-disc ratio above 0.5 and a notched rim; bilateral but asymmetric

Acute angle closure

  • SymptomsSudden severe eye pain, red eye, blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting
  • SignsFixed, mid-dilated pupil, corneal edema, ciliary flush, shallow anterior chamber, and a firm eye
  • IOP30–80 mmHg

Complications

  • BlindnessIrreversible; glaucoma is the second leading cause of blindness
  • After acute closureRetinal vascular occlusion, ischemic optic neuropathy, and peripheral anterior synechiae

Diagnosis

  1. TonometryIOP above 21 mmHg is raised
  2. GonioscopyOpen or closed angle
  3. Fundoscopy and OCTCup-to-disc ratio and nerve fiber layer
  4. Visual fieldsPeripheral and arcuate loss

Gonioscopy

  • MethodA mirrored lens on the cornea shows the angle between iris and cornea
  • Open angleThe angle structures are visible
  • Acute angle closureClosed for 360°; the other eye is often narrow
  • After an attackRepeat to confirm the angle has reopened

Workup

If there isObtain
Painless field loss or a large cupTonometry, gonioscopy, OCT, and visual fields
Sudden painful red eye with halosUrgent tonometry and gonioscopy
Disc damage at normal pressureAssess vascular risks for normal-tension glaucoma

Note: IOP can fall after an attack because the ciliary body is ischemic, even if the angle stays closed.

Treatment

Treatment lowers IOP, by increasing the outflow of aqueous humor or decreasing its production.

Open-angle glaucoma

  1. DropsProstaglandin analog first
  2. Laser trabeculoplastyIf drops fail
  3. SurgeryTrabeculectomy, tube shunt, or MIGS

Acute angle closure

  1. Lower IOP nowAcetazolamide 500 mg, timolol, and apraclonidine
  2. Mannitol1–2 g/kg IV, if needed
  3. PilocarpineOnce IOP is below 40 mmHg
  4. Laser peripheral iridotomyTreatment of choice; or lens extraction

Increase outflow

  • Prostaglandin analogsLatanoprost; increase uveoscleral outflow; first line, once daily; lengthen eyelashes and darken the iris
  • Cholinergic agentsPilocarpine; contract the ciliary muscle and constrict the pupil, opening the trabecular meshwork; poorly tolerated
  • α2-agonistsBrimonidine and apraclonidine; also increase uveoscleral outflow

Decrease production

  • β-blockersTimolol; block ciliary β receptors; avoid in asthma, COPD, heart block, and bradycardia
  • α2-agonistsBrimonidine and apraclonidine; brimonidine can cause apnea in children
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitorsDorzolamide drops, or acetazolamide by mouth or IV; less bicarbonate, less aqueous humor

Avoid

  • Mydriatics and cycloplegicsAtropine and cyclopentolate dilate the pupil and can trigger angle closure
  • SympathomimeticsAdrenaline, and phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine in decongestants, also dilate the pupil and can trigger closure

Note: An iridotomy lets aqueous humor bypass the pupil, relieving pupillary block.

Review article

Glaucoma: aqueous outflow, intraocular pressure, and optic nerve damage

Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy in which slow drainage of aqueous humor raises IOP and damages the optic nerve. In open-angle glaucoma, aqueous humor exits slowly through a resistant trabecular meshwork, causing painless, gradual peripheral vision loss. In angle closure, the iris blocks the angle, through pupillary block or a thickened iris base after the pupil dilates, and acute angle closure is a medical emergency. Gonioscopy distinguishes the two. Treatment lowers IOP by increasing outflow or decreasing production of aqueous humor. Here, we review the flow of aqueous humor, the mechanisms and features of each type, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • Most aqueous humor drains through the trabecular meshwork, and a minority through the uveoscleral route.
  • Open-angle glaucoma is slow exit of aqueous humor through the trabecular meshwork.
  • Angle closure follows pupillary block or a thickened iris base after the pupil dilates, and mydriatics can trigger it.
  • Gonioscopy shows whether the angle is open or closed.
  • Prostaglandin analogs and cholinergic agents increase outflow, and β-blockers, α2-agonists, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease production.
  • Acute angle closure is lowered medically, then treated with laser peripheral iridotomy.

Pathophysiology

Aqueous humor drains too slowly, through a resistant trabecular meshwork in open-angle glaucoma or past an iris that blocks the angle in angle closure, so IOP rises above 21 mmHg and damages the optic nerve. Ganglion cell axons are lost, the cup enlarges, and vision is lost irreversibly, peripheral first. Glaucoma can occur at normal pressure, and raised pressure does not always cause it.

The ciliary body secretes aqueous humor behind the iris, with β2 receptors increasing and α2 receptors decreasing secretion. It flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber. Most drains through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal, the site of resistance in open-angle glaucoma, and a minority leaves through the ciliary muscle by the uveoscleral route, which prostaglandin analogs increase.

Open-angle glaucoma is chronic and painless and makes up most glaucoma. Angle closure, about a third of cases but more often blinding, presses the iris against the trabecular meshwork and can be an acute emergency or chronic.

Etiology

In open-angle glaucoma, aqueous humor exits slowly although the angle is open. Angle closure has three main mechanisms. In pupillary block, the most common, the iris presses on the lens, aqueous humor builds behind it, and the iris bows forward onto the cornea. When the pupil dilates, mydriatics contract the radial dilator muscle, and the bunched iris base narrows the angle. A lens that thickens with age, or swells with cataract, pushes the iris forward.

Risks for open-angle glaucoma are older age, African ancestry, which raises risk 4-fold, family history, myopia, a thin cornea, and type 2 diabetes. Risks for angle closure are age 55–65, female sex, which raises risk 2–4 times, East Asian and Inuit ancestry, hyperopia, and a shallow anterior chamber. Dilating drops, such as atropine and cyclopentolate, topiramate, sulfonamides, and darkness can trigger closure. Secondary glaucoma follows steroids, pseudoexfoliation, neovascularization, trauma, or cataract.

Clinical presentation

Open-angle glaucoma has no early symptoms, and over half of cases are undetected. Vision is lost gradually in the periphery, with arcuate defects, while central vision is kept until late, and the disc shows a cup-to-disc ratio above 0.5 and a notched rim, bilaterally but asymmetrically.

Acute angle closure causes sudden severe eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting. The pupil is fixed and mid-dilated, with corneal edema, ciliary flush, a shallow anterior chamber, and a firm eye, and IOP is 30–80 mmHg. Glaucoma is the second leading cause of blindness, and acute closure can cause retinal vascular occlusion, ischemic optic neuropathy, and peripheral anterior synechiae.

Diagnosis

Tonometry measures IOP, gonioscopy shows whether the angle is open or closed, fundoscopy and OCT assess the cup and nerve fiber layer, and visual fields show peripheral and arcuate loss. In gonioscopy, a mirrored lens on the cornea shows the angle; in acute angle closure, it is closed for 360°, and the other eye is often narrow. Gonioscopy is repeated after an attack, because IOP can fall from ischemia of the ciliary body even if the angle stays closed. Disc damage at normal pressure prompts assessment of vascular risks for normal-tension glaucoma.

Management

Open-angle glaucoma is treated with drops, a prostaglandin analog first, then laser trabeculoplasty, then trabeculectomy, a tube shunt, or MIGS. Acute angle closure is treated with acetazolamide 500 mg, timolol, and apraclonidine, then IV mannitol 1–2 g/kg if needed, and pilocarpine once IOP is below 40 mmHg. Laser peripheral iridotomy, which lets aqueous humor bypass the pupil, is the treatment of choice, with lens extraction as an alternative.

Treatment lowers IOP, by increasing the outflow of aqueous humor or decreasing its production. Prostaglandin analogs, such as latanoprost, increase uveoscleral outflow and are first line; they lengthen eyelashes and darken the iris. Cholinergic agents, such as pilocarpine, contract the ciliary muscle and constrict the pupil, opening the trabecular meshwork, but are poorly tolerated. α2-agonists, brimonidine and apraclonidine, both decrease production and increase uveoscleral outflow, and brimonidine can cause apnea in children. β-blockers, such as timolol, block ciliary β receptors and are avoided in asthma, COPD, heart block, and bradycardia. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, dorzolamide drops or acetazolamide by mouth or IV, reduce bicarbonate and so aqueous humor. Mydriatics and cycloplegics, such as atropine and cyclopentolate, are avoided because they dilate the pupil and can trigger angle closure. Sympathomimetics, such as adrenaline, and phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine in decongestants, also dilate the pupil and can trigger angle closure in predisposed eyes.

Relationships to other conditions

. A swollen cataract can push the iris forward and close the angle, and a hypermature cataract can leak proteins that clog the trabecular meshwork. A cataract alone causes painless blurring without raised IOP.

. Acute angle closure is a cause of a painful red eye with reduced vision, like bacterial keratitis. A fixed, mid-dilated pupil, halos, and high IOP favor angle closure, whereas a corneal infiltrate after contact lens wear favors keratitis.

Cataract

Pathophysiology

Lens proteins change with age or injury, so the crystalline lens opacifies and scatters light, causing gradual, painless vision loss.

  1. Lens protein changePigment, hydration, or metaplasia
  2. OpacificationOf the crystalline lens
  3. Light scatterGlare and halos
  4. Blurred visionGradual and painless

How the lens clouds

  • NuclearUrochrome pigment collects in the center
  • CorticalWater collects between lens fibers
  • SubcapsularLens epithelium undergoes fibrous metaplasia
  • DiabetesSorbitol accumulates and draws water into the lens

Note: Both lens-induced glaucomas are untreated cataracts and are treated by removing the lens.

Etiology

  • Age-related
  • 1Nuclear sclerosisThe most common; the center turns yellow-brown, and a myopic shift lets some read again without glasses
  • 2CorticalWedge-shaped spokes from the edge of the lens
  • 3Posterior subcapsularAt the back of the lens, near the eye's nodal point, so it affects vision most; its growth predicts surgery most strongly

Causes

  • AgeThe most common cause; fifth and sixth decades
  • SteroidsTopical or systemic; posterior subcapsular
  • DiabetesSnowflake cortical opacities
  • TraumaA common cause of unilateral cataract in young adults
  • UveitisThe most common cause of secondary cataract
  • OthersRadiation, myotonic dystrophy, atopic dermatitis, smoking, and alcohol
  • CongenitalGenetic causes, intrauterine infection, and galactosemia; leukocoria, with a risk of amblyopia, so treatment is early

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Blurred visionGradual and painless
  • Glare and halosHeadlights and sunlight; worst with posterior subcapsular cataract
  • Faded colorsObjects look yellow
  • Frequent glasses changesFrom the myopic shift
  • Monocular diplopiaLight refracts through clear gaps

Complications

  • Lens-induced glaucomaPhacomorphic or phacolytic, if left untreated
  • DementiaAssociated with dementia over age 65; cataract surgery is linked to lower risk (hazard ratio 0.71)
  • BlindnessA major cause worldwide, but reversible

Lens-induced glaucoma

  • APhacomorphic glaucomaA swollen, intumescent lens pushes the iris forward and closes the angle
  • BPhacolytic glaucomaA hypermature lens leaks proteins, and macrophages clog the trabecular meshwork while the angle stays open

Diagnosis

  1. Visual acuitySnellen chart
  2. Slit lampUndilated and dilated; type and density
  3. Red reflexDimmed by the opacity
  4. Fundus and pupilsExclude retinal or optic nerve disease

Workup

If there isObtain
Gradual painless blurringVisual acuity and slit lamp
Sudden pain, red eye, and high IOP with a cataractGonioscopy: lens-induced glaucoma
Planned surgeryMedication history: tamsulosin causes floppy iris; anticoagulants

An RAPD with a cataract points to retinal or optic nerve disease, because a cataract alone does not cause one.

Treatment

Surgery is the only treatment.

Surgery

  • WhenVision limits daily activities, such as reading or night driving; troublesome glare; or lens-induced glaucoma
  • PhacoemulsificationUltrasound breaks up the lens through a small incision, and an IOL replaces it
  • Manual small-incision surgeryFor dense, black cataracts

Note: Cataract surgery is associated with a lower risk of dementia in older adults.

Review article

Cataract: opacification of the crystalline lens

A cataract is an opacification of the crystalline lens that scatters light and causes gradual, painless vision loss. Age-related nuclear sclerosis is the most common type, and posterior subcapsular cataract affects vision most and progresses to surgery most often. Untreated cataracts can cause phacomorphic or phacolytic glaucoma, and cataract is associated with dementia in people over 65. Diagnosis is clinical, and surgery, usually phacoemulsification with an IOL, is the only treatment. Here, we review the mechanisms, types, causes, complications, and treatment of cataract.

Key points

  • Nuclear sclerosis, the most common type, is age-related and causes a myopic shift.
  • Posterior subcapsular cataract sits near the nodal point, causes glare, and its growth predicts surgery most strongly.
  • Steroids, diabetes, trauma, and uveitis are causes beyond age.
  • Phacomorphic glaucoma closes the angle, and phacolytic glaucoma clogs the trabecular meshwork with macrophages.
  • Cataract is associated with dementia over age 65, and cataract surgery with lower dementia risk.

Pathophysiology

Lens proteins change with age or injury, so the crystalline lens opacifies and scatters light, causing glare, halos, and gradual, painless blurring. In nuclear cataract, urochrome pigment collects in the center; in cortical cataract, water collects between lens fibers; and in subcapsular cataract, lens epithelium undergoes fibrous metaplasia. In diabetes, sorbitol accumulates and draws water into the lens.

Etiology

Nuclear sclerosis is the most common type; the center turns yellow-brown, and a myopic shift lets some patients read again without glasses. Cortical cataract forms wedge-shaped spokes from the edge of the lens. Posterior subcapsular cataract forms at the back of the lens, near the eye's nodal point, so it affects vision most, and its growth predicts progression to surgery most strongly.

Age is the most common cause, typically in the fifth and sixth decades. Topical or systemic steroids cause posterior subcapsular cataract, diabetes causes snowflake cortical opacities, trauma is a common cause of unilateral cataract in young adults, and uveitis is the most common cause of secondary cataract. Radiation, myotonic dystrophy, atopic dermatitis, smoking, and alcohol also contribute.

Congenital cataracts follow genetic causes, intrauterine infection, and metabolic disease such as galactosemia; they present with leukocoria and are treated early because they cause amblyopia.

Clinical presentation

Cataract causes gradual, painless blurring, glare and halos from headlights and sunlight, worst with posterior subcapsular cataract, faded, yellowed colors, frequent changes of glasses from the myopic shift, and monocular diplopia as light refracts through clear gaps. Untreated cataract can cause phacomorphic or phacolytic glaucoma. Cataract is associated with dementia in people over 65, and cataract surgery is linked to a lower risk of dementia, with a hazard ratio of 0.71. Cataract is a major cause of blindness worldwide, but it is reversible.

Untreated cataracts can cause lens-induced glaucoma. In phacomorphic glaucoma, a swollen, intumescent lens pushes the iris forward and closes the angle. In phacolytic glaucoma, a hypermature lens leaks proteins, and macrophages clog the trabecular meshwork while the angle stays open. Both are treated by removing the lens.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is clinical, with visual acuity on a Snellen chart, slit lamp examination before and after dilation to grade type and density, a dimmed red reflex, and examination of the fundus and pupils to exclude retinal or optic nerve disease. An RAPD with a cataract points to retinal or optic nerve disease, because a cataract alone does not cause one. Sudden pain, a red eye, and high IOP with a cataract call for gonioscopy to look for lens-induced glaucoma, and before surgery, tamsulosin, which causes a floppy iris, and anticoagulants are noted.

Management

Surgery is the only treatment. It is offered when vision limits daily activities, such as reading or night driving, when glare is troublesome, or for lens-induced glaucoma. Phacoemulsification breaks up the lens with ultrasound through a small incision, and an IOL replaces it, whereas manual small-incision surgery suits dense, black cataracts.

Relationships to other conditions

. A swollen cataract can close the angle, and a hypermature cataract can clog the trabecular meshwork. Painless blurring with normal IOP favors cataract alone, whereas raised IOP, field loss, or a painful red eye favors glaucoma.

. Cataract is a cause of gradual painless vision loss, like retinitis pigmentosa. Glare and a dimmed red reflex favor cataract, whereas night blindness and tunnel vision favor retinitis pigmentosa.

. Cataract is associated with dementia in people over 65, and cataract surgery is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Review article

Vision loss and red eye: telling eye conditions apart by presentation

Eye conditions can be distinguished by how they present: a red eye, painful vision loss, sudden painless vision loss, or gradual painless vision loss. Viral and bacterial conjunctivitis and bacterial keratitis cause a red eye, with vision spared in conjunctivitis. Optic neuritis causes painful vision loss, retinal detachment and wet macular degeneration cause sudden painless loss, and retinitis pigmentosa and dry macular degeneration cause gradual loss. Each sits in a different part of the eye, from the conjunctiva to the optic nerve. Here, we review these eight conditions by presentation.

Key points

  • Viral conjunctivitis, usually adenovirus, causes a red eye with watery discharge and normal vision and resolves within 3 weeks.
  • Bacterial conjunctivitis causes mucopurulent discharge with lids stuck together, and topical antibiotics shorten it.
  • Bacterial keratitis follows contact lens wear and needs scraping and urgent topical antibiotics.
  • Optic neuritis causes painful monocular vision loss with an RAPD and is often the first sign of MS.
  • Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters, and a curtain and needs urgent surgery.
  • Wet macular degeneration causes central distortion and is treated with anti-VEGF injections.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness, then tunnel vision, with bone spicule pigment.
  • Dry macular degeneration, most AMD, causes gradual central loss with drusen, and AREDS supplements slow it.

Red eye

Viral conjunctivitis, caused by adenovirus in up to 90% of cases, causes a sudden red eye with watery discharge, itching, and foreign body sensation, and vision is normal. Follicles and preauricular lymph nodes are typical, often after a respiratory infection. It is highly contagious for 10–14 days and resolves within 3 weeks with artificial tears, cool compresses, and hand hygiene, and antibiotics do not help.

Bacterial conjunctivitis, caused mainly by Staphylococcus aureus in adults and by Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella in children, accounts for most childhood cases. It causes a red eye with mucopurulent discharge and lids stuck together on waking, often bilaterally, with normal vision. It is often self-limited, and topical antibiotics, such as chloramphenicol, polymyxin B with trimethoprim, or a fluoroquinolone, 4 times daily for 5–7 days, shorten it. Hyperacute conjunctivitis from Neisseria gonorrhoeae produces copious purulent discharge, can perforate the cornea, and needs Gram stain, culture, and urgent treatment.

Bacterial keratitis is a sight-threatening corneal infection, most often after contact lens wear, caused by organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas. It causes pain, redness, photophobia, discharge, and reduced vision, with an epithelial defect, a stromal infiltrate, and sometimes hypopyon. Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture precedes urgent topical antibiotics, moxifloxacin or fortified cefazolin and tobramycin. A painful red eye with halos and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil is acute angle closure instead.

Allergic conjunctivitis follows IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and causes itching, redness, tearing, and chemosis, often seasonally with atopy, and is treated with allergen avoidance, lubricating drops, and topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers. Anterior uveitis causes a painful red eye with blurred vision, photophobia, and ciliary flush, is associated with HLA-B27 disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, IBD, sarcoidosis, and Behçet disease, and is treated with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics.

Painful vision loss

Optic neuritis causes sudden vision loss in one eye, with pain on eye movement that often comes first and reduced color vision. An RAPD is present, and the disc is normal or, in a third, swollen. It affects women more than men, at ages 20–50, and is often the first sign of MS. MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium is obtained, and IV methylprednisolone followed by an oral taper speeds recovery without changing the outcome. It is also the most common syndrome of MOGAD, in which it is often bilateral.

Sudden painless vision loss

Retinal detachment is rhegmatogenous, from a tear, in most cases, or tractional, as in diabetic retinopathy, or exudative. Myopia, lattice degeneration, and trauma raise risk. New floaters and flashes precede field loss that spreads from the periphery like a curtain. Urgent surgery, by pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, or vitrectomy, seals the break, and the outcome is best if the macula is still attached.

In wet macular degeneration, VEGF drives new vessels from the choroid through Bruch membrane, and they leak and bleed. It affects 10–15% of patients with AMD, with age, smoking, family history, and hypertension as risks. It causes central distortion and blurring, with a central scotoma on an Amsler grid. OCT shows fluid, fluorescein angiography confirms the vessels, and intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, ranibizumab or aflibercept, are the treatment; without them, 79–90% of eyes become legally blind.

CRAO, usually from carotid or cardiac emboli and occasionally from GCA, causes sudden, severe, painless vision loss with an RAPD and a pale retina with a cherry-red spot, and is treated as a stroke equivalent. CRVO, mostly after age 50 with hypertension, glaucoma, diabetes, or hyperlipidemia, gives a blood and thunder fundus of dilated, tortuous veins and hemorrhages in all quadrants. GCA, after age 50, causes new headache, jaw claudication, and polymyalgia rheumatica, and sudden vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; ESR and CRP are followed by temporal artery biopsy, and glucocorticoids are started at once to prevent blindness.

Gradual painless vision loss

In retinitis pigmentosa, gene mutations, inherited in an autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, or X-linked pattern, kill rods first, then cones; Usher syndrome adds hearing loss. Night blindness comes first, then tunnel vision, and central vision is lost late. The fundus shows bone spicule pigment, narrowed arterioles, and waxy disc pallor, and the ERG is reduced. There is no standard treatment beyond glasses and low-vision support, and gene therapy is emerging.

Dry macular degeneration makes up most AMD. Lipofuscin and lipid deposits, drusen, build up beneath the RPE, and the RPE and photoreceptors then atrophy, ending in geographic atrophy. Age over 60, smoking, family history and complement gene variants, and hypertension raise risk. It causes gradual loss of central vision, with yellow drusen and RPE pigment changes. Antioxidant and zinc supplements, as tested in AREDS, slow progression, smoking is stopped, and an Amsler grid detects conversion to wet AMD. Cataract and open-angle glaucoma also cause gradual painless vision loss.

Papilledema is bilateral optic disc swelling from raised ICP, with headache and transient visual obscurations, from tumors, CSF obstruction, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and calls for urgent imaging. Hypertensive retinopathy shows arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton wool spots, with papilledema in malignant hypertension. Horner syndrome, ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, follows lesions of the brainstem, lung apex, or internal carotid artery, and Argyll Robertson pupils, small pupils that constrict to near but not light, mark neurosyphilis.

Relationships to other conditions

. Acute angle closure causes a painful red eye like bacterial keratitis, and open-angle glaucoma causes gradual peripheral loss like retinitis pigmentosa. Raised IOP and a large cup favor glaucoma.

. Cataract causes gradual painless vision loss, like retinitis pigmentosa. Glare and a dimmed red reflex favor cataract, whereas night blindness and bone spicule pigment favor retinitis pigmentosa.

. Optic neuritis is often the first sign of multiple sclerosis, so MRI of the brain is obtained to look for other lesions.

. Optic neuritis is the most common syndrome of MOGAD. Bilateral optic neuritis with disc edema favors MOGAD.

Hearing Loss

Pathophysiology

Sound is lost before the cochlea in conductive hearing loss, at or after the cochlea in sensorineural hearing loss, or at both in mixed hearing loss; conductive loss makes sound quieter, whereas sensorineural loss makes it quieter and distorted.

  1. CollectionOuter ear and canal
  2. AmplificationEardrum and ossicles
  3. TransductionCochlear hair cells
  4. TransmissionCochlear nerve to the brainstem

Where sound is lost

  • AEar canalBlockage stops sound reaching the eardrum
  • BMiddle earThe eardrum and ossicles fail to amplify sound to the oval window
  • CCochleaHair cells fail to turn vibration into nerve signals
  • DCochlear nervePart of CN VIII; retrocochlear loss

Three types

ForConductiveSensorineuralMixed
SiteCanal, eardrum, or ossiclesCochlea or cochlear nerveBoth
SoundQuieterQuieter and distortedQuieter and distorted
AudiogramBone conduction normal; air-bone gapAir and bone both reduced; no gapBoth reduced, with a gap
ShareCommon in childrenThe most common typeLess common

Note: Otosclerosis can cause both conductive and sensorineural loss, giving mixed hearing loss.

  • Conductive

  • 2Otitis media with effusionThe most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children
  • 3Perforation or cholesteatomaCholesteatoma is trapped squamous debris that erodes the middle ear
  • 4OtosclerosisSpongy bone fixes the stapes; women twice as often; family history in over half; worse in pregnancy
  • Sensorineural
  • 5PresbycusisThe most common cause worldwide; bilateral, high-frequency
  • 6NoiseHair cell stereocilia are damaged; a notch at 3–6 kHz
  • 7Ototoxic drugsAminoglycosides, loop diuretics, and cisplatin
  • 8Ménière diseaseEndolymphatic hydrops; low-frequency and fluctuating
  • 9Vestibular schwannomaA benign Schwann cell tumor of CN VIII; unilateral

Other causes

  • ChildrenGenetic causes in over half; congenital CMV
  • SystemicMeningitis and diabetes
  • Sudden SNHLUsually idiopathic
  • NF2Autosomal dominant (merlin, chromosome 22): bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas

Genetic causes

  • ShareAbout 50% of childhood hearing loss; 70% nonsyndromic and 30% syndromic
  • NonsyndromicAutosomal recessive in 75–80%: prelingual, severe, and stable
  • ConnexinsGap junction proteins of the cochlea; their loss lowers the endocochlear potential
  • Waardenburg syndromeNeural crest cells fail to migrate, so melanocytes are missing from the hair, skin, iris, and stria vascularis
ForGeneFeatures
DFNB1GJB2 (connexin 26) and GJB6 (connexin 30), adjacent on chromosome 13q12Autosomal recessive; the most common genetic cause of severe to profound congenital deafness; a GJB6 deletion with one GJB2 mutation also causes it

  • PresbycusisTurning the television up, trouble in noise, and losing high-pitched consonants such as s, f, and k
  • NoiseTinnitus and hyperacusis; acoustic trauma after a single loud noise

  • ChildrenSpeech delay; hearing loss is its most common cause

Tinnitus

  • SubjectiveMost tinnitus; only the patient hears it; noise trauma is the most common cause, at the frequency lost
  • ObjectiveThe examiner can hear it, as with an aneurysm
  • UnilateralWith asymmetric hearing, suggests vestibular schwannoma

  • DrugsHigh-dose aspirin, reversibly; cisplatin and loop diuretics, possibly permanently

Review article

Hearing loss: conductive, sensorineural, and mixed

Hearing loss is conductive when sound is blocked before the cochlea, sensorineural when the cochlea or cochlear nerve fails, and mixed when both occur. Conductive causes include cerumen, effusion, perforation, cholesteatoma, and otosclerosis; sensorineural causes include presbycusis, noise, ototoxic drugs, Ménière disease, and vestibular schwannoma. The Weber and Rinne tests and audiometry separate the types, and tinnitus, vertigo, and asymmetry point to particular causes. Treatment addresses the cause, with hearing aids and cochlear implants for permanent loss. Here, we review the types, causes, clinical clues, diagnosis, and management of hearing loss.

Key points

  • Conductive loss makes sound quieter, and sensorineural loss makes it quieter and distorted.
  • In conductive loss, the Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear and bone conduction beats air on the Rinne test.
  • In sensorineural loss, the Weber test lateralizes to the better ear and air conduction beats bone.
  • Presbycusis is bilateral and high-frequency, noise causes a 4 kHz notch, and Ménière disease causes fluctuating low-frequency loss.
  • Asymmetric SNHL or unilateral tinnitus calls for MRI to look for vestibular schwannoma.
  • Sudden SNHL is an emergency treated with oral steroids.
  • GJB2 and GJB6 mutations at DFNB1 are the most common genetic cause, and PAX3 mutations cause Waardenburg syndrome types 1 and 3.

Pathophysiology

Sound is collected by the outer ear, amplified by the eardrum and ossicles, transduced by cochlear hair cells, and carried by the cochlear nerve, part of CN VIII, to the brainstem. Loss before the cochlea is conductive and makes sound quieter. Loss at or after the cochlea is sensorineural and makes sound quieter and distorted. Mixed loss involves both, as otosclerosis can.

In conductive loss, bone conduction is normal, leaving an air-bone gap on the audiogram. In sensorineural loss, air and bone conduction are both reduced without a gap. Sensorineural loss is the most common type, and conductive loss is common in children.

Etiology

Conductive loss follows cerumen impaction, foreign bodies, and otitis externa; otitis media with effusion, the most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children; eardrum perforation; cholesteatoma, trapped squamous debris that erodes the middle ear; and otosclerosis, in which spongy bone fixes the stapes. Otosclerosis affects women twice as often, runs in families in over half of cases, and worsens in pregnancy.

Sensorineural loss follows presbycusis, the most common cause worldwide; noise, which damages hair cell stereocilia; ototoxic drugs, such as aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, and cisplatin; Ménière disease, from endolymphatic hydrops; and vestibular schwannoma, a benign Schwann cell tumor of CN VIII. In children, genetic causes account for over half of cases, and congenital CMV is another cause. Meningitis and diabetes can also cause it, and sudden SNHL is usually idiopathic.

Genetic causes account for about half of childhood hearing loss, 70% of it nonsyndromic and 30% syndromic, and nonsyndromic loss is autosomal recessive in 75–80% of cases, prelingual, severe, and stable. The DFNB1 locus on chromosome 13q12 holds GJB2 and GJB6, which encode connexins 26 and 30, gap junction proteins whose loss lowers the endocochlear potential; DFNB1 mutations are the most common genetic cause of severe to profound congenital deafness, and a GJB6 deletion with one GJB2 mutation also causes it. Waardenburg syndrome follows failed migration of neural crest cells, so melanocytes are missing from the hair, skin, iris, and stria vascularis. Type 1, from PAX3 mutations, is autosomal dominant, with a white forelock, heterochromia, patchy depigmentation, dystopia canthorum, and SNHL in about 20%; type 2, from MITF mutations, lacks dystopia canthorum and causes SNHL in up to 50%; type 3, also from PAX3, adds upper limb anomalies; and type 4, from EDNRB or EDN3 mutations and usually autosomal recessive, adds Hirschsprung disease.

NF2, an autosomal dominant disorder of the merlin gene on chromosome 22, causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas with meningiomas and ependymomas.

Clinical presentation

Presbycusis causes difficulty in noise and loss of high-pitched consonants. Noise causes tinnitus and hyperacusis. Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive loss with a normal eardrum, sometimes with a red promontory, the Schwartze sign. Ménière disease causes fluctuating loss with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and aural fullness, and vestibular schwannoma causes unilateral loss, tinnitus, and imbalance, rarely with facial palsy. In children, hearing loss is the most common cause of speech delay.

Most tinnitus is subjective, heard only by the patient, and noise trauma is its most common cause, at the frequency lost. Objective tinnitus, which the examiner can hear, can arise from an aneurysm. Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing suggests vestibular schwannoma, and tinnitus with vertigo and fluctuating loss suggests Ménière disease. High-dose aspirin causes reversible tinnitus, whereas cisplatin and loop diuretics can cause permanent tinnitus. Tinnitus usually accompanies hearing loss, but 20% of people in tinnitus clinics hear normally.

Diagnosis

Otoscopy looks for wax, perforation, effusion, or cholesteatoma. With a 512 Hz tuning fork, the Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss, and the Rinne test shows bone louder than air in an ear with conductive loss, whereas air is louder than bone normally and in sensorineural loss.

Audiometry measures air and bone conduction. Presbycusis gives a bilateral, high-frequency, downsloping curve, noise gives a notch at 3–6 kHz, often 4 kHz, with recovery at 8 kHz, Ménière disease gives low- to mid-frequency SNHL, and conductive loss gives an air-bone gap. Sudden SNHL, a loss of over 30 dB at 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours, calls for audiometry and MRI of the internal auditory canals, and asymmetric SNHL or unilateral tinnitus calls for MRI with gadolinium to look for vestibular schwannoma. Speech delay in a child always calls for a formal hearing test, and congenital or childhood SNHL calls for GJB2 testing once acquired causes are excluded, with gene-specific testing if a syndrome is suspected.

Management

Conductive loss is treated by its cause: removal or microsuction of cerumen, ventilation tubes for persistent effusion, and hearing aids or stapes surgery for otosclerosis. Sudden SNHL is an emergency treated with oral prednisone 1 mg/kg daily, up to 60 mg, for 7 days, then tapered, because spontaneous recovery is most likely in the first 2 weeks. Chronic SNHL is treated with hearing aids, since lost hearing does not return, and cochlear implants help severe bilateral loss, working best when placed before age 2 in children born deaf. Families with genetic hearing loss receive genetic counseling, since parents of recessive cases are usually unaffected carriers. Ear protection and avoiding or monitoring ototoxic drugs prevent loss, and a small vestibular schwannoma may be observed, whereas surgery or radiation does not restore hearing.

Tinnitus with hearing loss is treated with hearing aids, distress with cognitive behavior therapy and sound therapy, and aspirin-induced tinnitus resolves when aspirin is stopped.

Relationships to other conditions

. Ménière disease, labyrinthitis, and vestibular schwannoma cause both hearing loss and vestibular symptoms. Hearing loss with vertigo points to the inner ear or CN VIII, whereas vestibular neuritis and BPPV spare hearing.

. Lateral pontine syndromes from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery can cause ipsilateral hearing loss with vertigo. Other brainstem signs favor stroke over an ear cause.

Vertigo

Pathophysiology

Unequal signals from the two vestibular systems are read as rotation, and the VOR drives the eyes in a slow drift with corrective fast phases, producing vertigo and nystagmus.

  1. Asymmetric vestibular inputOne side fails or is overstimulated
  2. VertigoA false sense of spinning
  3. VOR imbalanceThe eyes drift slowly toward the weaker side
  4. NystagmusFast phases beat away from the weaker side

The vestibular system

  • ASemicircular canalsThree perpendicular canals sense rotation
  • BUtricleIts otoconia sense gravity; loose otoconia cause BPPV
  • CVestibular nervePart of CN VIII; peripheral
  • DVestibular nuclei and cerebellumCentral; drive the eyes through the VOR

Peripheral and central vertigo

ForPeripheralCentral
ShareOver 90%Mostly ischemia of the cerebellum or brainstem
NystagmusHorizontal-torsional, one direction; never purely vertical or torsionalDirection-changing, vertical, or purely torsional
FixationSuppresses itDoes not suppress it
Head impulseAbnormal: a corrective saccadeNormal
Skew deviationAbsentCan be present
Hearing lossCan occur, pointing to the earUsually absent

Note: Nystagmus is named for its fast phase, and it strengthens when the patient looks toward the fast phase (Alexander law).

Etiology

  • Recurrent, triggered
  • 1BPPVOtoconia loose in a canal, usually the posterior; the most common peripheral cause
  • Acute, continuous
  • 2Vestibular neuritisPresumed viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve; hearing spared
  • 3LabyrinthitisInflammation of the labyrinth, usually viral; with hearing loss
  • Recurrent, spontaneous
  • 4Ménière diseaseEndolymphatic hydrops
  • Chronic
  • 5Vestibular schwannomaSlow-growing tumor of CN VIII
  • Central
  • 6Vestibular migraineA common central cause
  • 7Posterior circulation strokeCerebellum or brainstem; lateral medullary syndrome is the most common

Risk factors

  • BPPVAge and head injury, the most common secondary cause
  • Central causesOlder age and stroke risk factors
  • DrugsAnticonvulsants, salicylates, and antibiotics affect vestibular function

Symptoms and complications

By timing

  • Acute and continuousDays of vertigo with nausea and unsteadiness: vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, or posterior circulation stroke
  • Recurrent, triggeredUnder 1 minute, set off by rolling over, looking up, or bending: BPPV
  • Recurrent, spontaneous20 minutes to 12 hours with ear symptoms: Ménière disease; 5 minutes to 72 hours with migraine features: vestibular migraine; minutes: TIA
  • ChronicProgressive imbalance with unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus: vestibular schwannoma

Nystagmus

  • PeripheralHorizontal-torsional, beating away from the affected ear in every gaze; suppressed by fixation
  • Posterior canal BPPVUpbeat and torsional on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver; fatigues with repetition
  • Lateral canal BPPVHorizontal, geotropic or apogeotropic, on the head-roll test
  • CentralChanges direction with gaze, or is vertical or purely torsional; not suppressed by fixation
  • DownbeatCervicomedullary junction or midline cerebellum
  • UpbeatPons and midbrain
  • Gaze-evokedOnly in eccentric gaze; sedatives and other drugs
  • Periodic alternatingReverses direction every 90–120 seconds; brainstem and cerebellum

Complications

  • FallsFrom imbalance
  • Chronic dizzinessLong use of vestibular suppressants delays central compensation
  • Missed strokeAcute vertigo can be the only sign of a posterior circulation stroke

Diagnosis

  1. Confirm vertigoSpinning, not presyncope or imbalance
  2. Timing and triggersAcute, recurrent, or chronic
  3. HINTSIf vertigo is acute and continuous
  4. Dix-HallpikeIf vertigo is positional
  5. Audiometry and MRIIf there are ear or central signs

Hearing loss, tinnitus, and nystagmus as clues

ForHearing and tinnitusNystagmusOther clue
1. BPPVNormalUpbeat-torsional on Dix-Hallpike, fatigableEpisodes under 1 minute with head movement
2. Vestibular neuritisNormalSpontaneous, unidirectional, horizontal-torsionalRecent viral illness; abnormal head impulse
3. LabyrinthitisUnilateral hearing loss and tinnitusAs in vestibular neuritisRecent viral illness
4. Ménière diseaseFluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, and fullnessPeripheral, during attacksAttacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours
5. Vestibular schwannomaProgressive unilateral SNHL and tinnitus—Imbalance more than vertigo; asymmetric audiogram
6. Vestibular migraineUsually normal—Headache, photophobia, or aura
7. StrokeUsually normalDirection-changing or vertical; normal head impulseSkew deviation and other brainstem signs

HINTS

  • Head impulseAbnormal, with a corrective saccade, in peripheral loss; normal is worrying in acute vertigo
  • NystagmusUnidirectional is peripheral; direction-changing is central
  • Test of skewA vertical shift on cover testing is central
  • AccuracyMore sensitive for stroke than MRI in the first 48 hours

Dix-Hallpike maneuver

  • MethodHead turned 45° to the tested ear, then lying back with the head hanging
  • PositiveVertigo with upbeat, torsional nystagmus: posterior canal BPPV

Workup

If there isObtain
A central HINTS result, focal signs, new headache, or stroke riskMRI and MRA; CT is less sensitive
Unilateral hearing loss or tinnitusAudiometry and MRI with gadolinium

Note: The absence of focal neurologic signs does not exclude a central cause.

Treatment

Treatment targets the cause; vestibular suppressants only relieve acute symptoms.

By cause

  • BPPVEpley maneuver, which repositions otoconia out of the posterior canal; suppressants have little role
  • Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitisAntiemetics, antihistamines such as meclizine, or benzodiazepines for about 3 days, then vestibular rehabilitation; steroids lack evidence

  • AimTrains the brain to balance with visual and proprioceptive cues
