Review article

Vertigo: timing, nystagmus, and hearing as guides to the cause

Vertigo is a false sense of motion arising from asymmetric vestibular input, and the VOR turns that asymmetry into nystagmus. Peripheral causes account for over 90% of cases and include BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, Ménière disease, and vestibular schwannoma; central causes include vestibular migraine and posterior circulation stroke. Timing, triggers, the pattern of nystagmus, and whether hearing loss and tinnitus are present point to the cause, and the HINTS examination separates peripheral from central acute vertigo. Treatment targets the cause. Here, we review the vestibular system, causes of vertigo by timing, nystagmus, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-torsional, unidirectional, and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus can change direction or be vertical.
  • In acute vertigo, an abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus, and no skew suggest a peripheral cause.
  • BPPV causes episodes under 1 minute with upbeat, torsional nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver and is treated with the Epley maneuver.
  • Vestibular neuritis spares hearing, whereas labyrinthitis adds hearing loss.
  • Ménière disease causes attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and fullness.
  • Vestibular suppressants should be limited to a few days.

Pathophysiology

Unequal signals from the two vestibular systems are read as rotation. The VOR drives the eyes in a slow drift toward the weaker side, and corrective fast phases beat away from it, producing nystagmus, which is named for its fast phase and strengthens with gaze toward that phase. The semicircular canals sense rotation, the utricle senses gravity with its otoconia, and the vestibular nerve, part of CN VIII, carries signals to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.

Peripheral causes account for over 90% of vertigo. Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-torsional and unidirectional, never purely vertical or torsional, and is suppressed by fixation, with an abnormal head impulse and no skew. Central vertigo, mostly from ischemia of the cerebellum or brainstem, can cause direction-changing, vertical, or purely torsional nystagmus that fixation does not suppress, with a normal head impulse and sometimes skew deviation. Hearing loss points to the ear.

Etiology

BPPV, the most common peripheral cause, follows loose otoconia in a canal, usually the posterior, and age and head injury raise its risk. Vestibular neuritis is presumed viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve, and labyrinthitis inflames the whole labyrinth, usually after a viral infection. Ménière disease follows endolymphatic hydrops, and vestibular schwannoma is a slow-growing tumor of CN VIII. Vestibular migraine is a common central cause, and posterior circulation stroke, most often lateral medullary syndrome, is the cause not to miss. Anticonvulsants, salicylates, and antibiotics can affect vestibular function.

Clinical presentation

Acute, continuous vertigo lasting days with nausea and unsteadiness suggests vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, or posterior circulation stroke. Recurrent episodes under 1 minute triggered by rolling over, looking up, or bending suggest BPPV. Spontaneous attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours with ear symptoms suggest Ménière disease, attacks of 5 minutes to 72 hours with migraine features suggest vestibular migraine, and attacks of minutes suggest TIA. Progressive imbalance with unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus suggests vestibular schwannoma.

Posterior canal BPPV causes upbeat, torsional nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver that fatigues with repetition, and lateral canal BPPV causes geotropic or apogeotropic horizontal nystagmus on the head-roll test. Among central patterns, downbeat nystagmus points to the cervicomedullary junction or midline cerebellum, upbeat nystagmus to the pons and midbrain, gaze-evoked nystagmus to sedatives and other drugs, and periodic alternating nystagmus, which reverses every 90–120 seconds, to the brainstem and cerebellum. Complications include falls, chronic dizziness when suppressants are used too long, and missed stroke.

Diagnosis

Vertigo is first separated from presyncope and imbalance, then classified by timing and triggers. Hearing, tinnitus, and nystagmus then help point to the cause. Vestibular neuritis causes spontaneous, unidirectional, horizontal-torsional nystagmus with normal hearing, and labyrinthitis adds unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. Ménière disease causes fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, and fullness, with peripheral nystagmus during attacks, and vestibular schwannoma causes progressive unilateral SNHL and tinnitus, with imbalance more than vertigo. Stroke usually spares hearing and causes direction-changing or vertical nystagmus with a normal head impulse and skew deviation.

In acute, continuous vertigo, the HINTS examination combines the head impulse, nystagmus, and a test of skew: a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew suggests a central cause, and HINTS is more sensitive for stroke than MRI in the first 48 hours. In positional vertigo, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, with the head turned 45° to the tested ear and then hanging back, provokes upbeat, torsional nystagmus in posterior canal BPPV.

A central HINTS result, focal signs, a new headache, or stroke risk calls for MRI and MRA, since CT is less sensitive. Unilateral hearing loss or tinnitus calls for audiometry and MRI with gadolinium, and Ménière disease is diagnosed by 2 or more attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours with documented low-frequency loss. The absence of focal signs does not exclude a central cause.

Management

Treatment targets the cause, and vestibular suppressants only relieve acute symptoms. BPPV is treated with the Epley maneuver, which repositions otoconia out of the posterior canal. Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis are treated with antiemetics, antihistamines such as meclizine, or benzodiazepines for about 3 days, then vestibular rehabilitation, and steroids lack evidence. Ménière disease is treated with less salt, caffeine, and alcohol, thiazides or betahistine, intratympanic steroids, and intratympanic gentamicin if refractory. Vestibular migraine is treated as migraine, stroke with stroke care, and vestibular schwannoma with observation, surgery, or radiation. Vestibular rehabilitation trains the brain to balance with visual and proprioceptive cues, and suppressants beyond a few days delay central compensation.

Relationships to other conditions

. Ménière disease, labyrinthitis, and vestibular schwannoma cause hearing loss and tinnitus with vestibular symptoms. Normal hearing favors vestibular neuritis or BPPV.

. Lateral medullary and cerebellar strokes can present with acute vertigo. A normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, or other brainstem signs favor stroke.

. Brainstem demyelination is a central cause of vertigo. Other focal signs and internuclear ophthalmoplegia favor a central lesion.

Alzheimer Disease

Pathophysiology

Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles cause gliosis and neuronal loss, leading to progressive dementia.

  1. Aβ productionFrom amyloid precursor protein
  2. Plaques and NFTsOutside and inside neurons
  3. GliosisActivated microglia and astrocytes
  4. Neuronal lossCauses atrophy and dementia

Amyloid pathways

  • Aα-secretaseCuts APP inside the Aβ region, so no Aβ forms
  • Bβ-secretaseCuts APP at the start of the Aβ region
  • Cγ-secretaseCuts APP within the membrane; after β-secretase, this releases Aβ
  • DFibrillizationAβ aggregates into oligomers, then fibrils
  • EPlaque formationFibrils deposit outside neurons as plaques

Neurofibrillary tangles

  1. TauMicrotubule-associated protein that stabilizes axons
  2. HyperphosphorylationTau detaches from microtubules
  3. NFTsTau aggregates inside neurons
  4. Failed axonal transportNeurons die

Distribution of Aβ and NFTs

  • Aβ (Thal phases)Neocortex → allocortex, including the hippocampus → diencephalon and striatum → brainstem → cerebellum
  • NFTs (Braak stages)Entorhinal cortex (I–II) → limbic areas (III–IV) → neocortex (V–VI)

NFTs track symptoms better than plaques do, because they follow the circuits that fail.

Etiology

  • Age and vascular injury
  • 1AgeThe main risk factor
  • 2Vascular risk factorsHypertension, diabetes, obesity, and smoking
  • Decreased clearance
  • 3APOE ε4Slows Aβ clearance; raises the risk of late-onset disease
  • Increased production
  • 4Early-onset mutationsAPP, PSEN1, and PSEN2
  • 5Down syndromeExtra APP gene on chromosome 21

γ-secretase genetics

  • PSEN1 and PSEN2Presenilins, the catalytic component; mutations cause early-onset familial disease

Review article

Alzheimer disease: amyloid plaques, tau tangles, and progressive neuronal loss

Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles cause gliosis and neuronal loss, leading to progressive dementia. Plaques arise when β-secretase and γ-secretase cleave APP to release Aβ, and tangles arise when hyperphosphorylated tau leaves microtubules and aggregates inside neurons. Age is the main risk factor, and mutations in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 cause early-onset disease. Loss of neurons in the entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, and cholinergic and monoaminergic nuclei produces memory loss and later global decline. Diagnosis in life is clinical, with biomarkers, and the ABC score needs brain tissue, usually at autopsy. Here, we review these mechanisms, the symptoms they produce, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how Alzheimer disease relates to other neurologic conditions.

Key points

  • α-secretase cuts APP inside the Aβ region, so no Aβ forms, whereas β-secretase followed by γ-secretase releases Aβ.
  • PSEN1 and PSEN2 encode the catalytic component of γ-secretase, and their mutations cause early-onset familial disease.
  • Aβ begins in the neocortex and moves inward, whereas NFTs begin in the entorhinal cortex and move outward.
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors offset the loss of cholinergic neurons from the nucleus basalis of Meynert.
  • The ABC score grades Aβ plaques, NFTs, and neuritic plaques, and needs brain tissue, usually at autopsy.

Pathophysiology

Aβ is produced from APP, forms plaques outside neurons alongside NFTs inside them, and activates microglia and astrocytes, causing gliosis. Neuronal loss then causes atrophy and dementia.

APP is processed by two pathways. In the non-amyloidogenic pathway, α-secretase cuts inside the Aβ region, so no Aβ forms when γ-secretase then cuts within the membrane. In the amyloidogenic pathway, β-secretase cuts at the start of the Aβ region, and the γ-secretase cut releases Aβ. Aβ aggregates into oligomers and then fibrils, which deposit outside neurons as plaques.

Tau is a microtubule-associated protein that stabilizes axons. Hyperphosphorylation detaches tau from microtubules, and tau then aggregates inside neurons as NFTs. Axonal transport fails, and the neurons die.

The two lesions spread differently. Aβ follows the Thal phases, from the neocortex to the allocortex, including the hippocampus, then the diencephalon and striatum, the brainstem, and the cerebellum. NFTs follow the Braak stages, from the entorhinal cortex (I–II) to limbic areas (III–IV) and the neocortex (V–VI). NFTs track symptoms better than plaques do, because they follow the circuits that fail.

Etiology

Age is the main risk factor, and vascular injury from hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and smoking adds to neuronal loss. Decreased Aβ clearance is represented by APOE ε4, which slows clearance and raises the risk of late-onset disease. Increased Aβ production is represented by early-onset mutations in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2, and by Down syndrome, in which chromosome 21 carries an extra APP gene. The presenilins PSEN1 and PSEN2 are the catalytic component of γ-secretase, and PEN2, APH1, and nicastrin are the other components of the complex.

Clinical presentation

Symptoms follow the structures affected. The entorhinal cortex is the first cortical site of NFTs, causing early memory loss and getting lost, and early atrophy of hippocampus CA1 accompanies short-term memory loss. Noradrenergic loss in the locus coeruleus changes attention and behavior, and serotonergic loss in the raphe nuclei causes depression and sleep changes. Cholinergic neuron loss in the nucleus basalis of Meynert causes memory and attention decline.

Early disease causes short-term memory loss, then executive dysfunction. Middle disease adds language and visuospatial decline, apathy, agitation, and wandering, and late disease causes apraxia, mutism, incontinence, and total dependence. Complications are aspiration pneumonia from dysphagia; infection, with pneumonia the most common cause of death; falls, dehydration, and malnutrition; and agitation, delirium, wandering, and caregiver burden. Life expectancy is about 4–8 years after diagnosis at age 65 or older. Aβ in vessel walls causes cerebral amyloid angiopathy, with lobar ICH.

Diagnosis

Assessment begins with a history that includes a collateral source, followed by cognitive testing with the MMSE or MoCA. Bloods are FBC, TFTs, B12, and electrolytes, and MRI shows medial temporal atrophy. Biomarkers are added if the diagnosis is unclear: CSF shows decreased Aβ42 with increased tau and phosphorylated tau, and amyloid PET shows plaques in life. Genetic testing is considered with early onset and a strong family history.

The ABC score is a neuropathologic score that needs brain tissue, usually at autopsy. A grades Aβ plaques by Thal phase, with A0 for none, A1 for phases 1–2, A2 for phase 3, and A3 for phases 4–5. B grades NFTs by Braak stage, with B0 for none, B1 for stages I–II, B2 for III–IV, and B3 for V–VI. C grades neuritic plaques by CERAD score, with C0 for none, C1 sparse, C2 moderate, and C3 frequent. The three grades combine into a level of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change: not, low, intermediate, or high.

Dementia mimics

Delirium is favored by sudden onset, fluctuating attention, and an acute illness, and prompts a search for the cause. Depression shows low mood, poor effort, and awareness of memory problems. Hypothyroidism causes fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain, and is found with TFTs, and B12 deficiency causes anemia and neuropathy. Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait disturbance and urinary incontinence early, and is assessed with MRI. Dementia with Lewy bodies is favored by visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations. Vascular dementia shows stepwise decline with vascular risk factors, and frontotemporal dementia occurs at a younger age, with early behavior or language change; both are assessed with MRI.

Management

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors slow ACh breakdown, offsetting cholinergic neuron loss, and give a modest benefit in mild to moderate disease. The drugs are donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, and they can cause bradycardia and GI upset. Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist for moderate to severe disease. The anti-amyloid antibodies lecanemab and donanemab clear plaques in early disease, with monitoring for ARIA.

Supportive care covers safety, routine, and caregiver support. Behavior is managed with non-drug approaches first, vascular risk factors are treated, and advance care planning begins early.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause progressive dementia. Visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations favor dementia with Lewy bodies, whereas early short-term memory loss with medial temporal atrophy favors Alzheimer disease.

. Both cause progressive dementia. Early behavior or language change with spared memory favors frontotemporal dementia, whereas early episodic memory loss favors Alzheimer disease.

. Aβ links the two conditions, since Aβ in vessel walls causes cerebral amyloid angiopathy and lobar ICH. Sudden focal deficits with blood on imaging favor hemorrhage, whereas gradual cognitive decline favors Alzheimer disease.

. Alzheimer disease is a degenerative cause of seizures, so treatment targets the underlying disease as well.

Frontotemporal Dementia

Pathophysiology

Tau, TDP-43, or FUS inclusions kill neurons in the frontal and anterior temporal lobes, so behavior, personality, and language fail while memory is spared early.

  1. Protein inclusionsTau, TDP-43, or FUS
  2. Frontal and temporal neuron lossKnife-edge atrophy
  3. Behavior or language changeMemory spared early

Pathology

  • FTLD-tauTau inclusions, such as Pick bodies, with ballooned neurons
  • FTLD-TDPAbout half of FTLD; TDP-43 is also the protein of ALS
  • FTLD-FUSRare

Note: The clinical variant does not reliably predict which protein is present.

Etiology

  • Sporadic
  • 1SporadicMost cases
  • Genetic
  • 2MAPTTau gene; FTLD-tau
  • 3GRNGranulin gene; FTLD-TDP
  • 4C9orf72Repeat expansion; FTLD-TDP, and the most common cause of familial FTD and ALS
  • Risk factors
  • 5Head trauma3.3-fold risk
  • 6Thyroid disease2.5-fold risk

Who gets it

  • FamilialAbout 40% of cases
  • AgeMean onset 58; the second most common early-onset dementia
  • SexbvFTD and svPPA more in men; nfvPPA more in women

Symptoms and complications

Variants by site

  • ABehavioral variant (bvFTD)Frontal lobes; the most common form
  • BSemantic variant (svPPA)Left, dominant, anterior temporal lobe
  • CNonfluent variant (nfvPPA)Left inferior frontal and insular cortex
  • DRight temporal variantRight, nondominant, anterior temporal lobe

A. Behavioral changes

  • DisinhibitionSocially inappropriate, impulsive behavior
  • ApathyOften mistaken for depression
  • Loss of empathyDisregard for others' feelings
  • Compulsive behaviorRepetitive movements, rituals, and stereotyped speech
  • HyperoralityA sweet tooth, binge eating, and more alcohol
  • Executive dysfunctionMemory and visuospatial skills spared

Personality changes early, and patients develop anosognosia: they cannot see that their behavior has changed or explain why they act as they do.

B–D. Language and recognition

  • Semantic variantFluent speech that has lost meaning; anomia and poor single-word comprehension
  • Nonfluent variantEffortful, halting, agrammatic speech with apraxia of speech; word meaning kept
  • Right temporal variantProsopagnosia, getting lost, behavior change, and memory loss

Complications

  • Overlap syndromesMND, CBD, and PSP
  • SafetyFalls, hypersexuality, driving, and finances
  • SleepInsomnia and daytime sleepiness
  • PrognosisAverage survival 7.5 years

Diagnosis

  1. Informant historyBehavior and personality change
  2. Cognitive testingGo-no-go, letter fluency, and similarities
  3. MRI or CTFrontal and anterior temporal atrophy
  4. SPECT or FDG-PETFrontotemporal hypoperfusion or hypometabolism
  5. Genetic testingIf there is a family history

Diagnostic criteria

  • Possible bvFTD3 of the 6 behavioral features
  • Semantic variantAnomia and impaired single-word comprehension
  • Nonfluent variantAgrammatism or effortful speech with apraxia of speech

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Alzheimer diseaseEarly episodic memory and visuospatial lossAmyloid and tau biomarkers
Logopenic PPAWord-finding pauses and poor repetitionAmyloid biomarkers; usually AD
DepressionLow mood rather than apathy alonePsychiatric assessment
DLBVisual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuationsClinical assessment

Note: Imaging findings support the diagnosis but are not specific.

Treatment

No treatment slows FTD, so care targets behavior, safety, and support.

Drugs

  • BehaviorSSRIs; they do not improve cognition
  • Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantineNo proven benefit; donepezil can worsen behavior
  • AntipsychoticsMixed results; patients are prone to extrapyramidal effects

Support

  • Speech therapyPPA variants
  • Physical and occupational therapyFunction and safety
  • CaregiversEducation and support
  • Genetic counselingPatients and families
  • Daily activitiesMonitor finances, driving, and eating

Note: Unlike AD, FTD does not respond to cholinesterase inhibitors.

Review article

Frontotemporal dementia: frontal and temporal degeneration of behavior and language

Frontotemporal dementia is a group of syndromes caused by frontotemporal lobar degeneration, in which tau, TDP-43, or FUS inclusions kill neurons in the frontal and anterior temporal lobes. The behavioral variant causes disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior, hyperorality, and executive dysfunction with anosognosia, and the language variants cause semantic or nonfluent primary progressive aphasia. About 40% of cases are familial. Diagnosis rests on history, cognitive testing, and frontotemporal atrophy on imaging, and treatment is supportive. Here, we review its pathology, variants, diagnosis, and management.

Key points

  • FTLD inclusions contain tau, TDP-43, or, rarely, FUS, and the variant does not reliably predict the protein.
  • MAPT causes FTLD-tau, and GRN and C9orf72 cause FTLD-TDP; C9orf72 also causes ALS.
  • bvFTD causes disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior, hyperorality, and executive dysfunction, with anosognosia.
  • Left anterior temporal atrophy causes the semantic variant, and right anterior temporal atrophy causes prosopagnosia and getting lost.
  • SSRIs help behavior, but cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine have no proven benefit.

Pathophysiology

Tau, TDP-43, or FUS inclusions kill neurons in the frontal and anterior temporal lobes, producing knife-edge atrophy, so behavior, personality, and language fail while memory is spared early. FTLD-tau includes tau inclusions such as Pick bodies, with ballooned neurons. FTLD-TDP accounts for about half of FTLD, and TDP-43 is also the protein of ALS, whereas FTLD-FUS is rare. The clinical variant does not reliably predict which protein is present.

Etiology

Most cases are sporadic, but about 40% are familial. MAPT, the tau gene, causes FTLD-tau, and GRN and C9orf72 cause FTLD-TDP; the C9orf72 repeat expansion is the most common cause of familial FTD and ALS. Head trauma and thyroid disease raise risk by 3.3-fold and 2.5-fold. Mean onset is at 58 years, making FTD the second most common early-onset dementia, and bvFTD and svPPA are more common in men, nfvPPA in women.

Clinical presentation

The behavioral variant, the most common form, follows frontal involvement. It causes disinhibition, with socially inappropriate and impulsive behavior; apathy, often mistaken for depression; loss of empathy; compulsive behavior, including repetitive movements, rituals, and stereotyped speech; hyperorality, including a sweet tooth, binge eating, and more alcohol; and executive dysfunction, with memory and visuospatial skills spared. Personality changes early, and patients develop anosognosia, losing insight into their changed behavior, and cannot explain why they act as they do.

The semantic variant follows left, dominant, anterior temporal atrophy and causes fluent speech that has lost meaning, with anomia and poor single-word comprehension. The nonfluent variant follows left inferior frontal and insular atrophy and causes effortful, halting, agrammatic speech with apraxia of speech, while word meaning is kept. Right, nondominant, anterior temporal atrophy causes prosopagnosia, getting lost, behavior change, and memory loss.

FTD overlaps with MND, CBD, and PSP. Complications include falls, hypersexuality, unsafe driving and finances, and insomnia and daytime sleepiness, and average survival is 7.5 years.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis begins with an informant history of behavior and personality change and cognitive testing, such as go-no-go, letter fluency, and similarities. MRI or CT shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, and SPECT or FDG-PET shows frontotemporal hypoperfusion or hypometabolism, though these findings are not specific. Genetic testing is offered when there is a family history.

Possible bvFTD requires 3 of the 6 behavioral features. The semantic variant requires anomia and impaired single-word comprehension, and the nonfluent variant requires agrammatism or effortful speech with apraxia of speech. Early episodic memory and visuospatial loss favor Alzheimer disease, word-finding pauses with poor repetition favor logopenic PPA, which is usually caused by AD, low mood favors depression, and visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations favor DLB.

Management

No treatment slows FTD, so care targets behavior, safety, and support. SSRIs can improve behavior but not cognition. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine have no proven benefit, and donepezil can worsen behavior. Antipsychotics have mixed results, and patients are prone to extrapyramidal effects. Speech therapy helps the PPA variants, physical and occupational therapy support function and safety, caregivers need education and support, families are offered genetic counseling, and finances, driving, and eating are monitored.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause progressive dementia, and logopenic PPA is usually caused by AD. Early episodic memory and visuospatial loss favor Alzheimer disease, whereas early behavior or language change with spared memory favors frontotemporal dementia, which does not respond to cholinesterase inhibitors.

. PSP and CBD are 4R tauopathies that overlap with FTLD. Early parkinsonism, gaze palsy, falls, or asymmetric apraxia favors atypical parkinsonism.

. Both can cause early behavioral and executive change. Visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations favor dementia with Lewy bodies.

Dementia with Lewy Bodies

Pathophysiology

α-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies across the brainstem, limbic areas, and cortex, causing cholinergic and dopaminergic deficits and leading to dementia with parkinsonism.

  1. α-synuclein misfoldingOligomers may be the main toxic form
  2. Lewy bodiesα-synuclein and ubiquitin inside neurons
  3. Multifocal spreadBrainstem, limbic areas, and cortex
  4. Neurotransmitter lossCholinergic and dopaminergic

What Lewy bodies do

  • ACortexAttention, executive, and visuospatial decline
  • BNucleus basalis of MeynertCholinergic loss; attention and cognitive decline
  • CSubstantia nigraDopaminergic loss; parkinsonism
  • DBrainstem nucleiLocus coeruleus, dorsal raphe, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus; RBD
  • EOccipital cortexReduced metabolism; visual hallucinations
  • FMedial temporal lobeRelatively preserved, so memory is spared early
  • GAutonomic nervesLow cardiac MIBG uptake; autonomic dysfunction

Co-pathology

  • Aβ plaques and tau tanglesCommon; up to 30% of DLB meets the threshold for Alzheimer disease
  • EffectMore memory loss, faster progression, and higher mortality

Lewy body numbers track neuronal loss poorly, which is why oligomers may be the main toxic form.

Etiology

  • Age and co-pathology
  • 1AgeIncidence rises with age
  • 2APOE ε4Risk gene shared with Alzheimer disease
  • Decreased clearance
  • 3GBA1 variantsLysosomal enzyme; risk gene shared with Parkinson disease
  • Increased production
  • 4SNCA variantsThe α-synuclein gene; rare family multiplications

Note: Many studies find DLB more often in men, most people have no family history, and no single cause is known.

Symptoms and complications

Cognition

  • EarlyAttention, executive function, and visuoperceptual ability
  • LaterMemory impairment becomes evident

Core features

  • Fluctuating cognitionPronounced variations in attention and alertness
  • Visual hallucinationsRecurrent, well formed, and detailed
  • RBDActing out dreams; may precede cognitive decline
  • ParkinsonismBradykinesia, rest tremor, or rigidity

Supportive features

  • Autonomic dysfunctionOrthostatic hypotension (often early), constipation, and urinary incontinence
  • FallsPostural instability, repeated falls, syncope, and transient unresponsiveness
  • Sleep and smellHypersomnia and hyposmia
  • PsychiatricDelusions, misidentification, other hallucinations, apathy, anxiety, and depression

Complications

  • Antipsychotic reactionSudden change in consciousness, impaired swallowing, acute confusion, and worse parkinsonism
  • FallsTraumatic fractures
  • Life expectancy5–8 years after diagnosis
  • Causes of deathFalls, pneumonia, swallowing problems, cardiac complications, and suicide

Diagnosis

  1. HistoryWith a collateral source
  2. Cognitive testingMMSE or MoCA
  3. BloodsChemistry panel, TFTs, B12, syphilis, and HIV
  4. MRIMedial temporal lobes relatively preserved
  5. BiomarkersIf unclear

Consensus criteria

Dementia is essential: progressive cognitive decline that interferes with daily activities.

  • Probable DLB2 or more core features, or 1 core feature with 1 or more indicative biomarkers
  • Possible DLB1 core feature with no indicative biomarker, or an indicative biomarker with no core feature
  • Less likelyAnother illness explains the picture, or parkinsonism is the only core feature and first appears in severe dementia

Indicative biomarkers

  • DAT SPECT or PETReduced uptake in the basal ganglia
  • MIBG myocardial scintigraphyLow uptake
  • PolysomnographyREM sleep without atonia

Supportive biomarkers

  • CT or MRIRelative preservation of the medial temporal lobes
  • SPECT or PETLow occipital activity, with the cingulate island sign on FDG-PET
  • EEGProminent posterior slow-wave activity

Other tests

  • CSFα-synuclein seed amplification assay, over 90% sensitive and specific
  • AutopsyThe only definite diagnosis

DLB or PDD

  • DLBDementia before, with, or within 1 year of parkinsonism
  • PDDDementia 1 year or more after established Parkinson disease

DLB mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Alzheimer diseaseProminent early memory loss and medial temporal atrophyMRI
DeliriumSudden onset, an acute illness, and a reversible causeSearch for the cause
Vascular dementiaStepwise decline and vascular risk factorsMRI
Frontotemporal dementiaYounger age, with early behavior or language changeMRI
Prion diseaseRapid progression with myoclonusMRI and CSF
Drug-induced parkinsonismRecent dopamine-blocking drug useMedication review
Progressive supranuclear palsyEarly falls and vertical gaze palsyClinical examination

Biomarkers alone cannot make probable DLB; at least 1 core feature is needed.

Treatment

No treatment slows neuronal loss, so treatment targets each symptom.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors

  1. TargetAcetylcholinesterase
  2. MechanismSlows ACh breakdown, offsetting cholinergic loss
  3. ResponseBetter cognition, function, and hallucinations
  • DrugsRivastigmine, donepezil, and galantamine

Other symptoms

  • CognitionMemantine may add benefit
  • ParkinsonismLow-dose levodopa, increased slowly; less responsive than in Parkinson disease
  • RBDMelatonin, or cautious bedtime clonazepam
  • DepressionSSRIs, SNRIs, or mirtazapine
  • Autonomic dysfunctionTreat as in other diseases, with little DLB trial data
  • FallsSafety assessment, bone density, and vitamin D

Antipsychotics

  • If essentialLow-dose quetiapine, though a small trial was negative
  • Generally avoidHaloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, and aripiprazole

Supportive care

  • Daily lifeCaregiver education and home modifications
  • TherapiesPhysical, occupational, and speech therapy
  • PlanningEarly advance care planning

Avoid antipsychotics whenever possible, because serious reactions occur in up to 50% of people.

Review article

Dementia with Lewy bodies: α-synuclein, fluctuating cognition, and antipsychotic sensitivity

Dementia with Lewy bodies is a progressive dementia in which α-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies across the brainstem, limbic areas, and cortex, causing cholinergic and dopaminergic deficits. Its core features are fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, RBD, and parkinsonism, and attention, executive function, and visuoperceptual ability fail before memory. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by indicative biomarkers, and treatment targets each symptom, because no treatment slows neuronal loss. Antipsychotics carry a risk of serious reactions. Here, we review these mechanisms, the symptoms they produce, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how dementia with Lewy bodies relates to other neurologic conditions.

Key points

  • The four core features are fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, RBD, and parkinsonism.
  • Probable DLB needs 2 or more core features, or 1 core feature with an indicative biomarker.
  • Indicative biomarkers are reduced DAT uptake, low MIBG uptake, and REM sleep without atonia.
  • DLB is diagnosed when dementia begins before, with, or within 1 year of parkinsonism.
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors come first, and antipsychotics are avoided whenever possible.

Pathophysiology

α-synuclein misfolds and aggregates, and Lewy bodies form as inclusions of α-synuclein and ubiquitin inside neurons across the brainstem, limbic areas, and cortex. Oligomers may be the main toxic form, because Lewy body numbers track neuronal loss poorly.

Each site produces a different effect. Cortical involvement causes attention, executive, and visuospatial decline. Cholinergic loss from the nucleus basalis of Meynert contributes to attention and cognitive decline, and dopaminergic loss from the substantia nigra causes parkinsonism. Brainstem nuclei are also affected, including the locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, with REM sleep without atonia and RBD. The occipital cortex shows reduced metabolism, with visual hallucinations, whereas the medial temporal lobe is relatively preserved, so memory is spared early. Autonomic nerve involvement causes low cardiac MIBG uptake and autonomic dysfunction.

Aβ plaques and tau tangles commonly coexist, and up to 30% of DLB meets the threshold for Alzheimer disease. This co-pathology brings more memory loss, faster progression, and higher mortality.

Etiology

Many studies find DLB more often in men, most people have no family history, and no single cause is known. Incidence rises with age, and APOE ε4 is a risk gene shared with Alzheimer disease. Decreased clearance is represented by GBA1 variants, which affect a lysosomal enzyme and are shared with Parkinson disease. SNCA, the α-synuclein gene, represents increased production, with rare family multiplications.

Clinical presentation

Attention, executive function, and visuoperceptual ability are affected early, and memory impairment becomes evident later. Fluctuating cognition causes pronounced variations in attention and alertness. Visual hallucinations are recurrent, well formed, and detailed. RBD causes acting out of dreams and may precede cognitive decline, and parkinsonism causes bradykinesia, rest tremor, or rigidity.

Supportive features are autonomic dysfunction, with orthostatic hypotension, which is often early, constipation, and urinary incontinence; postural instability, repeated falls, syncope, and transient unresponsiveness; hypersomnia and hyposmia; and delusions, misidentification, other hallucinations, apathy, anxiety, and depression. Complications are antipsychotic reactions, with sudden change in consciousness, impaired swallowing, acute confusion, and worse parkinsonism, as well as traumatic fractures from falls. Life expectancy is 5–8 years after diagnosis, and causes of death include falls, pneumonia, swallowing problems, cardiac complications, and suicide.

Diagnosis

Assessment begins with a history that includes a collateral source, cognitive testing with the MMSE or MoCA, bloods with a chemistry panel, TFTs, B12, syphilis, and HIV, and MRI, which shows relatively preserved medial temporal lobes. Biomarkers are added if the diagnosis is unclear.

Dementia is essential, defined as progressive cognitive decline that interferes with daily activities. Probable DLB needs 2 or more core features, or 1 core feature with 1 or more indicative biomarkers, and biomarkers alone cannot make the diagnosis. Possible DLB is 1 core feature with no indicative biomarker, or an indicative biomarker with no core feature. DLB is less likely if another illness explains the picture, or if parkinsonism is the only core feature and first appears in severe dementia.

Indicative biomarkers are reduced basal ganglia uptake on DAT SPECT or PET, low uptake on MIBG myocardial scintigraphy, and REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography. Supportive biomarkers are relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes on CT or MRI, low occipital activity on SPECT or PET with the cingulate island sign on FDG-PET, and prominent posterior slow-wave activity on EEG. CSF α-synuclein seed amplification assays have over 90% sensitivity and specificity, and only autopsy gives a definite diagnosis. DLB is diagnosed when dementia begins before, with, or within 1 year of parkinsonism, and PDD when dementia begins 1 year or more after established Parkinson disease.

DLB mimics

Alzheimer disease is favored by prominent early memory loss and medial temporal atrophy on MRI. Delirium has a sudden onset, an acute illness, and a reversible cause. Vascular dementia shows stepwise decline with vascular risk factors. Frontotemporal dementia occurs at a younger age, with early behavior or language change, and prion disease causes rapid progression with myoclonus. Drug-induced parkinsonism follows recent dopamine-blocking drug use and is assessed with a medication review. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes early falls and vertical gaze palsy.

Management

No treatment slows neuronal loss, so treatment targets each symptom. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, rivastigmine, donepezil, and galantamine, slow ACh breakdown, offsetting cholinergic loss, and improve cognition, function, and hallucinations. Memantine may add benefit for cognition. Parkinsonism is less responsive than in Parkinson disease and is treated with low-dose levodopa, increased slowly. RBD is treated with melatonin, or cautious bedtime clonazepam, and depression with SSRIs, SNRIs, or mirtazapine. Autonomic dysfunction is treated as in other diseases, with little DLB trial data. Falls call for a safety assessment, bone density, and vitamin D.

Antipsychotics are avoided whenever possible, because serious reactions occur in up to 50% of people. If one is essential, low-dose quetiapine is used, though a small trial was negative, and haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, and aripiprazole are generally avoided. Supportive care covers caregiver education, home modifications, physical, occupational, and speech therapy, and early advance care planning.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause progressive dementia, the two pathologies often coexist, and both are treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Prominent early memory loss and medial temporal atrophy favor Alzheimer disease, whereas fluctuations, visual hallucinations, RBD, and parkinsonism favor dementia with Lewy bodies.

. Both involve α-synuclein and parkinsonism. Dementia before, with, or within 1 year of parkinsonism favors dementia with Lewy bodies, whereas dementia 1 year or more after established Parkinson disease is PDD.

Motor Signs and Syndromes

Where motor signs arise

  • ACortex and internal capsuleHemiparesis, supranuclear facial palsy, and apraxia
  • BBrainstemCrossed signs, nuclear facial palsy, and quadriplegia
  • CSpinal cordQuadriplegia from cervical lesions
  • DPeripheral nerveLMN weakness: wrist drop, claw hand, ape hand, and foot drop
  • EBasal gangliaResting tremor, dystonia, chorea, and ballismus
  • FCerebellumGait and limb ataxia and intention tremor; with the red nucleus, rubral tremor
  • GDorsal columnsSensory ataxia with a positive Romberg test

Upper motor neuron weakness

Hemiparesis and hemiplegia

A–C: UMN
Site
Contralateral cortex, internal capsule, or brainstem; ipsilateral if in the cord
Features
Weakness or paralysis of one side, worst in arm extensors and leg flexors; spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign

Involved if the lesion lies above the facial nucleus

Stroke, tumor, trauma, infection, and MS

Hemiparetic: the stiff leg circumducts

Quadriplegia

B–C: UMN; tetraplegia
Site
Cervical cord, or both sides of the brainstem

All four limbs weak; above C5, the diaphragm fails too
Central cord syndrome
The most common incomplete injury: arms weaker than legs, after neck hyperextension with stenosis
Causes
Vehicle collisions, falls, tumors, and degenerative cervical myelopathy

Posturing

A–B: UMN; above or below the red nucleus
Decorticate
Flexed arms with extended legs; a lesion above the red nucleus
Decerebrate
Extension of all limbs; a lesion at or below the red nucleus, in the midbrain or rostral pons
Meaning
Usually a response to noxious stimuli, and a sign of severe brain injury

Supranuclear facial palsy

A: UMN; central
Site
Contralateral cortex or corticobulbar tract
Features
Lower face weak; forehead spared, because the upper face receives input from both hemispheres
With
Hemiparesis, aphasia, or other stroke signs
Bilateral
Pseudobulbar palsy: slurred speech, dysphagia, brisk jaw jerk, and pseudobulbar affect

Lower motor neuron weakness

Nuclear and peripheral facial palsy

B or D: LMN
Site
Ipsilateral facial nucleus in the pons, or CN VII
Features
The whole half of the face, forehead included; hyperacusis, taste loss, and dry eye
Causes
Bell palsy in 38–83%; zoster (Ramsay Hunt), Lyme disease, tumors, Guillain-Barré, and pontine stroke
Bell palsy
Peaks within 72 hours after ear pain; steroids and antivirals, with eye protection
Outcome
70–80% recover untreated; over 95% with prompt treatment

Radial nerve

D: wrist drop
Site
Spiral groove of the humerus, the most common: Saturday night palsy or a humeral shaft fracture; crutches
Features
Cannot extend the wrist, fingers, or thumb; numb dorsoradial hand
Branch
Posterior interosseous nerve at the elbow: purely motor, so sensation is spared
Treatment
Splinting and rehabilitation; surgery if it does not recover

Ulnar nerve

D: claw hand
Site
Cubital tunnel at the elbow, the most common; Guyon canal at the wrist
Features
Tingling of the ring and little fingers; weak grip and pinch, with a Froment sign
Severe
Intrinsic hand wasting and clawing of the ring and little fingers

Median nerve

D: ape hand
Site
Carpal tunnel, the most common; the forearm in 7–10%
Features
Night pain and tingling of the thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring finger; Phalen and Tinel signs
Clue
Thenar sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome, because its branch leaves above the wrist
Severe
Thenar wasting and loss of opposition: ape hand
Risks
Repetitive or vibrating work, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, and obesity
Treatment
Surgical release if severe or refractory

Common peroneal nerve

D: foot drop
Site
Fibular head: leg crossing, casts, kneeling, squatting, surgery positioning, or trauma
Features
Foot drop from weak dorsiflexion and eversion; numb dorsum of the foot and lateral leg; steppage gait
Clue
Inversion is spared, because the tibial nerve supplies it
Mimic
L5 radiculopathy, the most common cause of foot drop, from disc herniation
Treatment
Usually conservative, with an AFO

Note: A pontine stroke also weakens the forehead, but brings other brainstem signs that Bell palsy does not.

Review article

Motor signs and syndromes: localizing weakness, abnormal movements, and nerve lesions

Motor signs localize lesions along a chain from the cortex through the brainstem and spinal cord to the peripheral nerve, with the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and dorsal columns tuning movement alongside. UMN lesions cause spastic weakness with brisk reflexes, whereas LMN lesions cause flaccid weakness with atrophy and fasciculations. Facial palsy that spares the forehead is supranuclear, gait patterns point to their lesion, ataxia separates cerebellar from sensory causes, and tremor type, dystonia, chorea, ballismus, myoclonus, and apraxia each have characteristic sites. Peripheral nerve lesions produce wrist drop, claw hand, ape hand, and foot drop. Here, we review these signs and what they localize.

Key points

  • UMN lesions cause spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign; LMN lesions cause flaccid weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations.
  • Supranuclear facial palsy spares the forehead, whereas nuclear and peripheral palsy weakens the whole half of the face.
  • Midline cerebellar lesions cause gait ataxia, hemispheric lesions cause limb ataxia on the same side, and dorsal column lesions cause sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg test.
  • Resting tremor suggests PD, postural tremor essential tremor, intention tremor the cerebellum, and rubral tremor a midbrain lesion.
  • Hemiballismus classically follows a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus and tends to resolve.
  • Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, ulnar claw hand, median ape hand, and common peroneal foot drop.

Where motor signs arise

Voluntary movement passes from the cortex through the internal capsule and brainstem to the spinal cord and peripheral nerve, while the basal ganglia and cerebellum tune it and the dorsal columns return position sense. UMN lesions, from cortex to cord, cause spastic, velocity-dependent tone, brisk reflexes, a Babinski sign, and weakness worst in arm extensors and leg flexors, as in stroke, MS, and cord injury. LMN lesions, from anterior horn cell to nerve, cause flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, atrophy, and fasciculations in the pattern of a nerve or root, as in polio, SMA, and nerve injury. A UMN lesion above the pyramidal decussation causes contralateral signs, and one below it, in the cord, causes ipsilateral signs.

Upper motor neuron weakness

Hemiparesis and hemiplegia follow lesions of the contralateral cortex, internal capsule, or brainstem, or of the ipsilateral cord, and cause one-sided weakness with spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign; the face is involved if the lesion lies above the facial nucleus. Stroke, tumor, trauma, infection, and MS are causes, and the gait is hemiparetic. Quadriplegia follows cervical cord or bilateral brainstem lesions, and injury above C5 also paralyzes the diaphragm. Decorticate posturing, with flexed arms and extended legs, follows lesions above the red nucleus, and decerebrate posturing, with extension of all limbs, follows lesions at or below it, in the midbrain or rostral pons; both are usually responses to noxious stimuli and signs of severe brain injury. Central cord syndrome, the most common incomplete injury, weakens the arms more than the legs after neck hyperextension with stenosis.

Supranuclear facial palsy, from a contralateral cortical or corticobulbar lesion, weakens the lower face and spares the forehead, which receives input from both hemispheres; bilateral lesions cause pseudobulbar palsy, with slurred speech, dysphagia, a brisk jaw jerk, and pseudobulbar affect.

Lower motor neuron weakness

Nuclear and peripheral facial palsy, from the ipsilateral facial nucleus or CN VII, weakens the whole half of the face, with hyperacusis, taste loss, and dry eye. Bell palsy causes 38–83% of cases and peaks within 72 hours after ear pain; it is treated with steroids, antivirals, and eye protection, and over 95% recover with prompt treatment. A pontine stroke also weakens the forehead but brings other brainstem signs.

Radial nerve injury at the spiral groove of the humerus, from Saturday night palsy, a humeral shaft fracture, or crutches, causes wrist drop with loss of wrist, finger, and thumb extension and a numb dorsoradial hand; posterior interosseous nerve lesions at the elbow are purely motor. Splinting and rehabilitation are the treatment, with surgery if it does not recover. Ulnar nerve compression, most often at the cubital tunnel and also at the Guyon canal, causes tingling of the ring and little fingers, weak grip and pinch with a Froment sign, and, when severe, intrinsic wasting and clawing.

Median nerve compression, most often in the carpal tunnel, causes night pain and tingling of the thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring finger, with Phalen and Tinel signs; thenar sensation is spared because its branch leaves above the wrist, and severe cases cause thenar wasting and ape hand. Repetitive or vibrating work, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, and obesity raise risk, and surgical release treats severe or refractory cases. Common peroneal nerve compression at the fibular head, from leg crossing, casts, kneeling, squatting, surgery positioning, or trauma, causes foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion, a numb dorsum of the foot and lateral leg, and a steppage gait. Inversion, supplied by the tibial nerve, is spared, which separates it from L5 radiculopathy, the most common cause of foot drop. An AFO and conservative care usually suffice.

Erb palsy, a birth traction injury of C5–C6 associated with shoulder dystocia, holds the arm in the waiter's tip position, with the shoulder adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, and wrist flexed, and abolishes the biceps reflex. Klumpke palsy, a C8–T1 injury from hyperabduction traction or an apical lung tumor, causes intrinsic hand weakness and clawing with medial forearm sensory loss, and Horner syndrome if sympathetic fibers are involved. Long thoracic nerve injury weakens the serratus anterior and wings the scapula; axillary nerve injury, from anterior dislocation or a proximal humerus fracture, weakens the deltoid and teres minor and numbs the regimental badge area; and musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm.

Ataxia

Midline vermis lesions cause gait ataxia, with a broad-based gait and truncal sway, from alcohol, drugs such as phenytoin, lithium, and carbamazepine, or degeneration. Hemispheric lesions cause limb ataxia on the same side, with dysmetria, past-pointing, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, rebound, pendular reflexes, scanning speech, and gaze-evoked nystagmus, from posterior circulation stroke, tumor, abscess, or MS. Sensory ataxia follows dorsal column or large-fiber loss, with lost position sense, a stomping gait, pseudoathetosis, and a positive Romberg test, as in B12 deficiency and tabes dorsalis. The Romberg test detects dorsal column disease, because cerebellar ataxia persists with the eyes open.

Tremor

Resting tremor, easing with movement and unilateral at onset, suggests PD. Postural tremor of both hands at 6–12 Hz, sometimes with head and voice tremor, is essential tremor, which is often familial and treated with propranolol or primidone. Intention tremor grows as the hand nears a target and follows cerebellar lesions. Rubral, or Holmes, tremor is slow, under 4.5 Hz, and coarse, and occurs at rest, in posture, and with intention, because midbrain and cerebellothalamic lesions, usually from stroke, disrupt both cerebellar and dopamine pathways; it begins weeks to 2 years after the lesion.

Dystonia, chorea, and ballismus

Dystonia is sustained co-contraction of agonists and antagonists that twists the body into abnormal postures, worsens with action, and eases with a sensory trick. Cervical dystonia is the most common in adults, with blepharospasm and writer's cramp as other focal forms, and early-onset generalized dystonia is linked to DYT1 and DYT6. Antipsychotics and dopa-responsive dystonia are other causes. Botulinum toxin treats focal dystonia, trihexyphenidyl childhood generalized dystonia, and levodopa dopa-responsive dystonia, with baclofen and benzodiazepines as alternatives.

Hemichorea and hemiballismus classically follow a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus. Chorea is irregular, flowing, and dance-like, and ballismus is violent, flinging, and high in amplitude. Ischemic stroke is the most common cause over 65, and nonketotic hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes is another. The movements tend to resolve, and treatment addresses the cause, with haloperidol or risperidone, tetrabenazine, clonazepam, or topiramate. Bilateral chorea with dementia and a family history suggests Huntington disease.

Myoclonus and apraxia

Myoclonus is a sign of sudden, brief, lightning-like jerks. Asterixis is negative myoclonus, brief lapses in tone of the outstretched wrists, as in liver failure. Physiologic myoclonus, such as hiccups, startle, and jerks on falling asleep, needs only reassurance, JME causes morning jerks from puberty, and secondary myoclonus follows hypoxic brain injury, drugs including anticonvulsants, and kidney or liver failure.

Apraxia is loss of learned, skilled movement despite normal strength, sensation, and coordination. Ideational apraxia loses the concept, ideomotor apraxia disconnects concept from output, limb-kinetic apraxia loses fine output, and constructional apraxia impairs drawing and copying. It follows lesions of the dominant parietal and premotor praxis network, occurring in 50–80% of left hemisphere strokes, and is a feature of Alzheimer disease and corticobasal syndrome; physical and occupational therapy are the treatment.

Gait

A spastic hemiparetic gait swings the extended leg in an arc, and a scissor gait, crouched with crossing legs, follows cerebral palsy. A neuropathic steppage gait lifts the foot high and lands on the toes because of foot drop from peroneal, L5, or neuropathic lesions. A cerebellar gait is broad-based and unsteady, a sensory ataxic gait stomps and worsens in the dark, as in B12 deficiency, a festinating gait shuffles with reduced arm swing and freezing in PD, and a waddling gait follows proximal weakness. Most gait disorders are not neurologic, and pain causes an antalgic gait.

Relationships to other conditions

. Stroke is the most common cause of hemiparesis, supranuclear facial palsy, hemiballismus, apraxia, and rubral tremor. A sudden onset in an arterial territory favors stroke.

. Resting tremor and a festinating gait point to Parkinson disease, whereas postural tremor without bradykinesia favors essential tremor.

. Chorea is the hallmark of Huntington disease. Bilateral chorea with dementia and a family history favors it over hemichorea from a focal lesion.

. Corticobasal degeneration causes apraxia, dystonia, and myoclonus, and multiple system atrophy causes cerebellar ataxia. Their combination with parkinsonism favors these disorders.

Typical Parkinson Disease

Pathophysiology

Genetic and environmental factors make α-synuclein aggregate into Lewy bodies, and dopamine neurons of the SNc die, leaving too little dopamine in the striatum to drive movement.

  1. α-synuclein aggregationLewy bodies and Lewy neurites
  2. Neuron stressMitochondria, oxidation, proteasome, glutamate
  3. SNc neuron lossThe substantia nigra loses its pigment
  4. Striatal dopamine lossMotor signs after 50–60% of neurons are lost

What kills dopamine neurons

  • Aα-synuclein aggregationMisfolded α-synuclein forms Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites
  • BMitochondrial dysfunctionMPTP and rotenone accumulate in mitochondria and impair them
  • COxidative stressReactive oxygen species damage the neuron; DJ-1 normally protects mitochondria
  • DUbiquitin-proteasome failureMisfolded proteins are not tagged and cleared; parkin is a ubiquitin ligase
  • EGlutamate excitotoxicityAn overactive subthalamic nucleus floods the SNc with glutamate
  • FDopamine lossLess dopamine reaches the striatum, so movement slows

Pathology

  • DepigmentationLoss of neuromelanin-containing dopamine neurons makes the SNc pale
  • Lewy bodiesα-synuclein-stained inclusions in neuron cell bodies
  • Lewy neuritesα-synuclein inclusions in neuron processes
  • Braak spreadGut, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, and olfactory bulb → locus coeruleus → SNc → cortex

Constipation, RBD, and anosmia can precede motor signs by years, because α-synuclein reaches the gut and brainstem first.

Etiology

  • Genetic
  • 1SNCAThe α-synuclein gene; extra copies cause familial PD
  • 2LRRK2The most common dominant gene; 40% of familial cases
  • 3PRKN, PINK1, and DJ-1Mitochondrial quality control
  • 4GBA1Lysosomal enzyme
  • Environmental
  • 5Pesticides and herbicidesRotenone accumulates in mitochondria
  • 6MPTPTaken up by DAT into dopamine neurons
  • 7Head injuryMild to moderate injury raises risk
  • Age
  • 8AgeAffects 1% of people over 60

Idiopathic PD

  • Gene–toxin interactionIncompletely penetrant genes, such as LRRK2, raise risk most with toxin exposure
  • Known genesExplain only about 3–5% of cases
  • Lower riskSmoking, caffeine, and physical activity

Drug-induced parkinsonism

  • MechanismD2 receptors in the striatum are blocked, or dopamine is depleted
  • Dopamine blockersFirst-generation antipsychotics, especially haloperidol and fluphenazine; risperidone and olanzapine more than quetiapine and clozapine; metoclopramide and prochlorperazine
  • Dopamine depletersVMAT2 inhibitors: tetrabenazine and reserpine
  • CluesSymmetric, widespread signs after starting the drug; normal DAT SPECT; most common at ages 60–80

Symptoms and complications

Motor features

  • BradykinesiaSlow movement with decreasing amplitude; the core feature
  • Rest tremorUnilateral at onset and reemerges at rest; not required
  • RigidityLead pipe or cogwheel; reduced arm swing
  • Postural instabilityLate; festination, freezing, and falls

Non-motor features

  • ProdromalConstipation, RBD, and anosmia
  • AutonomicOrthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, dysphagia, and erectile dysfunction
  • PsychiatricDepression and anxiety; dementia and psychosis later

Complications

  • Motor fluctuations'Off' periods as levodopa wears off
  • DyskinesiaLevodopa-induced involuntary movements
  • Impulse control disorderMainly with dopamine agonists
  • FallsFrom postural instability and freezing

Diagnosis

  1. Clinical diagnosisHistory and examination
  2. ParkinsonismBradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity
  3. Exclusions and red flagsNone, or red flags balanced
  4. Supportive criteriaStrengthen the diagnosis
  5. DAT SPECTIf unclear

MDS criteria (2015)

Clinically probable PD needs parkinsonism, no absolute exclusion criteria, and any red flags balanced by supportive criteria. Clinically established PD needs at least 2 supportive criteria and no red flags.

Absolute exclusion criteria
  • Cerebellar abnormalities
  • Downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy
  • bvFTD or primary progressive aphasia
  • Parkinsonism limited to the legs for over 3 years
  • No response to high-dose levodopa
  • Cortical sensory loss, limb apraxia, or progressive aphasia
  • Normal DAT imaging
Red flags
  • Wheelchair within 5 years
  • No progression over 5 years
  • Early severe bulbar dysfunction
  • Inspiratory stridor
  • Severe autonomic failure within 5 years
  • Recurrent falls within 3 years
  • Disproportionate anterocollis
  • No non-motor features after 5 years
  • Unexplained pyramidal signs
Supportive criteria
  • Clear, dramatic response to dopaminergic therapy
  • Levodopa-induced dyskinesia
  • Rest tremor of a limb
  • Olfactory loss or cardiac MIBG denervation

DAT imaging

  • ¹²³I-ioflupane SPECTShows presynaptic dopamine transporters in the striatum
  • Reduced uptakeDopamine loss: PD, MSA, PSP, CBD, and DLB
  • Normal uptakeEssential tremor, drug-induced, and vascular parkinsonism

Atypical parkinsonism and mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Progressive supranuclear palsyVertical gaze palsy and early fallsClinical examination

Corticobasal degenerationAsymmetric apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limbClinical examination

Essential tremorBilateral postural or action tremorDAT SPECT if unclear

A clear response to levodopa supports PD; a poor response suggests another diagnosis.

Treatment

No treatment slows PD, so treatment restores dopamine signaling and manages symptoms.

Dopaminergic drugs

  • Levodopa with carbidopaLevodopa crosses the BBB and becomes dopamine; carbidopa blocks peripheral conversion; the most effective drug
  • PramipexoleDopamine agonist, selective for D3 receptors
  • RasagilineSelective MAO-B inhibitor; MAO-B is the main form in the brain
  • EntacaponeCOMT inhibitor that prolongs each levodopa dose

Other drugs

  • AmantadineA weak NMDA antagonist that increases dopamine release and blocks its reuptake; eases bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, often briefly
  • AnticholinergicsTrihexyphenidyl blocks muscarinic receptors; mainly for tremor; dry mouth and other anticholinergic effects
  • Drug-induced parkinsonismStop the causative drug; an atypical antipsychotic if one is still needed; anticholinergics such as benztropine

Treatment complications

  • Wearing off'On' time shortens as neurons are lost; add entacapone or extended-release levodopa
  • Impulse control disorderGambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping, and binge eating; reduce or stop the agonist
  • Refractory motor fluctuationsDBS

Non-motor symptoms

  • ConstipationPEG
  • Depression and anxietySSRIs
  • DementiaCholinesterase inhibitors
  • PsychosisPimavanserin or other antipsychotics
  • Impulsive behaviorCognitive behavior therapy

Note: Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole are the main trigger of impulse control disorders.

Review article

Parkinson disease: α-synuclein, dopamine neuron loss, and dopaminergic treatment

Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which α-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies and dopamine neurons of the SNc die, depleting dopamine in the striatum. Genetic factors, such as SNCA and LRRK2, interact with environmental exposures, such as pesticides and MPTP, and with age. Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, failure of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and glutamate excitotoxicity drive neuron loss. Diagnosis is clinical, by the MDS criteria, with DAT SPECT when unclear, and treatment restores dopamine signaling, because no treatment slows the disease. Here, we review these mechanisms, the symptoms they produce, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how Parkinson disease relates to other neurologic conditions.

Key points

  • Lewy bodies are α-synuclein-stained inclusions, and the SNc loses its pigment as dopamine neurons die.
  • Motor signs appear once 50–60% of nigrostriatal neurons are lost.
  • Parkinsonism means bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity.
  • The MDS criteria weigh absolute exclusions, red flags, and supportive criteria.
  • Levodopa with carbidopa is the most effective treatment, and dopamine agonists cause impulse control disorders.

Pathophysiology

Genetic and environmental factors make α-synuclein aggregate into Lewy bodies, and dopamine neurons of the SNc die, leaving too little dopamine in the striatum to drive movement. Motor signs appear once 50–60% of nigrostriatal neurons are lost.

Several mechanisms kill dopamine neurons. Misfolded α-synuclein forms Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. MPTP and rotenone accumulate in mitochondria and impair them. Reactive oxygen species cause oxidative stress, which DJ-1 normally counters by protecting mitochondria. Failure of the ubiquitin-proteasome system leaves misfolded proteins uncleared, and parkin is a ubiquitin ligase in this system. An overactive subthalamic nucleus floods the SNc with glutamate, causing excitotoxicity.

Loss of neuromelanin-containing dopamine neurons makes the SNc pale. Lewy bodies are α-synuclein-stained inclusions in neuron cell bodies, and Lewy neurites are inclusions in neuron processes. By Braak staging, pathology spreads from the gut, the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, and the olfactory bulb to the locus coeruleus, the SNc, and finally the cortex, so constipation, RBD, and anosmia can precede motor signs by years.

Etiology

SNCA, the α-synuclein gene, causes familial PD when extra copies are present. LRRK2 is the most common dominant gene, accounting for 40% of familial cases, and PRKN, PINK1, and DJ-1 serve mitochondrial quality control, while GBA1 encodes a lysosomal enzyme. Environmental factors include pesticides and herbicides, such as rotenone, MPTP, which is taken up by DAT into dopamine neurons, and mild to moderate head injury. Age is a major factor, and PD affects 1% of people over 60.

Most PD is idiopathic: incompletely penetrant genes, such as LRRK2, raise risk most with toxin exposure, and known genes explain only about 3–5% of cases. Drug-induced parkinsonism follows D2 receptor blockade in the striatum, by first-generation antipsychotics, especially haloperidol and fluphenazine, by risperidone and olanzapine more than quetiapine and clozapine, and by metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, or dopamine depletion by the VMAT2 inhibitors tetrabenazine and reserpine. Its signs are symmetric and widespread after starting the drug, DAT SPECT is normal, and it is most common at ages 60–80. Smoking, caffeine, and physical activity are linked to lower risk.

Clinical presentation

Bradykinesia, slow movement with decreasing amplitude, is the core feature. Rest tremor is unilateral at onset and reemerges at rest but is not required. Rigidity is lead pipe or cogwheel, with reduced arm swing, and postural instability, with festination, freezing, and falls, appears late.

Non-motor features include prodromal constipation, RBD, and anosmia; autonomic orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, dysphagia, and erectile dysfunction; and depression and anxiety, with dementia and psychosis later. Complications are motor fluctuations, with 'off' periods as levodopa wears off, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, impulse control disorders, mainly with dopamine agonists, and falls.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is clinical. Parkinsonism means bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity. By the 2015 MDS criteria, clinically probable PD needs parkinsonism, no absolute exclusion criteria, and any red flags balanced by supportive criteria, and clinically established PD needs at least 2 supportive criteria and no red flags.

Absolute exclusion criteria are cerebellar abnormalities, downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, bvFTD or primary progressive aphasia, parkinsonism limited to the legs for over 3 years, no response to high-dose levodopa, cortical sensory loss, limb apraxia, or progressive aphasia, and normal DAT imaging. Red flags are a wheelchair within 5 years, no progression over 5 years, early severe bulbar dysfunction, inspiratory stridor, severe autonomic failure within 5 years, recurrent falls within 3 years, disproportionate anterocollis, no non-motor features after 5 years, and unexplained pyramidal signs. Supportive criteria are a clear, dramatic response to dopaminergic therapy, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor of a limb, and olfactory loss or cardiac MIBG denervation.

¹²³I-ioflupane SPECT shows presynaptic dopamine transporters in the striatum. Uptake is reduced with dopamine loss, in PD, MSA, PSP, CBD, and DLB, and normal in essential tremor and drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism. A clear response to levodopa supports PD, and a poor response suggests another diagnosis.

Atypical parkinsonism and mimics

Progressive supranuclear palsy causes vertical gaze palsy and early falls. Multiple system atrophy causes early autonomic failure, with cerebellar and pyramidal signs, and corticobasal degeneration causes asymmetric apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limb. Dementia with Lewy bodies brings early dementia and visual hallucinations. Drug-induced parkinsonism follows dopamine-blocking drugs, and essential tremor causes a bilateral postural or action tremor; both have normal DAT imaging.

Management

No treatment slows PD, so treatment restores dopamine signaling and manages symptoms. Levodopa crosses the BBB and becomes dopamine, and carbidopa blocks its peripheral conversion; together they are the most effective treatment. Pramipexole is a dopamine agonist, selective for D3 receptors, rasagiline is a selective MAO-B inhibitor, and entacapone is a COMT inhibitor that prolongs each levodopa dose.

Amantadine, a weak NMDA antagonist, increases dopamine release and blocks its reuptake, easing bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, often only briefly. Anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl block muscarinic receptors and mainly help tremor, at the cost of dry mouth and other anticholinergic effects. Drug-induced parkinsonism is treated by stopping the causative drug, using an atypical antipsychotic if one is still needed, and anticholinergics such as benztropine.

As neurons are lost, 'on' time shortens, and entacapone or extended-release levodopa is added. Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole are the main trigger of impulse control disorders, including gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping, and binge eating, which call for reducing or stopping the agonist. DBS treats refractory motor fluctuations. Non-motor symptoms are treated with PEG for constipation, SSRIs for depression and anxiety, cholinesterase inhibitors for dementia, pimavanserin or other antipsychotics for psychosis, and cognitive behavior therapy for impulsive behavior.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both involve α-synuclein, Lewy bodies, and parkinsonism. Dementia before, with, or within 1 year of parkinsonism favors dementia with Lewy bodies, whereas dementia 1 year or more after established Parkinson disease is Parkinson disease dementia.

. Progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, and corticobasal degeneration also cause parkinsonism with reduced DAT uptake, but they respond poorly to levodopa and add features such as vertical gaze palsy, early autonomic failure, or asymmetric apraxia.

Atypical Parkinsonism

Pathophysiology

An abnormal protein collects in neurons and glia, and the cells of the basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum, or cortex die, causing parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa.

  1. Protein aggregationα-synuclein in MSA; 4R tau in PSP and CBD
  2. Neuron and glia lossBeyond the substantia nigra
  3. Parkinsonism plus other signsAutonomic, cerebellar, gaze, or cortical
  4. Poor levodopa responseStriatal targets are lost too

Which protein collects

  • Aα-synucleinPD and DLB in neurons; MSA in oligodendrocytes
  • BAβ plus 3R and 4R tauAD; its tangles mix both tau forms
  • C4R tauPSP and CBD, in neurons and astrocytes
  • DTDP-43MND and LATE, and about half of FTLD

Pathology

ForInclusionsWhere
Multiple system atrophyGCIs of α-synuclein in oligodendrocytes, with widespread neuron lossPutamen, pons, MCP, and cerebellum; increased putaminal iron
Progressive supranuclear palsyNeuronal and glial 4R tau; tufted astrocytesBasal ganglia and brainstem, with variable cortex
Corticobasal degenerationNeuronal and glial 4R tau; astrocytic plaques and ballooned neuronsPosterior frontal and anterior parietal cortex and basal ganglia, asymmetric

Note: Lewy bodies sit in neurons, but the α-synuclein of MSA collects mainly in oligodendrocytes.

Causes

  • Family historyParkinsonism or ataxia in relatives argues against MSA
  • Prion-like spreadMisfolded tau seeds neighboring cells in CBD

1. Multiple system atrophy

Treatment

No treatment slows MSA, PSP, or CBD, so all three are treated the same way, by symptom.

Motor symptoms

  • ParkinsonismLevodopa trial, up to 900–1200 mg daily for at least a month; taper if there is no benefit
  • DystoniaBotulinum toxin if focal; baclofen or clonazepam
  • Falls and gaitPhysical and occupational therapy with balance training
  • DBSNot recommended in PSP

Non-motor symptoms

  • Orthostatic hypotensionMidodrine or fludrocortisone
  • Urinary dysfunctionα-blockers, mirabegron, or selective antimuscarinics
  • ConstipationFiber, fluids, and osmotic laxatives
  • RBDMelatonin, then low-dose clonazepam
  • SialorrheaBotulinum toxin
  • Dysphagia and speechEarly speech pathology referral
  • CognitionCholinesterase inhibitors, which may worsen motor function in PSP

Care

  • TeamNeurology, physical, occupational, and speech therapy
  • Palliative careEarly advance care planning, then hospice

Note: A clear levodopa response points back toward typical PD.
