Review article

Atypical parkinsonism: multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, and corticobasal degeneration

Atypical parkinsonism describes neurodegenerative disorders that cause parkinsonism with a poor response to levodopa and additional signs. Multiple system atrophy is an α-synucleinopathy with GCIs in oligodendrocytes, whereas progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration are 4R tauopathies. Each damages a characteristic pattern of structures, producing early autonomic failure and cerebellar signs, vertical gaze palsy and early falls, or asymmetric cortical signs. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI patterns, and treatment is symptomatic. Here, we review the proteinopathies, clinical features, imaging, and management of these disorders.

Key points

  • α-synuclein collects in PD, DLB, and MSA, 4R tau in PSP and CBD, Aβ with 3R and 4R tau in AD, and TDP-43 in MND and LATE.
  • MSA presents with parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, or pyramidal signs, with early autonomic failure.
  • PSP causes vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, early falls, akinesia, and cognitive dysfunction.
  • CBD causes asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, and myoclonus with apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limb.
  • The hot cross bun sign suggests MSA, and midbrain atrophy suggests PSP.
  • No treatment slows these disorders, so all three are treated by symptom.

Pathophysiology

An abnormal protein collects in neurons and glia, and cells of the basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum, or cortex die, causing parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa because striatal targets are lost too.

Neurodegenerative diseases can be grouped by the protein that collects. α-synuclein collects in PD and DLB in neurons and in MSA in oligodendrocytes. AD combines Aβ with tangles that mix 3R and 4R tau. PSP and CBD are 4R tauopathies affecting neurons and astrocytes. TDP-43 collects in MND, LATE, and about half of FTLD.

In MSA, GCIs of α-synuclein in oligodendrocytes accompany widespread neuron loss in the putamen, pons, MCP, and cerebellum, with increased putaminal iron. In PSP, neuronal and glial 4R tau, including tufted astrocytes, affects the basal ganglia and brainstem, with variable cortical involvement. In CBD, neuronal and glial 4R tau, astrocytic plaques, and ballooned neurons affect the posterior frontal and anterior parietal cortex and basal ganglia asymmetrically.

Etiology

All three disorders are sporadic, and their causes are unknown. A family history of parkinsonism or ataxia argues against MSA. In CBD, misfolded tau is thought to spread from cell to cell in a prion-like manner, seeding further pathology.

Clinical presentation

MSA presents with parkinsonism (MSA-P), with bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and postural instability, from striatonigral degeneration; with cerebellar signs (MSA-C), including gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and nystagmus, from olivopontocerebellar atrophy; or with both, and pyramidal signs, such as hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign, are common. MSA-P accounts for 70–80% of cases in Western populations, whereas MSA-C accounts for 67–84% in Asian populations and begins earlier. Its features include early autonomic failure, with orthostatic hypotension, urinary dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction, a poor levodopa response, dysphagia, hypometric saccades, falls, myoclonus, RBD, which often comes first, and stridor and sleep apnea.

The hallmark of PSP is vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, beginning with slow vertical saccades, with downgaze affected before upgaze. Postural instability causes early backward falls with a stiff, upright gait, and akinesia is symmetric and axial. Cognitive dysfunction includes apathy, disinhibition, and executive dysfunction. The 2017 MDS criteria describe subtypes: PSP-RS, the classic form, with gaze palsy, early falls, and cognitive change, leads to death about 7 years from onset; PSP-P, which may respond to levodopa, and PSP-PAGF, with gait freezing, allow survival of a decade or more; and cortical variants include PSP-CBS, PSP-bvFTD, and PSP-PNFA.

CBD causes asymmetric limb rigidity or akinesia, dystonia, and myoclonus, with cortical signs: limb apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limb. Nonfluent aphasia and executive dysfunction can occur.

Complications include falls with head injury, dysphagia with aspiration pneumonia, and, in MSA, stridor and sleep apnea from vocal cord paralysis. Patients with PSP become dependent within 3–4 years, and median survival in CBD is about 8 years.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is clinical: parkinsonism with red flags and a poor or short-lived response to a levodopa trial. MRI shows the pattern of atrophy, and DAT SPECT is reduced in all three, as in PD, so it does not separate them from PD. Only autopsy confirms the protein.

Early autonomic failure, cerebellar or pyramidal signs, and stridor favor MSA, in which MRI shows the hot cross bun sign in the pons, atrophy of the putamen, MCP, pons, and cerebellum, and putaminal iron. Vertical gaze palsy and early falls favor PSP, in which MRI shows midbrain atrophy, the hummingbird sign. Asymmetric apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limb favor CBD, in which MRI shows asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy and FDG-PET shows asymmetric hypometabolism. Probable CBS is asymmetric, with 2 of limb rigidity or akinesia, limb dystonia, and limb myoclonus, plus 2 of orobuccal or limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficit, and alien limb; possible CBS may be symmetric, with 1 of each. CBS is not specific, since PSP, AD, and other pathologies can cause it.

Management

No treatment slows MSA, PSP, or CBD, so all three are treated the same way, by symptom. Parkinsonism is treated with a levodopa trial of up to 900–1200 mg daily for at least a month, tapered if there is no benefit. Focal dystonia is treated with botulinum toxin, with baclofen or clonazepam as alternatives, and falls with physical and occupational therapy and balance training. DBS is not recommended in PSP.

Orthostatic hypotension is treated with midodrine or fludrocortisone, urinary dysfunction with α-blockers, mirabegron, or selective antimuscarinics, and constipation with fiber, fluids, and osmotic laxatives. RBD is treated with melatonin, then low-dose clonazepam, and sialorrhea with botulinum toxin. Early speech pathology referral addresses dysphagia and speech, and cholinesterase inhibitors may help cognition but can worsen motor function in PSP. Care involves neurology and physical, occupational, and speech therapy, with early advance care planning and later hospice.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause parkinsonism with reduced DAT uptake. A clear, lasting levodopa response and rest tremor favor typical Parkinson disease, whereas a poor response with early autonomic failure, gaze palsy, early falls, or asymmetric cortical signs favors atypical parkinsonism.

. Both are α-synucleinopathies when the atypical disorder is MSA. Early dementia and visual hallucinations favor dementia with Lewy bodies.

. PSP and CBD are tauopathies that overlap with FTLD and can cause behavior and language change. Behavior or language change first, without early parkinsonism, favors frontotemporal dementia.

Huntington Disease

Pathophysiology

An expanded CAG repeat in HTT adds a polyglutamine stretch to huntingtin, which kills the medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen; loss of the indirect pathway releases the thalamus, causing chorea, with psychiatric change and dementia.

  1. CAG expansion in HTTChromosome 4p16.3
  2. Polyglutamine huntingtinToxic gain and loss of function; nuclear inclusions
  3. Striatal neuron lossOver 90% of GABA medium spiny neurons
  4. Chorea, then hypokinesiaWith psychiatric change and dementia

Basal ganglia circuit

  • ACortexDrives the striatum with glutamate
  • BIndirect-pathway neuronsEnkephalin neurons projecting to the GPe; lost first
  • CGPe, STN, and GPiThe GPi inhibits the thalamus less
  • DThalamusReleased, it overdrives the cortex: chorea
  • EDirect-pathway neuronsProjecting to the GPi; lost later: rigidity and bradykinesia

Course of degeneration

  • Where it startsThe tail and head of the caudate and the dorsal putamen
  • DirectionDorsomedial to ventrolateral, and caudal to rostral
  • Grade 0No visible change; some neuron loss in the caudate head
  • Grades 1–250% of caudate head neurons lost; the caudate still bulges into the ventricle
  • Grades 3–4The caudate flattens, then becomes concave, with 95% of its neurons lost
  • LaterCortex, globus pallidus, cerebellum, amygdala, and hippocampus

Note: The Vonsattel grade tracks clinical disability, and caudate atrophy tracks repeat length and motor score.

Etiology

  • 126 or fewerNormal
  • 227–35, intermediateNo disease, but unstable: can expand into the disease range in children
  • 336–39, reduced penetranceMay or may not cause disease
  • 440 or moreAlmost always causes disease; longer repeats bring earlier onset
  • 5Over 55Juvenile onset, usually over 60

Inheritance

  • Autosomal dominantEach child of an affected parent has a 50% chance
  • AnticipationRepeats lengthen during spermatogenesis, so onset comes earlier when inherited from the father
  • No family historyEarly parental death, late onset in the parent, an intermediate allele, or an unrecognized diagnosis
  • HomozygotesSimilar onset, but faster progression

Who gets it

  • Prevalence2.7 per 100000 worldwide; 10.6–13.7 per 100000 in people of European descent
  • OnsetMean age 45

Symptoms and complications

Clinical triad

  • MotorChorea, starting distally and spreading to the face, trunk, and proximal limbs; later bradykinesia, dystonia, and rigidity; dysarthria, dysphagia, and falls
  • PsychiatricOften first: irritability, impulsivity, and aggression; apathy, the most common feature; depression; psychosis late; little insight
  • CognitiveExecutive dysfunction first; a subcortical dementia with slow retrieval, sparing aphasia and apraxia

Stages

  • PresymptomaticGene positive, no signs; imaging may change
  • ProdromalSubtle motor and cognitive signs, apathy, and depression
  • ManifestMotor and cognitive signs that impair daily life

Variants

  • JuvenileBefore age 20: rigidity and bradykinesia (Westphal variant), dystonia, learning difficulty, and seizures in 30–50% before age 10
  • Late onsetAfter 50 in about 25%: chorea and gait problems, with a milder, longer course

Complications

  • Aspiration pneumoniaThe most common cause of death
  • SuicideThe second cause of death; about 25% attempt it
  • SurvivalMedian 15–18 years from onset

Diagnosis

  1. Family history and triadChorea with behavior or cognitive change
  2. Genetic testingCAG repeat length; the gold standard
  3. MRIEarly caudate atrophy, even before symptoms

Testing

  • Predictive testingFor at-risk adults, with genetic counseling
  • PrenatalChorionic villus sampling at 10–12 weeks or amniocentesis at 15–17 weeks
  • Imaging courseCaudate first; cortex and cerebellum later

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain

Treatment

No treatment slows HD, so treatment targets symptoms.

Chorea

Tetrabenazine VMAT2 inhibitor
  1. TargetVMAT2 on presynaptic vesicles
  2. MechanismBlocks loading of dopamine into vesicles
  3. ResponseLess dopamine release; less chorea
  • VMAT2 inhibitorsTetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, and valbenazine; first line; can cause depression, suicidality, fatigue, and akathisia
  • AntipsychoticsOff label: olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, or aripiprazole, which matches tetrabenazine; extrapyramidal effects and tardive dyskinesia

Review article

Huntington disease: CAG repeat expansion, striatal degeneration, and chorea

Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in HTT, which adds a polyglutamine stretch to huntingtin. Medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen degenerate, indirect-pathway neurons first, causing chorea, followed by hypokinesia, psychiatric change, and a subcortical dementia. Repeat length predicts penetrance and age of onset, and anticipation follows paternal transmission. Diagnosis rests on genetic testing, and treatment is symptomatic, with VMAT2 inhibitors such as tetrabenazine for chorea. Here, we review the genetics, pathology, clinical course, diagnosis, and treatment of Huntington disease.

Key points

  • HD is autosomal dominant: 36–39 CAG repeats have reduced penetrance, and 40 or more almost always cause disease.
  • Anticipation occurs mainly with paternal transmission, because repeats lengthen in spermatogenesis.
  • Indirect-pathway medium spiny neurons are lost first, causing chorea; direct-pathway loss later causes rigidity.
  • Degeneration starts in the caudate and dorsal putamen and spreads dorsomedial to ventrolateral; the Vonsattel grade tracks disability.
  • Tetrabenazine inhibits VMAT2, reducing dopamine release and chorea, but can worsen depression.
  • Aspiration pneumonia is the most common cause of death, followed by suicide.

Pathophysiology

An expanded CAG repeat in HTT, on chromosome 4p16.3, adds a polyglutamine stretch to huntingtin, which causes both a toxic gain and a loss of function and forms nuclear inclusions. Over 90% of the GABA medium spiny neurons of the striatum degenerate. Indirect-pathway neurons, which contain enkephalin and project to the GPe, are lost first, so the GPi inhibits the thalamus less and the released thalamus overdrives the cortex, causing chorea. Direct-pathway neurons, projecting to the GPi, are lost later, causing rigidity and bradykinesia.

Degeneration starts in the tail and head of the caudate and the dorsal putamen and proceeds dorsomedial to ventrolateral and caudal to rostral. By Vonsattel grade, grade 0 shows no visible change, grades 1–2 show 50% loss of caudate head neurons with the caudate still convex, and grades 3–4 show a flat, then concave caudate, with 95% of its neurons lost. The cortex, globus pallidus, cerebellum, amygdala, and hippocampus are affected later. The grade tracks clinical disability, and caudate atrophy tracks repeat length and motor score.

Etiology

HD is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Repeats of 26 or fewer are normal, and 27–35 cause no disease but are unstable and can expand in children. Repeats of 36–39 have reduced penetrance, 40 or more almost always cause disease, with longer repeats bringing earlier onset, and over 55, usually over 60, cause juvenile disease. Repeats lengthen during spermatogenesis, so anticipation occurs mainly with paternal transmission. The family history can be negative after early parental death, late onset in the parent, an intermediate allele, or an unrecognized diagnosis, and homozygotes have a similar onset but faster progression.

Prevalence is 2.7 per 100000 worldwide and 10.6–13.7 per 100000 in people of European descent, and mean onset is at 45 years.

Clinical presentation

Chorea starts distally and spreads to the face, trunk, and proximal limbs, and later gives way to bradykinesia, dystonia, and rigidity, with dysarthria, dysphagia, and falls. Psychiatric change often comes first, with irritability, impulsivity, and aggression; apathy is the most common feature, depression is frequent, psychosis appears late, and insight is poor. Cognitive change begins with executive dysfunction and progresses to a subcortical dementia with slow retrieval that spares aphasia and apraxia.

The disease passes from presymptomatic, gene positive without signs, through prodromal, with subtle motor and cognitive signs, apathy, and depression, to manifest, when signs impair daily life. Juvenile disease, before age 20, causes rigidity and bradykinesia (the Westphal variant), dystonia, learning difficulty, and seizures in 30–50% before age 10. Late-onset disease, after 50 in about 25%, causes chorea and gait problems with a milder, longer course. Aspiration pneumonia is the most common cause of death, followed by suicide, which about 25% attempt, and median survival is 15–18 years from onset.

Diagnosis

A family history with chorea and behavioral or cognitive change suggests HD, and genetic testing of CAG repeat length is the gold standard. MRI shows early caudate atrophy, even before symptoms, with cortical and cerebellar atrophy later. Predictive testing is offered to at-risk adults with genetic counseling, and prenatal testing uses chorionic villus sampling at 10–12 weeks or amniocentesis at 15–17 weeks.

Chorea-acanthocytosis, autosomal recessive, causes orofacial chorea worse with eating, tongue biting, myopathy, and onset around 30, with acanthocytes on the blood film. McLeod syndrome, X-linked, causes acanthocytes, hemolysis, and myopathy, with absent Kell antigen. Wilson disease causes orofacial dystonia with parkinsonism, and spinocerebellar ataxias cause prominent ataxia; marked ataxia points away from HD.

Management

No treatment slows HD, so treatment targets symptoms. Tetrabenazine inhibits VMAT2 on presynaptic vesicles, blocking the loading of dopamine and reducing its release, which lessens chorea. Tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, and valbenazine are first line but can cause depression, suicidality, fatigue, and akathisia, so mood and suicidal thoughts are monitored. Antipsychotics are used off label, with aripiprazole matching tetrabenazine, at the cost of extrapyramidal effects and tardive dyskinesia.

Rigidity in the Westphal variant is treated with levodopa, dopamine agonists, or amantadine, and focal dystonia with botulinum toxin. Depression, anxiety, and OCD are treated with SSRIs or TCAs, with limited evidence, and no drug helps cognition. Supportive care covers diet, nursing, and equipment, smoking and alcohol are avoided, and patients and families receive counseling and genetic counseling.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both disturb the basal ganglia, in opposite directions. Loss of indirect-pathway neurons in HD causes excess movement, whereas dopamine loss in Parkinson disease causes too little; the Westphal variant of HD, with rigidity, responds to the same antiparkinsonian drugs.

. Both cause dementia. HD causes a subcortical dementia with slow retrieval that spares aphasia and apraxia, whereas Alzheimer disease causes a cortical dementia with early memory loss.

Localizing a Lesion

Approach

Each finding points to a level, from cortex to muscle, and a side; when every finding fits one site, the lesion is there, and when they cannot, several lesions or a diffuse process is more likely.

  1. LevelCortex, capsule, brainstem, cord, nerve, or muscle
  2. SideSame side or opposite
  3. One site?Do all findings fit together?
  4. Then the causeOnset and course narrow it
  • Sudden onset in an arterial territoryStroke
  • Lesions separated in space and timeMultiple sclerosis
  • Symptoms that spread over minutesMigraine aura or a seizure march
  • Gradual onset, or feverTumor or abscess

Weakness and sensory loss

Crossed or uncrossed

  • ACortex or internal capsuleOpposite face, arm, and leg; with aphasia, neglect, or field loss if the cortex is involved, and pure motor or sensory loss if the lesion is small and deep
  • BBrainstemCrossed signs: a cranial nerve palsy on the side of the lesion, with weakness of the opposite body
  • CSpinal cordThe face is spared; weakness on the same side below the lesion, with a sensory level; hemisection adds opposite pain and temperature loss
  • DNerve or rootLMN weakness and sensory loss in the pattern of one nerve or dermatome

Homunculus

  • Leg more than armMedial cortex, in the ACA territory
  • Face and arm more than legLateral cortex, in the MCA territory
  • Face, arm, and leg equallyInternal capsule, where the fibers are packed together
  • Symptoms spreading to the next body partA Jacksonian march: a seizure spreading along the cortex
  • Proximal arm and shoulder, sparing hand and faceMCA/ACA watershed: the man-in-a-barrel pattern if bilateral

UMN or LMN

  • UMNSpasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign; weakness worst in arm extensors and leg flexors
  • LMNFlaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, atrophy, and fasciculations in one nerve or root
  • Above the pyramidal decussationSigns on the opposite side
  • Below it, in the cordSigns on the same side

Note: The face is involved only by lesions above the facial nucleus, so facial weakness rules out a cord lesion.

Review article

Localizing a neurologic lesion: from signs to level and side

Each neurologic finding points to a level of the nervous system, from cortex to muscle, and to a side, and a lesion is localized where all the findings fit together; when they cannot, several lesions or a diffuse process is more likely. Crossed signs place a lesion in the brainstem, the homunculus separates ACA from MCA territory, and cranial nerve, pupil, eye movement, nystagmus, and visual field patterns pinpoint the level. Cortical and diencephalic signs, headache features, and gait add further clues. Here, we review how to move from the signs to the site.

Key points

  • A lesion is localized where every finding fits; findings that cannot fit one site suggest several lesions or a diffuse process.
  • A cranial nerve palsy with weakness of the opposite body places the lesion in the brainstem at the level of that nerve.
  • Leg weakness more than arm points to the medial ACA territory, face and arm more than leg to the lateral MCA territory, and equal weakness to the internal capsule.
  • Central nystagmus changes direction, is vertical or purely torsional, and is not suppressed by fixation.
  • A thunderclap headache, a new headache over 50, and papilledema each call for urgent investigation.

Approach

Each finding points to a level, from cortex to muscle, and a side; when every finding fits one site, the lesion is there, and when they cannot, several lesions or a diffuse process is more likely. Localization proceeds from level to side, then asks whether all findings fit together, before onset and course narrow the cause. Sudden onset in an arterial territory suggests stroke, lesions separated in space and time suggest multiple sclerosis, symptoms that spread over minutes suggest a migraine aura or a seizure march, and gradual onset or fever suggests a tumor or abscess.

Weakness and sensory loss

A cortical or internal capsule lesion weakens the opposite face, arm, and leg, with aphasia, neglect, or field loss if the cortex is involved, and pure motor or sensory loss if the lesion is small and deep. A brainstem lesion causes crossed signs, a cranial nerve palsy on the side of the lesion with weakness of the opposite body. A spinal cord lesion spares the face and weakens the same side below it, with a sensory level, and hemisection adds opposite pain and temperature loss. A nerve or root lesion causes LMN weakness and sensory loss in the pattern of one nerve or dermatome.

In the homunculus, the leg lies on the medial cortex in the ACA territory, and the arm, hand, and face lie on the lateral cortex in the MCA territory, so leg weakness more than arm points to the ACA, face and arm more than leg to the MCA, and equal weakness of face, arm, and leg to the internal capsule, where the fibers are packed together. Symptoms spreading to the next body part are a Jacksonian march, a seizure spreading along the cortex, and proximal arm and shoulder weakness sparing the hand and face is the MCA/ACA watershed pattern, the man-in-a-barrel pattern if bilateral.

UMN lesions cause spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign, with weakness worst in arm extensors and leg flexors, whereas LMN lesions cause flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, atrophy, and fasciculations in one nerve or root. A lesion above the pyramidal decussation causes signs on the opposite side, and one below it, in the cord, on the same side. The face is involved only by lesions above the facial nucleus, so facial weakness rules out a cord lesion.

Cranial nerves

A CN III palsy with a dilated pupil suggests compression, as by a PComm aneurysm or uncal herniation, whereas one sparing the pupil suggests microvascular ischemia, as in diabetes. A CN IV palsy, with the head tilted away, often follows trauma, and a CN VI palsy can be a false localizing sign of raised ICP or reflect a pontine lesion. Weakness of the whole half of the face, forehead included, localizes to the facial nucleus or nerve on that side, as in Bell palsy, whereas lower facial weakness sparing the forehead localizes to the opposite cortex or corticobulbar tract.

The jaw deviates toward a CN V lesion, the uvula away from a CN X lesion, and the tongue toward a CN XII lesion. CN V, VII, and VIII together point to the cerebellopontine angle, as with a vestibular schwannoma; CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI together to the cavernous sinus; and CN IX, X, and XI together to the jugular foramen. A brisk jaw jerk with slurred speech and dysphagia is pseudobulbar palsy from bilateral corticobulbar lesions. A cranial nerve palsy with weakness of the opposite body places the lesion in the brainstem, at the level of that nerve.

Eyes and pupils

A small pupil with mild ptosis and anhidrosis is Horner syndrome, from a lesion anywhere along the sympathetic pathway, from hypothalamus and brainstem to cord, lung apex, and carotid. A large pupil with ptosis and an eye turned down and out is a CN III palsy. Pupils that constrict to a near target but not to light show light-near dissociation, from an Adie pupil or the dorsal midbrain, and a pupil that dilates with the swinging light test has an RAPD from an optic nerve lesion, as in optic neuritis.

Double vision that goes when either eye is covered is binocular, from misaligned eyes due to a nerve, muscle, or junction problem, whereas double vision that persists with one eye covered is monocular, from the eye itself. Failure to adduct one eye with nystagmus of the other is INO from an MLF lesion, bilateral in young people with MS and unilateral in older people with stroke. Impaired upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and light-near dissociation make up Parinaud syndrome of the dorsal midbrain, from a pineal tumor or midbrain stroke. Vertical gaze palsy with early falls suggests progressive supranuclear palsy, and eyes deviated toward one side suggest a hemispheric lesion on that side, as in MCA stroke.

Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-torsional, beats away from the affected ear in every gaze, and is suppressed by fixation, as in vestibular neuritis or BPPV. Direction-changing nystagmus, which changes with gaze and is not suppressed by fixation, is central, and so is purely torsional nystagmus; downbeat nystagmus points to the cervicomedullary junction or midline cerebellum and upbeat nystagmus to the pons and midbrain.

Visual loss in one eye localizes to the retina or optic nerve, bitemporal hemianopia to the optic chiasm, as with a pituitary tumor, and homonymous hemianopia to the opposite optic tract, radiation, or occipital cortex. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing points to the opposite occipital cortex in the PCA territory, and superior quadrantanopia to the opposite temporal lobe through the Meyer loop.

Cortical and diencephalic signs

Nonfluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension localizes to the Broca area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, fluent speech with paraphasias and poor comprehension to the Wernicke area in the dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus, and isolated poor repetition to the arcuate fasciculus in conduction aphasia. Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation make up Gerstmann syndrome of the dominant angular gyrus, and hemispatial neglect with anosognosia localizes to the nondominant parietal lobe. Alexia without agraphia points to the dominant PCA territory and prosopagnosia to the nondominant PCA territory.

Disinhibition, impulsivity, and tactlessness point to the orbitofrontal cortex; apathy, abulia, and reduced speech to the anterior cingulate cortex, with akinetic mutism if bilateral; and poor planning, fluency, and working memory to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Sensory loss of all types on one side points to the opposite thalamus, as in a pure sensory lacunar stroke, and disordered temperature, appetite, thirst, or sleep points to the hypothalamus. Cortical signs such as aphasia and neglect place a hemiparesis in the cortex rather than the internal capsule or brainstem.

Headache

A headache reaching peak intensity almost at once, the worst ever, is a thunderclap headache, from SAH, RCVS, ICH, dissection, or venous sinus thrombosis, and calls for non-contrast CT, with a lumbar puncture if it is normal after 6 hours. One-sided, pulsating headache lasting 4–72 hours, with nausea and light and sound sensitivity and worse with activity, is migraine. One-sided orbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes, with tearing or nasal congestion on that side, restlessness, and attacks at night, is cluster headache, three times more common in men and relieved by 100% oxygen within 10 minutes in at least two thirds. Bilateral, band-like, pressing pain for 30 minutes to 7 days without nausea is tension-type headache, the most common primary headache.

Papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, and CN VI palsy in a young woman with obesity suggest IIH once a mass is excluded, and call for imaging and then a lumbar puncture with opening pressure. A new headache over 50, with jaw claudication, vision loss, or raised ESR and CRP, suggests GCA, which needs prompt high-dose glucocorticoids to prevent blindness. Headache on 15 or more days a month with frequent analgesic use is medication overuse headache.

Gait and balance

A stiff leg swung in an arc is a hemiparetic gait from a UMN lesion, and crouched, crossing legs are a scissor gait from bilateral UMN lesions, as in cerebral palsy. High stepping that lands on the toes is a steppage gait from foot drop due to a peroneal nerve, L5, or neuropathic lesion. A broad-based, unsteady gait is cerebellar, from the vermis, whereas a stomping gait that worsens in the dark with a positive Romberg test is sensory ataxia from the dorsal columns or large fibers. Shuffling with reduced arm swing and freezing is the festinating gait of Parkinson disease, a waddling gait reflects proximal muscle weakness, and gait disturbance with urinary incontinence and cognitive decline suggests NPH.

On the Romberg test, unsteadiness that worsens with the eyes closed indicates lost proprioception, whereas unsteadiness with the eyes open as well is cerebellar. Limb ataxia localizes to the cerebellar hemisphere on the same side.

Relationships to other conditions

. That page starts from each arterial territory and lists its deficits, whereas this one starts from the deficit and works back to the territory. A sudden deficit that fits one arterial territory favors stroke over the other causes considered here.

. Both separate UMN from LMN weakness and read the gait. That page describes each sign in detail, whereas this one combines them with cranial nerve, eye, and cortical findings to place the lesion.

. Localization gives the site of a lesion, and the next step is to ask what else could cause the same findings; that page covers the mimics of the main conditions.

Ruling Out Mimics

Approach

A presentation suggests a diagnosis, but findings it cannot explain point to a mimic, so the treatable and dangerous mimics are excluded first with the test that best separates them.

  1. Leading diagnosisFrom the presentation
  2. Misfit findingsWhat it cannot explain
  3. Must not missTreatable or dangerous mimics
  4. Targeted testThe one that separates them

Stroke

  1. GlucoseRule out hypoglycemia

Review article

Ruling out mimics in stroke, seizure, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, and Parkinson disease

A presentation suggests a diagnosis, but findings that the diagnosis cannot explain point to a mimic. Treatable and dangerous mimics are excluded first, with the test that best separates them. For stroke, glucose and non-contrast CT come first; for seizure, glucose, bloods, CT, then EEG and MRI; for multiple sclerosis, MRI, CSF, and antibodies; for dementia, delirium, depression, B12, and thyroid function; and for parkinsonism, a medication review, a levodopa trial, and DAT SPECT. Here, we review the signs that point away from each diagnosis and the tests that settle the question.

Key points

  • Findings a diagnosis cannot explain point to a mimic, and treatable or dangerous mimics are excluded first.
  • A normal early CT does not exclude ischemic stroke, because DWI shows an infarct within minutes.
  • A normal EEG during a typical event points to PNES, whereas a normal routine EEG between events does not exclude epilepsy.
  • Severe or bilateral optic neuritis, LETM, or intractable hiccups and vomiting point away from MS toward NMOSD.
  • DAT SPECT is reduced in Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism alike, so it separates them from drug-induced parkinsonism and essential tremor, not from each other.

Approach

A presentation suggests a diagnosis, but findings it cannot explain point to a mimic, so the treatable and dangerous mimics are excluded first with the test that best separates them. The leading diagnosis comes from the presentation, misfit findings are sought, must-not-miss mimics are excluded, and a targeted test separates the remaining possibilities.

Stroke

Evaluation starts with glucose to rule out hypoglycemia and non-contrast CT to rule out hemorrhage, then CT angiogram for LVO, and CT perfusion or MRI at 4.5–24 hours or when onset is unknown. Low glucose with deficits that resolve when it is corrected indicates hypoglycemia. A witnessed seizure, tongue biting, and a post-ictal state suggest a seizure with Todd paralysis, confirmed by EEG. Positive symptoms spreading over minutes with past similar attacks suggest migraine with aura, with MRI if unclear, and inconsistent signs with a positive Hoover sign suggest a functional neurologic disorder, with MRI.

Gradual onset or fever suggests a brain tumor or abscess, shown by CT or MRI with contrast; isolated facial weakness that includes the forehead suggests Bell palsy on clinical examination; isolated vertigo with a reassuring HINTS examination suggests peripheral vertigo, with MRI if unclear; and sepsis, hyponatremia, or new drugs can unmask an old deficit, found with bloods and cultures. A normal early CT does not exclude ischemic stroke, because DWI shows an infarct within minutes, long before CT changes.

Seizure

Evaluation starts with glucose and vital signs, treating hypoglycemia first, then bloods for electrolytes and drug levels, non-contrast CT after a first seizure, and EEG and MRI to classify the seizure and find its cause. A trigger, lightheadedness, brief jerks, and rapid recovery suggest syncope, assessed with ECG and orthostatic BP. Closed eyes, side-to-side head movement, asynchronous limbs, and no post-ictal state suggest PNES, confirmed by video EEG. Palpitations, exertional collapse, or a family history of sudden death suggest a cardiac arrhythmia, assessed with ECG and telemetry, and negative symptoms such as weakness or numbness without a march suggest TIA, assessed with MRI and vascular imaging.

Symptoms spreading over minutes and followed by headache suggest migraine with aura; events only during sleep suggest a sleep disorder, assessed by a sleep study; fear, palpitations, and hyperventilation with awareness preserved suggest a panic attack; and tics or dystonia with awareness preserved suggest a movement disorder, with EEG if unclear. A normal EEG during a typical event points to PNES, whereas a normal routine EEG between events does not exclude epilepsy.

Multiple sclerosis

Evaluation uses MRI brain and spine with gadolinium and the McDonald criteria of space plus time or a substitute, with CSF if MRI falls short and bloods to exclude mimics. Severe or bilateral optic neuritis, LETM, or intractable hiccups and vomiting suggest NMOSD, tested by AQP4-IgG, and bilateral optic neuritis with disc edema or a conus lesion suggests MOGAD, tested by MOG-IgG. One episode after an infection with encephalopathy in a child suggests ADEM, on MRI. Dorsal column and corticospinal signs with anemia suggest B12 deficiency; rash, joint pain, and kidney disease suggest SLE, tested by ANA; and lung disease with CN palsies suggests neurosarcoidosis, tested by CXR and serum ACE.

Risk factors for syphilis, HIV, or Lyme disease call for serology, and older age, vascular risk factors, and no oligoclonal bands suggest small vessel disease, on MRI and CSF. Progressive worsening from onset suggests primary progressive MS or a mimic, since NMOSD rarely progresses, and calls for MRI, CSF, and antibodies.

Alzheimer disease

Evaluation first excludes delirium, with its sudden onset and fluctuating attention, screens for depression, checks B12 and TFTs, and uses MRI for the pattern of atrophy. Sudden onset, fluctuating attention, and an acute illness indicate delirium, which needs a search for its cause, and low mood, poor effort, and awareness of memory problems suggest depression. Fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain suggest hypothyroidism, tested by TFTs, and anemia with neuropathy suggests B12 deficiency.

Early gait disturbance and urinary incontinence suggest NPH, on MRI; visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations suggest dementia with Lewy bodies, supported by DAT SPECT; stepwise decline with vascular risk factors suggests vascular dementia, on MRI; younger age with early behavior or language change suggests frontotemporal dementia, on MRI; and rapid progression with myoclonus suggests prion disease, on MRI and CSF. Early memory loss with medial temporal atrophy favors Alzheimer disease, whereas preserved medial temporal lobes favor dementia with Lewy bodies.

Parkinson disease

Evaluation confirms bradykinesia with rest tremor or rigidity, reviews medications for dopamine-blocking drugs, uses a levodopa trial, in which a clear response supports PD, and adds DAT SPECT if still unclear. Vertical gaze palsy and early falls suggest progressive supranuclear palsy, with the hummingbird sign on MRI; early autonomic failure with cerebellar or pyramidal signs suggests multiple system atrophy, with the hot cross bun sign; and asymmetric apraxia, cortical sensory loss, and alien limb suggest corticobasal degeneration, with asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy. Early dementia and visual hallucinations suggest dementia with Lewy bodies.

Symmetric signs after starting a dopamine-blocking drug suggest drug-induced parkinsonism, found by medication review, with a normal DAT SPECT; bilateral postural or action tremor without bradykinesia suggests essential tremor, also with a normal DAT SPECT; and chorea with a family history suggests Huntington disease, confirmed by genetic testing. DAT SPECT is reduced in PD and in atypical parkinsonism alike, so it separates them from drug-induced parkinsonism and essential tremor, not from each other.

Relationships to other conditions

. Localization gives the site, and ruling out mimics gives the cause. Findings that cannot fit one site are themselves a clue to a mimic, such as several lesions or a diffuse process.

. Most mimics here are settled by a test, and that page explains which imaging sequence or EEG pattern answers each question.

Choosing Imaging and EEG

Choosing a test

The question sets the test: CT is fast and best for fresh blood, MRI shows tissue in detail and acute ischemia within minutes, angiography shows vessels, and EEG shows electrical activity rather than structure.

If there isObtainTo find

Thunderclap headacheNon-contrast CT; lumbar puncture if normal after 6 hoursSAH
Lobar ICH in an older personMRI with SWIMicrobleeds of amyloid angiopathy
A first seizureNon-contrast CT, then MRI and EEGA structural cause; the seizure type

Acute vertigo with a central HINTS resultMRI and MRAPosterior circulation stroke

CT

Non-contrast CT

  • ReadsDensity in HU: fat about −50, CSF +15, white matter +25, gray matter +40, and blood +30–45
  • Acute bloodBright, so hemorrhage is ruled in or out in minutes
  • Early ischemia, under 12 hoursOften normal; loss of gray-white differentiation, insular ribbon blurring, or lentiform nucleus effacement
  • Hyperdense MCA signThrombus in the artery; highly specific for LVO
  • ASPECTS10 points, minus 1 for each MCA region with early change; 6 or more is a small to moderate core

CT angiogram

  • ShowsVessels from the aortic arch to the vertex, with iodinated contrast
  • FindsLVO, dissection, aneurysm, AVM, and vasculitis
  • MultiphaseCollateral circulation; good collaterals predict a larger penumbra

CT perfusion

  • MapsCBV, CBF, MTT, and Tmax
  • CorerCBF under 30% of the other side: likely lost
  • PenumbraTmax over 6 seconds with rCBF 30% or more: still salvageable
  • UseMismatch selects thrombectomy at 6–24 hours, and thrombolysis in some late or wake-up strokes

  • DWI-FLAIR mismatchInfarct bright on DWI but not yet on FLAIR: under 4.5 hours, so thrombolysis can be considered when onset is unknown
  • T2 shine-throughOld edema or gliosis can be bright on DWI; true acute infarct is dark on ADC
  • GadoliniumAvoided in severe renal impairment, for NSF, and where possible in pregnancy

Review article

Choosing imaging and EEG in neurology, and the signs to look for

The clinical question sets the test. Non-contrast CT is fast and best for fresh blood, CT angiogram shows vessels, CT perfusion separates ischemic core from salvageable penumbra, and MRI shows tissue in detail, with DWI revealing ischemia within minutes. T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI with ADC, SWI, and gadolinium each make different tissue bright, and conditions carry characteristic signs, from Dawson fingers in MS to the hot cross bun sign in multiple system atrophy. EEG shows electrical activity rather than structure, and nuclear medicine shows dopamine terminals, glucose use, and amyloid. Here, we review which test to order and what to look for.

Key points

  • Non-contrast CT rules hemorrhage in or out in minutes but is often normal in the first hours of ischemia; DWI shows an infarct within minutes.
  • On CT perfusion, the core has rCBF under 30%, and the penumbra has Tmax over 6 seconds with rCBF 30% or more.
  • An acute infarct is bright on DWI and dark on ADC, and an infarct bright on DWI but not yet on FLAIR is under 4.5 hours old.
  • SWI shows blood products as dark, revealing microbleeds and hemorrhage.
  • Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave suggests absence seizures, and a normal EEG during a typical event points to PNES.

Choosing a test

The question sets the test: CT is fast and best for fresh blood, MRI shows tissue in detail and acute ischemia within minutes, angiography shows vessels, and EEG shows electrical activity rather than structure. Suspected stroke calls for non-contrast CT, then CT angiogram, to find hemorrhage and then LVO, and stroke at 4.5–24 hours or of unknown onset calls for CT perfusion or MRI to find salvageable penumbra. A thunderclap headache calls for non-contrast CT, with a lumbar puncture if it is normal after 6 hours, to find SAH, and a lobar ICH in an older person calls for MRI with SWI to find the microbleeds of amyloid angiopathy.

A first seizure calls for non-contrast CT, then MRI and EEG, to find a structural cause and the seizure type, and suspected demyelination calls for MRI brain and spine with gadolinium, with the orbits for NMOSD. Acute vertigo with a central HINTS result calls for MRI and MRA to find posterior circulation stroke, and asymmetric SNHL or one-sided tinnitus for MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium to find a vestibular schwannoma. Cognitive decline calls for MRI, with PET or SPECT if unclear, and parkinsonism of uncertain cause for DAT SPECT.

CT

Non-contrast CT reads density in HU: fat about −50, CSF +15, white matter +25, gray matter +40, and blood +30–45. Acute blood is bright, so hemorrhage is ruled in or out in minutes. Early ischemia under 12 hours often looks normal or shows loss of gray-white differentiation, insular ribbon blurring, or lentiform nucleus effacement, and a hyperdense MCA sign reflects thrombus in the artery and is highly specific for LVO. ASPECTS starts at 10 and loses 1 point for each MCA region with early change, and 6 or more indicates a small to moderate core.

CT angiogram shows vessels from the aortic arch to the vertex with iodinated contrast and finds LVO, dissection, aneurysm, AVM, and vasculitis, and multiphase imaging shows collateral circulation, with good collaterals predicting a larger penumbra. CT perfusion maps CBV, CBF, MTT, and Tmax. The core, with rCBF under 30% of the other side, is likely lost, whereas the penumbra, with Tmax over 6 seconds and rCBF 30% or more, is still salvageable, and the mismatch selects thrombectomy at 6–24 hours and thrombolysis in some late or wake-up strokes.

MRI sequences

T1 makes fat and gadolinium bright and shows anatomy, and T2 makes fluid, edema, and most lesions bright, showing MS plaques and edema. FLAIR makes lesions bright with fluid made dark, showing periventricular plaques, SAH in the sulci, and infarcts after 4.5–6 hours. DWI with ADC shows acute infarct as bright on DWI and dark on ADC within minutes. SWI or gradient echo shows blood products as dark, revealing microbleeds, hemorrhage, and thrombus. T1 with gadolinium shows enhancing lesions, such as active MS plaques, tumors, and abscesses, and MRA shows flowing blood, finding occlusion, dissection, and stenosis without iodinated contrast. On non-contrast CT, by contrast, fresh blood is bright, CSF dark, and bone white.

An infarct bright on DWI but not yet on FLAIR, a DWI-FLAIR mismatch, is under 4.5 hours old, so thrombolysis can be considered when onset is unknown. Old edema or gliosis can also be bright on DWI, T2 shine-through, but true acute infarct is dark on ADC. Gadolinium is avoided in severe renal impairment, because of NSF, and where possible in pregnancy.

Signs by condition

Acute ischemic stroke shows restricted diffusion on DWI, and core and penumbra on CT perfusion; lacunar stroke a small deep infarct on MRI; intracerebral hemorrhage hyperdense blood on non-contrast CT, deep in hypertension; cerebral amyloid angiopathy lobar microbleeds on MRI with SWI; cerebral venous sinus thrombosis the empty delta sign on CT or MR venography; and subarachnoid hemorrhage blood in the subarachnoid space on non-contrast CT, or xanthochromia on lumbar puncture.

Multiple sclerosis shows periventricular Dawson fingers, plaques in 2 of 5 sites, and the central vein sign on MRI with gadolinium; NMOSD shows LETM over 3 or more segments, a dorsal medulla lesion, and a long posterior optic nerve lesion; and MOGAD shows a long anterior optic nerve lesion with disc edema, a conus lesion, and the H-sign.

Alzheimer disease shows medial temporal atrophy on MRI and amyloid plaques on amyloid PET; frontotemporal dementia frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, with hypometabolism there on FDG-PET; and dementia with Lewy bodies preserved medial temporal lobes, reduced DAT uptake, and the cingulate island sign. Parkinson disease shows reduced striatal uptake on DAT SPECT; multiple system atrophy the hot cross bun sign with atrophy of the putamen, MCP, pons, and cerebellum; progressive supranuclear palsy midbrain atrophy, the hummingbird sign; corticobasal degeneration asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy and hypometabolism; and Huntington disease caudate atrophy, even before symptoms. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy shows hippocampal volume loss with bright T2 and FLAIR signal, and vestibular schwannoma, brain tumor, and abscess show an enhancing mass on MRI with gadolinium.

EEG

EEG rhythms are beta at 13–30 Hz, alpha at 8–12 Hz, theta at 4–7 Hz, and delta under 4 Hz, and a normal adult at rest has a posterior dominant alpha rhythm at 8–12 Hz. EEG classifies and localizes seizures and assesses encephalopathy, coma, and brain death. A routine 30-minute EEG often misses interictal discharges, so repeated or prolonged recordings find more, and video EEG captures events to separate seizures from PNES.

Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave provoked by hyperventilation suggests absence seizures, focal spikes or sharp waves a focal epileptic source, a normal EEG during a typical event PNES, triphasic waves a metabolic encephalopathy such as hepatic or uremic, prominent posterior slow waves dementia with Lewy bodies, and seizure activity without convulsions nonconvulsive status epilepticus.

Nuclear medicine

DAT SPECT shows presynaptic dopamine terminals, reduced in PD and atypical parkinsonism and normal in drug-induced parkinsonism and essential tremor. FDG-PET shows glucose use, low at a seizure focus between seizures, with patterns of dementia, and ictal SPECT shows increased perfusion at a seizure focus when injected within 90 seconds of onset. Amyloid PET shows amyloid plaques in life, in Alzheimer disease.

Relationships to other conditions

. That page lists the mimics of each condition and the test that separates them, and this one explains how to read those tests.

. Imaging decides stroke treatment: non-contrast CT excludes hemorrhage before thrombolysis, CT angiogram finds LVO for thrombectomy, and perfusion or DWI-FLAIR mismatch extends treatment to late or unknown onset.
